### Social media

If you endorse or incorporate social media in content, ensure that you follow the policies in the IBM Social Computing Guidelines. The guidelines are reviewed and updated periodically to reflect emerging technologies and online social tools.

For more information about guidelines that address issues such as privacy, proper identiﬁcation, inappropriate content, copyright protection, and branding, see the [Corporate governance documents](https:/www.ibm.com/investor/governance/corporate-governance-documents) . From this site, you can access other key resources such as the IBM Business Conduct Guidelines.

If you want to include links to social media in IBM content, consult your designated legal counsel for approval. Examples of social media include Facebook, Twitter, or blogs. Generally, you should not include links to uncontrolled information in client-facing IBM content because of the unpredictable nature of the medium.

Consider carefully whether to link to an external blog, because you cannot predict or control the future content of the blog, and the resulting message might be contrary to IBM objectives. If you want to link to a blog, consider the website, the author, and possible future content, and determine whether they support IBM goals.

For more information about linking, see [Citations and references](.) . For more information about embedding or linking to videos that are hosted on social media sites, such as YouTube, see [Videos](.) .

#### Related resources


- For information about using social media buttons and icons, see [IBM Web Standards: Social brand guidelines .](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-web-standards-external/quality-guidelines/social-media)
- To learn more about social computing platforms and tools, see [Social Computing  Guidelines .](https:/w3.ibm.com/hr/web/empdata/social_computing_guidelines)

### Third-party tools

IBMers often use third-party tools to help them with writing and editing tasks.

Some tools introduce data privacy, copyright infringement, and information integrity risks to IBM. Learn about tools that are IBM-approved and others to avoid when you’re looking for help with certain tasks.

- [Generative AI](.)
- [Copy editing](.)
- [Translation](.)

For more information about using third-party tools to conduct IBM business, see [Free and open source tools .](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/open-source-tools)

#### Generative AI

IBMers may not use third party generative AI tools for IBM business or with IBM or client data. Do not submit or otherwise disclose IBM proprietary, conﬁdential, client, or personal information, or any intellectual property of IBM to these tools. Information shared with generative AI tools may be used to further train the tools and may be stored externally. This could result in the loss of ownership of this data, loss of IBM or client intellectual property, or even constitute a data breach.


Rules about who at IBM can use IBM Watson Code Assistant (WCA@IBM) and for what purposes are in flux. For the latest information, see [Gen AI Policy.](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/orai-microsite/legal-policy)

##### ChatGPT

Do not use the output from ChatGPT or other non-IBM large language model and generative AI tools in any IBM materials. The output from a third-party generative AI tool might infringe intellectual property rights, or it might not be unique, accurate, fair, bug-free, or even suited for the purpose for which it is intended.


For more information, see [Third Party Generative AI Tools .](https:/pages.github.ibm.com/ciso-psg/main/supplemental/GenAI.html)

#### Copy editing


The recommended tool for copy editing IBM content is Acrolinx. Acrolinx is an AI system that helps content creators write effective, high-quality content. For more information, see [Acrolinx .](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/drupal-in-support/additional-programs/acrolinx)

##### Vale


If your organization does not have licenses for Acrolinx, you can evaluate whether Vale is a viable solution for you. Vale ( [https://vale.sh/](https:/vale.sh) ) is a customizable, open source linter for Markdown, HTML, CSV, AsciiDoc, DITA, and text ﬁles. (A linter is a tool that checks source code for bugs or deviations from an established style sheet or programming language coding conventions.) The IBM Cloud team created custom rules that are based on IBM Style that you can reuse. However, there is no dedicated support team; the resources are community owned and maintained. For more information, see the [IBM Vale wiki .](https:/github.ibm.com/ibmcloud/ibm-vale/wiki)

##### Grammarly

Do not use Grammarly to copy edit written content. Grammarly does not ensure the privacy of data that you submit to it in the public cloud. Using Grammarly risks exposing IBM conﬁdential information.

#### Translation


To translate proprietary IBM content, use the IBM approved translation tool named [Translate@IBM . The tool generates a quick translation for you right away, and then sends a subsequent email with a more precise translation of your text. You can alternatively pay for Advanced- or Premium-level translations. For more information, see the](https:/translate.g11n.ibm.com)

Do not use third-party translation tools, such as Google Translate, to translate proprietary IBM content.

### Tone

Tone is the perceived attitude of a writer toward the subject or reader. Use a tone that is appropriate for your subject, goals, and audience.

#### Contents

- [Importance of tone](.)
- [Guidance for all tones](.)
- [Guidance for conveying  an appropriate tone](.)

#### Importance of tone

The primary goal of most IBM content is to convey information in a direct, clear, and thoughtful way. The words that you choose and the way that you arrange those words (word choice and syntax) should always serve that goal.

When you create IBM content, consider the ways that tone might support or detract from this goal. For example, in marketing content, you might use a friendly and relatively informal tone to attract attendees to an IBM event that promotes a product.


Clouds are gathering, but there’s no storm in sight. Come to IBM BluCirrus 2014, where organizations from around the world will showcase their implementations of public, private, and hybrid clouds. If you’re quick, you can get one of the few remaining tickets for our opening day demo, where you’ll see how IBM Cloud uses Cloud Foundry technology to help developers manage cloud applications.

In online installation documentation for the same product, the informal tone that is appropriate in the marketing context might distract users and detract from the core goal of helping users to accomplish their tasks. Instead, be as direct and concise as possible.


Before you use IBM Cloud to build and deploy cloud applications, choose the predeﬁned services and runtime frameworks for your implementation.

Both examples are effective, but their tones are not interchangeable.

Write content that is as universal and timeless as possible. For all content that you create, use what you know about your audience to inform your decisions about tone. Consider the wide scope of IBM as an organization and the resulting variation in IBM audiences.

Because your prospective readers come from diverse backgrounds, countries, and cultures, it is important to balance the needs of one group against the whole. See speciﬁc guidance on [Global audiences](.) .


*Ineffective. Targets too narrow an audience:* The new IBM BladeCenter blade server runs at up to 1866 MHz – that’s tons of data transferred in the time it takes you to view an Instagram! :&gt;)


*Informal but effective* : With the new IBM BladeCenter blade server, the University of San Dimas transferred twice as much data at half the speed. “We used 40% less power to achieve better results”, said Fernando Guerrera, systems analyst at San Dimas. “I can’t tell you how good that looks on our budget reports.”

#### Guidance for all tones

IBM Style supports various writing styles and tones. Regardless of the tone that you choose for your content, use IBM Style topics and IBM resources to ﬁnd standards and guidelines for clear, direct, and consistent communication.

To write content that is appropriate for [all audiences](.) , apply the following guidelines:

- Write clearly and directly. Wherever possible, use the second person ( *you* ). Where appropriate, use ﬁrst person ( *we* , *our* to refer to IBM). See speciﬁc guidance on ﬁrst and second person in [Verbs](.) .


When the folder is opened, the plugin.jar ﬁle can be identiﬁed and deleted. Open the folder, and then delete the plugin.jar ﬁle.


In the showroom, there will be ﬁve demos per day for each breakout session cluster. Pick demonstrations from 10 different clusters and 50 different demonstrations in all every day. Register for your breakout sessions today!


Come to the showroom to register for the demos that you want to attend. Demos are organized into clusters based on subject area. You can attend up to ﬁve demos a day.


In this lesson, the user creates a service that contains the user interface that the hiring manager uses. In this lesson, you create a service that contains the user interface that the hiring manager uses.


IBM has seen IoT devices become more powerful and ubiquitous We’ve seen IoT devices become more powerful and ubiquitous

- Be succinct, and keep sentences as short and simple as possible. Omit wordy or redundant phrases.


at the end of the day at this point in time

each and every one of you going forward

in any shape, manner, or form to all intents and purposes

- Organize information cohesively.


If you get an error when you compile a job, ensure that the output columns for each operator match the input columns for the next operator. Make sure that you have added all of the operators to transform the data before the data is written to a target database. Compile and run jobs in a development environment before you try to run the jobs in a production environment. You can use operators such as the Transformation or Sort operators to transform data.


Add all of the operators to transform the data before any operator that writes the data to a target database. You can use operators such as the Transformation or Sort operators to transform data.

*In a separate section of the content or in another deliverable altogether:*

Compile and run jobs in a development environment before you try to run the jobs in a production environment. If you get an error when you compile a job, ensure that the output columns for each operator match the input columns for the next operator.

- Use the simplest term that is appropriate for your audience. For example, use *large* instead of *voluminous* , and use *small*

instead of *diminutive* .

- Explain concepts or terms that might be new for your audience, and spell out acronyms. For example, in content about cloud services, spell out *PaaS* as *platform as a service* , and briefly deﬁne the term. See speciﬁc guidance for acronyms in [Abbreviations](.) .
- Use appropriate and consistent terminology. See speciﬁc guidance in [Terminology](.) .


Choose your favorite repos to use as the metadata repository, and then import the data Choose the repository to use as the metadata repository, and then import the data.


You can use the System Connector to connect one system to another. The systems connector is an optional feature. You can have more than one connector working in parallel.


You can use the system connector to connect one system to another. The system connector is an optional feature. You can have more than one system connector working in parallel.

In the ﬁrst incorrect example, the terms *repos* and *repository* are used to mean the same thing. In the second incorrect example, the terms *System Connector* , *systems connector* , and *connector* are used to mean the same thing.

- Use simple present tense, as much as possible.

After you have identiﬁed the market theme for your analysis, you will be able to conﬁgure the options and run the analysis tool.


After you identify the market theme for your analysis, conﬁgure the options, and run the analysis tool.

- Use active voice, where appropriate.


The default application layout can be replaced. You can replace the default application layout.

#### Guidance for conveying an appropriate tone

The audience for IBM information is often much broader than you might ﬁrst realize. If you write content that is targeted to a speciﬁc reader, anchored in a speciﬁc place and time, your content might become less effective over time or even offend readers in the present. When you write, consider all your potential readers, and try to transcend your current surroundings and personal experiences to offer content that appeals to the widest possible audience.

To communicate clearly and effectively, write content that focuses on the information that you want to convey rather than on the author, narrator, or style. Writing that calls attention to the author, narrator, or the style of language can obscure the core information, distract readers, and convey an inappropriate tone.

Apply the following guidelines to help avoid an inappropriate tone in your writing:

- Although a friendly or conversational style might be appropriate in some contexts, do not write content that replicates the way that people sometimes speak. On the page or screen, this type of writing can seem rambling or verbose.

Okay, so suppose that you have a data store that is growing at an incredible rate, and things just keep coming in faster and faster. I mean, what do you do with all that data? You might be worried about security, or backup and recovery, and maybe you

want to deduplicate the data or perform some analytics on it.


Use IBM data storage solutions to manage data growth and get business value from your data. IBM Smarter Storage addresses these business needs:

- Analytics
- Backup and recovery
- Data deduplication
- Avoid jokes or other content that is intended to be humorous. Humor is subjective, culturally speciﬁc, and often anchored to a speciﬁc place and time.

If your data streams are rising faster than Seattle’s minimum wage, an IBM big data solution will make your IT managers want to do the happy dance.

- Avoid content that requires knowledge that is speciﬁc to a culture, language, or age group. Instead, use expressive but clear wording. Where appropriate, use ﬁctional scenarios, real-world examples, quotations, and illustrations. To write content that is accessible across cultures and demographic groups, apply the following guidelines:

Avoid ﬁgurative language

If you don’t want to be left high and dry, account for peak memory usage.

WebSphere Translation Server is a Rosetta Stone that organizations can use to provide content for customers around the globe.


If you allow data to enter your data mart without implementing data quality rules, you might be on a slippery slope that

leads to a point of no return.


Avoid idioms bit the dust

elephant in the room hit the ground running it’s not rocket science low-hanging fruit


Avoid sports metaphors in the ballpark

full-court press

in your wheelhouse a slam dunk


Avoid ﬁgurative use of military terms blow away the competition

kill the critics collateral damage drop a bombshell surgical strike

weaponize your marketing approach convene a digital war room


Avoid pop culture references Wildcard characters

Use ? for any single character and * for a string of one or more characters. For example, use A? Rock to ﬁnd search results about Ad Rock, A* Rock to ﬁnd search results about Aesop Rock, and A* Rock? to ﬁnd search results about A$AP Rocky.


If your marketing conversion rates look as strong as the 2003 Detroit Tigers win-loss record, consider the predictive analytics capabilities of IBM Tealeaf software.


Avoid unnecessary or inappropriate jargon

Ensure that your database is ACID compliant before you CRUD any data in a production environment. To troubleshoot the memory issues, take a dump, and then send it to IBM Support.


To troubleshoot the memory issues, generate a memory dump, and then send it to IBM Support.


Avoid religious references Let there be data.

And we saw the data, and it was good. Like the good Samaritan,

Cloud computing casts out the inefﬁciencies.

- Use casual expressions in error messages with care. For more information, see [Messages](.) .
- Do not use words or syntax that conveys a stilted, academic, or overly formal tone. Follow this advice to avoid constructions that are unnecessarily complex or formal:
    - Do not change the word order in a sentence to avoid ending the sentence with a preposition.


Specify the name of the database to which the source ﬁle should be written. Specify the name of the database to write the source ﬁle to.

- Avoid complex sentences that overuse punctuation such as commas and semicolons.

Use Data Protection for IBM Domino on Windows to back up and restore Domino databases and transaction logs; when archival logging is used on the Domino server, the server archives transaction log ﬁles, retrieves the ﬁles as required for a database recovery, and then stores database backups and archived transaction log ﬁles on the Tivoli Storage Manager server.


Use Data Protection for IBM Domino on Windows to back up and restore Domino databases and transaction logs. When archival logging is used on the Domino server, the server archives transaction log ﬁles and retrieves the ﬁles as required for a database recovery. Database backups and archived transaction log ﬁles are stored on the Tivoli Storage Manager server.

- In technical information, avoid terms of politeness, such as *please* and *thank you* . These terms are inappropriate or offensive in some cultural contexts.

### Videos

Follow these guidelines when you create your own videos, or link to or embed videos that were created by others.

#### Contents

- [Creating  videos](.)
    - Captions and accessibility considerations
- [Linking  to videos](.)

#### Creating videos

Although you might think of videos as a more informal way to provide information, almost all standard IBM Style guidelines apply. Use this topic as an extra set of style guidelines when you create videos.

The following deﬁnitions provide context for the guidance in this topic:

- The video consists of what the user sees (which can include graphics, animation, and text) and sometimes audio.
- An external-use transcript accompanies the video. The transcript is not the same as the script, which is used for internal planning purposes. The transcript contains text versions of the audio and text that describes the actions that the user sees. For [accessibility reasons, only minor discrepancies between the audio and transcript are allowed, as speciﬁed in the following table.](https:/www.ibm.com/able/toolkit/design/content/#video-captions)
- Captions are a text version of the audio content, displayed in synchronization with the video. The most common form of captions are closed captions, which the viewer can choose to turn off or on, and which are typically displayed near the bottom of the video screen. The captions are similar to the transcript in that they represent a transcribed version of the audio. Therefore, the guidance for the transcript also applies to the closed captions.

The following table contains three categories of information:

- Exceptions to standard IBM Style guidance
- Extra advice for videos
- Reminders about standard IBM Style guidance that might be overlooked for videos

| **Topic name**            | **Guidance**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Abbreviations             | If an abbreviation is not commonly known, or if you are unsure whether it is commonly known, say the entire term at its ﬁrst occurrence, followed by the abbreviation. For example, in the audio, say “Business Process Modeling Notation, known as BPMN, is a standardized graphical notation ...” In the transcript and the captions, follow the standard IBM Style guideline of putting the abbreviation in parentheses after the spelled-out form: “Business Process Modeling Notation (BPMN) is a standardized graphical notation ...” |
| Capitalization            | Use headline-style capitalization for titles of videos. Use sentence-style capitalization for titles of screens within videos.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Citations and references  | In the audio, do not provide the web address unless it is short. For a video, follow the guidelines for a publication without a preface or bibliography, with one exception: provide the document number in only the transcript, not in the audio or captions. Also, two or three short citations at the end of a video are acceptable. If you need more, mention in the audio that more citations are available in the transcript.                                                                                                         |
| Code and command examples | If space is limited, avoid overly long code examples. In a video, it is harder to maintain an understanding of a long example that is broken up across several screens than it is to maintain an understanding of the same long example online or in print. Limit an example to a screen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Command syntax            | If space is limited or there is less time to absorb information, show only basic syntax, and use text, not syntax diagrams. A complicated syntax diagram is not suitable for a video, where space is limited and syntax must be quickly understood.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Copyright notices         | For information about copyright notices, see legal guidance for videos.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Currency                  | In the audio, state the name of the currency after the numeric amount. For example, say “1,000 Canadian dollars”. In the captions and transcript, follow the normal IBM Style guideline for referring to currency. For example, write “CAD 1,000”.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Date                      | In the audio and transcript, refer to the day in whatever way sounds natural, such as “the ﬁrst of October 2013” or “October ﬁrst, 2013”, but use a word rather than a number for the month.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Files and directories     | Remember to pronounce the period (.) in a ﬁle name or ﬁle extension, as “dot”. For example, pronounce  *.doc*  as “dot doc”, not just “doc”.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Global audiences          | Avoid slang, jargon, humor, sarcasm, colloquialisms, idioms, emoticons (also called  *smileys*  ), and metaphors. Instead, rewrite the sentence to use clearer, more direct language.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|                           | You can use questions such as “When should you install a client?” However, do not overuse questions in headings, and make sure that headings that use questions are meaningful.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Keyboard keys             | In the audio, use the spelled-out names of keys, not the abbreviations that are printed on the keys (for example, say “function” not “fn”), except for the following abbreviations: Alt, Caps Lock, and Num Lock.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Lists                     | Use full-sentence introductions, whether in the audio, transcript, or captions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Numbers                   | If there is no space between the unit and number, do not repeat the unit of measurement in the audio.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Phone numbers             | If you expect content to be used only in the same country from which a telephone number originates, use the national form of the number. Group the numerals according to the format that is normally used in the area or country.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Procedures                | If space is limited, ensure that an entire supertask procedure can be viewed at one time so that it is easier for users to understand the overall task. In a video, limit a supertask procedure to approximately a screen. Subtasks for that procedure can use additional screens.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

| **Topic name**               | **Guidance**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Product and service names    | Use only approved names and abbreviations. For example, use WebSphere Application Server, not WAS. Also, do not use code names. In addition, follow the trademark guidelines. For information about trademark requirements for videos, see legal guidance for videos.                                                                                                                           |
| Pronouns                     | If it adds value to the content of the videos or if the presenters are visible, the presenters can introduce themselves but should not use the ﬁrst person elsewhere in the video.                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Punctuation and symbols      | In the audio, if you refer to a special character that is not common or that might be confused with another special character, show the special character in the captions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Slashes                      | Even if space is limited, do not use the construction  *and/or*  , which can be ambiguous and causes problems for translation. Instead, consider whether both conjunctions are needed; if not, use  *and*  or  *or*  . If both conjunctions are needed, use the construction  *option A*  ,  *option B*  , or  *both*  .                                                                        |
| Tables                       | Avoid using a long or complex table. Limit a table to one screen. Also, the table must be legible without requiring the viewer to adjust the screen resolution. In addition, the table must be simple enough that the narrator can easily describe it and the viewer can understand it without having to pause the video.                                                                       |
| Time                         | Include the colons in the transcript and captions, regardless of how you pronounce the time in the audio.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Trademarks                   | For information about trademark requirements, see legal guidance for videos.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Verbs                        | In general, do not use ﬁrst person in videos. Generally, the content should focus on the material and viewer, not on the presenters of the material. However, if it adds value to the content of the videos or the presenters are visible, the presenters can introduce themselves. The presenters should not use the ﬁrst person elsewhere in the video, though.                               |
| Web, IP, and email addresses | In the transcripts, provide both a descriptive label and the web address for a site. In the audio, provide only the descriptive label unless the web address is short; in that case, you can also provide the web address. Also, two or three short citations at the end of a video are acceptable. If you need more citations, mention in the audio that more citations are in the transcript. |

##### Videos and accessibility considerations


Videos need to include captions for those who cannot hear well. For those who cannot see well, if a video contains information that is not fully described in the audio track or in the text that surrounds the video, then you must provide an alternative. The alternative can either be a text ﬁle that describes any content in the video (including onscreen text and titles) or a descriptive audio track. For more information, see [IBM Web Content Accessibility Guidelines .](https:/www.ibm.com/able/toolkit/design/content/#visual-content-in-videos)

#### Linking to videos

You need permission from IBM to post videos on social media sites such as YouTube. This is the case whether you link to such a video or embed it on your page. See the [Video topic on IBM Content](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/en/technical-content?topic=practices-video) for more information.

If you add a link to a video, include the term *video* , and the name of the hosting site so that your readers know they will be taken to a video on an external website.

- Inline link

For more information, watch the [XYZ Technology Overview video  on YouTube.](.)

### Writing content for large language model consumability

Large language models (LLMs) are being used increasingly in chatbots and other support and help system applications to help answer technical questions.

A popular pattern that is used to create AI apps is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). With RAG, a question that is submitted by a user is ﬁrst used to search a trusted knowledge base for relevant information. Then, the top search results are submitted with the original question as contextual information to a large language model. The added contextual information helps the large language model answer the user's question accurately.

The content that you write and publish about IBM products and services is an example of the type of trusted knowledge that is ideal for use in RAG-based applications. As you author IBM content, follow these guidelines to write in a manner that is consumable by AI models without reducing consumability for humans.

If you follow IBM Style, you already write content that large language models can use. Large language models perform best when the following general rules are applied:

*Write content that is grammatically correct, clear, concise, appropriate for global audiences, accessible, and easy to translate.*

#### Adapting content for large language model consumption

Follow these extra guidelines to adapt content to be more consumable by large language models:

- Avoid duplicating information in more than one topic in your documentation set.

Aim to cover each subject comprehensively in a dedicated topic and link to the information where necessary. When you include fragments of information in multiple places, search might ﬁnd and feed the incomplete information to the LLM, which can result in incomplete and misleading answers.

- In complex conceptual topics, include explicit statements and comparisons that address common or likely questions about the concept. LLMs cannot always infer accurate and complete ideas from information that is expressed over many paragraphs.
- If you author content that is published in IBM Documentation, avoid tiny topics (approximately 5 or fewer sentences).

Tiny topics are not indexed and cannot be returned as search results. RAG implementations can only ﬁnd information that is returned in search results. For tiny topics with important information, add more content or combine the information with another topic.

- Check the consumability of accordions.

LLMs cannot always process text within a collapsed accordion. Test whether the LLM you're using can understand accordions. If not, try reorganizing the information into separate sections or child topics. If the order of the information is important, you can use child topics with navigation to next and previous topics. If you must use accordions, do not put complex tables, instructions, or formatting within content in accordions.

- Check the consumability of deﬁnition lists.

Some LLMs do not interpret deﬁnition lists as lists and cannot answer questions that require returning the list. Test whether the LLM you're using can understand deﬁnition lists. If not, try reorganizing the information into bulleted lists or subsections. If you must use deﬁnition lists, keep them short.

- Keep tables simple.

LLMs are better at reading tables that have column headers, values in the ﬁrst column, and a simple structure without spanned cells. If possible, do not include empty cells, symbols, or footnotes in tables.

If your LLM-based application cannot effectively process text formats such as accordions, deﬁnition lists, or tables that you want to keep for human consumability, your application might need to preprocess these elements to capture their meaning in text before the content can be used by the LLM.

### Abbreviations

Abbreviations include initialisms, acronyms, and shortened words. An *initialism* is an abbreviation that is pronounced as individual letters, for example, IBM. An *acronym* is an abbreviation that forms a pronounceable word, for example, NATO.

#### General guidelines

Use an abbreviation in the following situations:

- Its meaning is clear: the spelled-out form is well known or is stated at the ﬁrst instance in text.
- It makes the information easier to understand.
- It is recognized more easily than its spelled-out form, for example, HTML.
- It reduces text when space is limited, such as in a table or detailed diagram.

Do not use an abbreviation in the following situations:

- It is unnecessary: the spelled-out form is short, clear, and does not beneﬁt from abbreviation.
- It is invented: the abbreviation is created for speciﬁc content and does not have widespread use.
- Its meaning is unclear: the spelled-out form is not well known or is not stated at the ﬁrst instance in text.
- It makes the information more difﬁcult to understand.
- It occurs infrequently in the information, such as only two or three times in a large amount of content.
- It has several possible spelled-out forms, and the variations create confusion.
- It creates an inappropriate or undesirable letter combination or word.
- It is derived from Latin.
- It abbreviates an IBM product name. Legal and branding representatives must ofﬁcially approve abbreviations for product names, such as RUP or TADDM.
- It abbreviates a name or entity that is owned by another company, and the owning company does not use that abbreviation.
- It might be a registered trademark for a different product or entity. Follow these general guidelines for abbreviations:
- Do not abbreviate or otherwise abridge text if doing so sacriﬁces clarity. In the following example, writing both parameter options in full is clearer than saving a little space by referring to both options by using a single term with the preﬁx in parentheses.


Set the (UN)ABRIDGED option of the INFO parameter.

Set the ABRIDGED or UNABRIDGED option of the INFO parameter.

- Choose the indeﬁnite article *a* or *an* according to how an abbreviation is spoken. Use *a* before an abbreviation that begins with a consonant sound. Use *an* before an abbreviation with a vowel sound. For more information about which indeﬁnite article to use, see [Articles](.) .

a PDF document, an SAP project, an XML activity

- If an abbreviation can be plural, form the plural by adding a lowercase *s* . The abbreviation for a unit of measurement is both singular and plural.

user IDs, RFPs, 1 mm, 10 mm

- Do not use an abbreviation as a noun unless the sentence makes sense when you substitute the spelled-out form of the term.


The tutorials are available as PDFs. [portable document formats] The tutorials are available as PDF ﬁles.


Enhancements in this release include a redesigned GUI. The procurement process begins with an RFP.

- Do not use abbreviations as verbs.


You can FTP the ﬁles to the server.

You can use the FTP command to send the ﬁles to the server.

- Do not use an apostrophe and the letter *s* (’s) to show the possessive form of an abbreviation. Make the abbreviation an adjective, or use the abbreviation in a prepositional phrase.


HTML’s properties are editable. HTML properties are editable.

The properties of HTML are editable.

- Do not abbreviate a unit of measurement in general text if no numeric value is associated with it.


Record the size of the package in mm. Record the size of the package in millimeters.


Download times are reduced from 10 ms to less than a ms. Download times are reduced from 10 ms to less than a millisecond.

- Do not abbreviate a multiplier to a letter, such as “thousand” to K or “million” to M. Use letters only as preﬁxes to units of measurement, such as “km” for “kilometers” or “MB” for “megabytes”. For correct usage of multiplier preﬁxes, including k (for x1,000) and K (for x1,024), see [Units of measurement](.) .


The company has 10K employees.

The company has 10 thousand employees. The company has 10,000 employees.


The contract is worth USD 4M.

The contract is worth USD 4 million. The contract is worth USD 4,000,000.


Each turbine can generate 30 MW of power. The power line is 50 km long.

The client system has only 100 KB of memory.

**Exception:** Using an uppercase letter as an abbreviation for a multiplier is allowed when space is limited (as on some user interfaces or websites, and as in some mobile apps), and when readers can be expected to know or easily determine the meaning of the abbreviation. In such instances, do not insert a blank between the number and the multiplier.


100 K visitors/yr. 100K visitors/yr. Sales: $4M

[Start of page](.)

#### Spelled-out forms

Follow these guidelines for spelling out abbreviations:

- Do not spell out an abbreviation that is commonly known to the target audience. Commonly known terms vary by audience; each writing and editing team must determine which abbreviations are familiar to the audience.

*When known to the audience:* DOS, HTML, HTTP, PDF, TCP/IP

- If an abbreviation is not commonly known, or if you are unsure whether it is commonly known, spell out the term at its ﬁrst occurrence in text, followed by the abbreviation in parentheses. If information has a deﬁned, linear reading path, consider spelling out an abbreviation at its ﬁrst occurrence in a major section, such as at the beginning of each chapter in a book, or in an overview topic instead of in each subtopic. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .


massively parallel processing (MPP) minimum recovery time (MRT) customer service representative (CSR)

- Conﬁrm the capitalization for the spelled-out form of an abbreviation; many spelled-out abbreviations do not require initial uppercase letters.

IBM only To conﬁrm the capitalization, ﬁrst search for the term in the [IBM Terminology database . The database is not exhaustive, so you might also have to search the internet. If you ﬁnd instances of the spelled-out form with initial lowercase letters in reliable sources, use that capitalization because IBM Style prefers a lowercase style.](https:/w3.terminology.g11n.ibm.com/standards/terminology/termsearch)


graphical user interface (GUI) local area network (LAN)

service-oriented architecture (SOA)

- Most spelled-out forms of language and protocol names have initial uppercase letters.


Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Uniﬁed Modeling Language (UML)

Web Services Description Language (WSDL) Wireless Application Protocol (WAP)

- When you spell out an abbreviation, do not capitalize letters in the middle of a word to show the origin of an initialism.


eXtensible markup language (XML) Extensible Markup Language (XML)

- In most cases, when you spell out an abbreviation, do not include wording that repeats part of the spelled-out version of the abbreviation. For example, do not use *DASD device* , because the second *D* stands for *device* , or *JCL language* , because the *L* stands for *language* . However, there are rare exceptions. For example, it is standard to refer to a *CICS system* , although *CICS* stands for *Customer Information Control System* .

[Start of page](.)

#### Periods with abbreviations

Follow these guidelines for using periods with abbreviations:


- Omit periods in uppercase abbreviations.  EST, ID, US
- Omit periods in abbreviations for academic degrees.  BA, MA, PhD
- Include periods in abbreviations for social titles.

Dr., Ms., Jr.


- If an abbreviation that requires a period occurs at the end of a sentence, do not include another period.  In American system units, the dimensions are 4 in. x 6 in. x 12 in.

For guidance about using periods with abbreviated units of measurement, see [Units of measurement](.) .

#### Indexes

For abbreviations that are unambiguous and that are recognized more easily than their spelled-out forms, index only the abbreviations. Examples are *AIX, CORBA, HTML, SQL, PDF, XML, TCP/IP* , and *UNIX* .


**&lt;i1&gt;AIX**

For other abbreviations, create main entries for both the abbreviation and the spelled-out form. Place the secondary and tertiary entries under the abbreviation. Under the spelled-out form, place a *See* reference to the abbreviation.


**&lt;i1&gt;ECI**

**&lt;i2&gt;requests**

**&lt;i2&gt;security**

**&lt;i2&gt;transaction IDs**

**&lt;i2&gt;transaction IDs**

**&lt;i1&gt;External Call Interface**

**&lt;i2&gt;See ECI**

#### Latin abbreviations

Do not use Latin abbreviations; use their English equivalents instead. Latin abbreviations are sometimes misunderstood.

| **Latin**   | **English equivalent**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| e.g.        | Use  *for example*  .                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| etc.        | Use  *and so on*  when you list a clear sequence of elements, such as “1, 2, 3, and so on” or “Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and so on”. Otherwise, rewrite the sentence to replace  *etc.*  with something more descriptive, such as “and other output”. |
| i.e.        | Use  *that is*  .                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

#### Legal considerations

If you create an abbreviation, check with your Intellectual Property Law (IPL) department before you use it. Your IPL department must verify that abbreviations are not trademarks of other companies. Do not use abbreviations for terms if the abbreviations are trademarks of other companies.

Do not create an abbreviation that is the same as an IBM trademark but that has a different meaning. For example, do not use *AFS* as an abbreviation for *advanced ﬁle system* . *AFS* is a trademark of IBM.

For legal reasons, do not use abbreviations on front covers unless they are IBM trademarks. See also [Legal information](.) .

### Adverbs - only

The word *only* can be used as an adverb, an adjective, or a conjunction. When *only* is used as an adverb, the meaning of the sentence can change, depending on the location of the word *only* .

Place the word *only* immediately before the word or phrase that it modiﬁes.


Deleting a host group only removes it from the server and not from the business application. Deleting a host group removes it only from the server and not from the business application.


If a user only belongs to a Guest group that is not a primary group, that user cannot access the client. If a user belongs only to a Guest group that is not a primary group, that user cannot access the client.


You can only charge a ﬁle plan component to one user at a time. You can charge a ﬁle plan component to only one user at a time.

In the following table, each sentence has a different meaning, depending on where you place the word *only* .

| **Sentence**                                                           | **Meaning**                                                                                        |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| *Only*  an administrator can open the XML ﬁles in the latest browser.  | Administrators, but not other users, can open the XML ﬁles in the latest browser.                  |
| An administrator can  *only*  open the XML ﬁles in the latest browser. | The administrator can open, but cannot edit, close, or delete, the XML ﬁles in the latest browser. |
| An administrator can open  *only*  the XML ﬁles in the latest browser. | The administrator can open the XML ﬁles, but not other ﬁles, in the latest browser.                |
| An administrator can open the XML ﬁles in  *only*  the latest browser. | The administrator can open the XML ﬁles in the latest browser, but not in older browsers.          |

### Anthropomorphism

Do not assign human characteristics to inanimate objects, which are incapable of human behaviors and emotions. As much as possible, focus technical information on users and their actions, not on a product and its actions. See speciﬁc guidance for [Marketing](.) .


*Product focus:* The Delivery Information window *allows* you to specify the name of the sender.

*User focus:* In the Delivery Information window, specify the name of the sender.


*Product focus:* This menu *enables* you to create diagrams.

*User focus:* Use this menu to create diagrams.


*Product focus:* The conﬁguration *expects* the disk to have parity protection.

*User focus:* Before you conﬁgure the disk, ensure that it has parity protection.


*Product focus:* The Replicator page *lets* you synchronize your local database with replica databases.

*User focus:* On the Replicator page, you can synchronize your local database with replica databases. Double-click a ﬁle to download it to your local directory.


*Product focus:* The website *permits* you to save your credit card information.

*User focus:* You can save your credit card information on the website.

In cases where you must focus on a product, do not use verbs that humanize objects, such as *ask, decide, expect, say, see, think,* or *want* . However, inanimate objects such as hardware and software can perform actions, and some verbs are appropriate for both people and things. For example, a program can *search* for a text string, or an application can *read* data from a ﬁle.

Use appropriate verbs to avoid anthropomorphism.


The application *asks* you for a value. The application *prompts* you for a value.


The control partition *decides* to switch roles. The control partition *switches* roles.


If the system *sees* a new device, it changes the settings automatically.

If the system *detects* a new device, it changes the settings automatically.


The Merge Certiﬁcate window *tells* you about the new certiﬁcate information. The Merge Certiﬁcate window *displays* the new certiﬁcate information.


If a connector is disabled, the system *thinks* that the entire channel is disabled.

If a connector is disabled, the system *operates* as if the entire channel is disabled.


When the controller *wants* to create a resource, it constructs a list of storage locations. Before the controller *creates* a resource, it constructs a list of valid storage locations.

### Articles

Articles increase clarity and ease translation.

The articles “a” and “an” are indeﬁnite articles. Use them to refer to things in the abstract or not in the particular. “An offering” or “a product” means any offering or any product, as opposed to a speciﬁc offering or product.

“The” is a deﬁnite article. Use it to refer to a particular thing or things, meaning that “the offering” or “the product” is about that particular offering or product.

Do not omit an article that belongs in a sentence to save space because the omission creates a sentence that sounds stilted and unnatural.


Create project. Create a project.


File cannot be found. The ﬁle cannot be found.


Delete object from editor.

*Refers to any object* : Delete an object from the editor.

*Refers to a speciﬁc object that was discussed previously* : Delete the object from the editor.

In some cases, articles can be omitted. For example, you can omit the article from a sentence that expresses a general sentiment.


The servers talk to the clients. Servers talk to clients.


Only the administrators can create the projects. Only administrators can create projects.

For more information about when to keep or omit articles, refer to a grammar tutorial, such as [When to Use 'A,' 'An,' or 'The'](https:/gallaudet.edu/student-success/tutorial-center/english-center/grammar-and-vocabulary/when-to-use-a-an-or-the) .

**When to use** ***a*** **or** ***an***

Choose the indeﬁnite article *a* or *an* according to how an abbreviation, word, or number is spoken.

If an abbreviation is pronounced as a series of letters, choose the article according to the pronunciation of the ﬁrst letter. If an abbreviation is pronounced as a word, choose the article according to the pronunciation of the word. Assume that the period in a ﬁle name extension, such as .exe, is pronounced as *dot* , and use the indeﬁnite article *a* .

Use *a* before an abbreviation, word, or number that begins with a consonant sound.

| **Takes the article**  ***a***   | **Consonant sound**   |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------|
| **.mbtest**  ﬁle                 | D, as in  *dot*       |
| historical                       | H, as in  *hit*       |
| LAN                              | L, as in  *land*      |
| one                              | W, as in  *won*       |
| ROM                              | R, as in  *romp*      |
| SYSGEN                           | S, as in  *system*    |
| unit                             | Y, as in  *you*       |
| x4                               | B, as in  *by four*   |

Use *an* before an abbreviation, word, or number that begins with a vowel sound.

| **Takes the article**  ***an***   | **Vowel sound**      |
|-----------------------------------|----------------------|
| HTTP                              | A, as in  *ache*     |
| IoT                               | I, as in  *iced*     |
| LU                                | E, as in  *elf*      |
| MVS                               | E, as in  *empty*    |
| RPQ                               | A, as in  *are*      |
| SOA                               | E, as in  *estimate* |
| SQL                               | E, as in  *estimate* |

#### Capitalization styles

Items such as headings, captions, labels, or interface elements generally follow one of two capitalization styles, depending on the item: sentence-style capitalization or headline-style capitalization.

##### Sentence-style capitalization

This style is predominantly lowercase; capitalize only the initial letter of the ﬁrst word in the text and other words that require capitalization, such as proper nouns. Examples of proper nouns include the names of speciﬁc people, places, companies, languages, protocols, and products.


Business models

Creating Boolean expressions Planning network architectures Properties and settings for printing

Requirements for Linux and UNIX operating systems

##### Headline-style capitalization

This style uses initial uppercase letters for all signiﬁcant words in the text. In headline-style capitalization, capitalize the initial letter of the following words:

- The ﬁrst and last words of the text
- All nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, and subordinating conjunctions, such as *after* , *although* , *because* , *before* , *how* , *if* , *than* , *that* , *though* , *until* , *when* , *where* , *whether* , and *while*
- Any word in a hyphenated compound that is not an article, preposition, or coordinating conjunction
- The last word in a hyphenated compound, regardless of its part of speech

In headline-style capitalization, do not capitalize the initial letter of the following words:

- Articles, except as the ﬁrst word
- Coordinating conjunctions
- Prepositions, except as the ﬁrst or last word
- The word *to* in an inﬁnitive, except as the ﬁrst word


Punctuating Lists and Glossaries

Variables to Be Determined by the Program IBM 3684 Point-of-Sale Terminal

#### Colons

Use a lowercase letter after a colon when the colon occurs within a sentence and introduces an inline list or independent clause (unless the word that follows the colon is a proper noun or otherwise requires capitalization).


Three security measures are evaluated: a ﬁrewall, an encryption key, and a password. The deletion is ﬁnal: you cannot restore an element after you delete it.

You can use the editor with the following programming languages: Java, C, and C++.

- Vertical list

Blue


Green


Red

In a database: This distributed storage option is known as database persistent sessions. Input and output operations: Move mode and locate mode

- Quotation

The manager’s instructions were clear: “Submit the report by Monday.”

- Subheading or subtitle

#### General text

As much as possible, use a lowercase style in general text. Do not use all uppercase letters except when necessary for accuracy, such as when writing acronyms, initialisms, command names, trademarked names, or caution and danger labels for notices. Apply the following capitalization guidelines:

- Use lowercase for names and terms unless the name or term is a proper noun. Translators are wary of translating terms that have initial uppercase letters. In general, if a term should be translated, use lowercase.


To illustrate the concept, create a Class diagram. To illustrate the concept, create a class diagram.


Run the Transformation. Run the transformation.


The company is hiring Software Developers. The company is hiring software developers.

- Do not use uppercase letters for emphasis. To emphasize a word, use italic font. To call attention to important hints, tips, guidance, restrictions, or advice that might be overlooked, consider using a note that has a meaningful label.


Do NOT disconnect from the server. Do not disconnect from the server.


YOU CANNOT CREATE A SUBSCRIPTION UNTIL YOU FINISH THIS TASK.

Restriction: You cannot create a subscription until you ﬁnish this task.

- Do not create terms with internal uppercase letters.


CopyPool copy pool

- Do not start a sentence with a lowercase term; rewrite the sentence.


**onmouseover** events can add visual interest.

You can add visual interest by using **onmouseover** events.


**if** expressions, unlike **if** statements, return a value. Unlike **if** statements, **if** expressions return a value.

- Do not capitalize the names of features and components unless they are sold separately or are trademarked.


Use the Command-Line Interface to ... Use the command-line interface to ...


Open the Table Partitioning feature. Open the table partitioning feature.

- Do not capitalize collective or generic terms, such as agent names.


The Dispatcher The dispatcher


The Image Display Monitor The image display monitor


The Paging Supervisor The paging supervisor

[Start of page](.)

#### Glossaries

Use the following capitalization in glossaries:

- Use lowercase for glossary terms unless a term is a proper noun or requires capitalization for other reasons.
- Use sentence-style capitalization for glossary deﬁnitions.

For more information about glossaries beyond capitalization, see [Glossaries](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Headings, titles, and banners

In general, use sentence-style capitalization for headings.

Use sentence-style capitalization for these items:

- Titles and headings in online information, such as websites, presentations, tutorials, samples, IBM Developer articles, and technotes
- Titles of white papers and marketing content
- Titles of parts, tracks, or sessions in events
- Titles of screens within videos
- Titles and headings in topic-based information
- Headings in books (except the book title) Use headline-style capitalization for these items:
- Titles of books
- Titles of CDs
- Titles of stand-alone information units, such as quick start guides or discrete sets of product documentation
- Titles of events, such as training courses or programs
- Titles of videos

If a headline-style title has a subtitle, apply these capitalization guidelines:

- Use headline-style capitalization for a subtitle that is displayed on the same line as the title, is short, or is essential to the title.
- Use sentence-style capitalization for a subtitle that is displayed separately from the title, is lengthy, or is supplementary to the title.

When you cite a heading in text, use the capitalization that is used in the source unless the original heading is in all uppercase letters. In that case, use headline-style capitalization in the citation.

Use sentence-style capitalization for banners. Capitalize names of IBM products in banners according to trademark conventions. Limit capitalization in banners; avoid words in all uppercase except to conform to trademark conventions, as in terms such as *UNIX* .

#### Hyphens

Apply the following capitalization guidelines to hyphenated words:

- When a hyphenated word occurs at the beginning of a sentence, capitalize only the ﬁrst element in the word unless a subsequent element is a proper noun or proper adjective.


Power-Saving techniques are important for notebook users. Power-saving techniques are important for notebook users.


All-american manufacturing is less common than it used to be. All-American manufacturing is less common than it used to be.

- When a hyphenated word occurs at the beginning of a heading with sentence-style capitalization, capitalize only the ﬁrst element in the word unless a subsequent element is a proper noun or proper adjective.


Case-Sensitive languages Case-sensitive languages


Non-European-Based companies Non-European-based companies

- When a hyphenated word occurs in a heading with headline-style capitalization, capitalize the ﬁrst element in the word; the last element in the word, regardless of its part of speech; and any element that is not an article, preposition, or coordinating conjunction.


Designing Interfaces for Non-English-speaking Users Designing Interfaces for Non-English-Speaking Users


Self-contained Sensors Self-Contained Sensors


Once-a-day Notiﬁcations Once-a-Day Notiﬁcations

For more information about hyphens beyond capitalization, see [Hyphens](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Indexes

Use lowercase for index terms unless a term is a proper noun or requires capitalization for other reasons. For more information about indexes beyond capitalization, see Indexes .

[Start of page](.)

#### Letters as letters

If you refer to a letter, use the capitalization that is appropriate for the context unless it causes confusion. For example, if you refer to a letter in the middle of a word, use the capitalization that occurs in the middle of the word.


The *M* in *HTML* stands for *Markup* .

Double the letter *m* in the word *programming* .

Before the repair, the printer did not print uppercase *A’s* or lowercase *t’s* . To form the plural of a single letter, add an apostrophe and the letter *s* .

If you refer to a letter and the capitalization is irrelevant, use an uppercase letter.


With some fonts, readers can mistake *N’s* for *M’s* . Beginner typists often mistype *P’s* and *Z’s* .

[Start of page](.)

#### Lists

Capitalize the ﬁrst word of each item in a vertical list.


*Correct example:*

The routine makes the following conversions:

- An EBCDIC value to a real number
- A real number to an EBCDIC value
- An EBCDIC value to an integer
- An integer to an EBCDIC value

In deﬁnition lists, capitalize the ﬁrst word of each term or descriptive name, unless it must be lowercase, and capitalize the ﬁrst word of each deﬁnition.


*Correct example:*

###### All

You can perform all operations on resources.

###### Create

You can view, edit, and add resources.

###### Modify

You can view and edit resources.

For more information about lists beyond capitalization, see [Lists](.) .

#### Nouns

Common nouns, also known as generic nouns, refer generally to people, places, things, or ideas. Do not capitalize common nouns in the middle of a sentence.


Ensure that each User speciﬁes a unique password. Ensure that each user speciﬁes a unique password.


Ask an Administrator to grant you permission to access the database. Ask an administrator to grant you permission to access the database.


In Java, an Object refers to an actual instance of a Class. In Java, an object refers to an actual instance of a class.


Marie is a Software Engineer. Marie is a software engineer.


John is a Subject Matter Expert. John is a subject matter expert.

Proper nouns refer to names of speciﬁc people, places, things, or ideas. Always capitalize proper nouns. For details about how to capitalize place names, see [Geographic locations](.) .


John is a subject matter expert in IBM Enterprise Design Thinking. Marie works from the Bangalore ofﬁce as a software engineer.

Maria Martinez, director of international sales, opened the meeting of employees from Europe and Africa. A technical writer, a journalist, and an editor applied for the position of senior information developer.

The president of IBM was the ﬁrst speaker at the conference.

Civil titles, professional titles, military ranks, and similar ofﬁcial designations are usually lowercase. However, titles are capitalized in these cases:

- When the title immediately precedes a personal name and is used as part of the name; for example, President Lincoln
- In other contexts, for reasons of courtesy or diplomacy
- When referring to an individual in combination with their job title

Arvind Krishna, President and Chief Executive Ofﬁcer of IBM, was the ﬁrst speaker at the conference.

To distinguish whether a noun is a common noun or a proper noun, consider whether the noun refers to any one of many items (common noun) or whether it refers to the speciﬁc name of one item (proper noun).

For more information about names and titles, see [Names and titles](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Tables

Use sentence-style capitalization for these table elements:

- Cell contents
- Column headings
- Row labels
- Table captions

For more information about tables beyond capitalization, see [Tables](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### User interfaces

The primary reference for capitalization in a product interface is the design guidelines for that product. When you write about an item that is displayed in an interface or on a device, match the capitalization and spelling of the item in your writing. If an item uses all uppercase letters, use the same capitalization to refer to the item, even though use of all uppercase letters in general is discouraged. If a product does not have interface design guidelines, use sentence-style capitalization for all interface elements.

#### Computer-related terms

Use lowercase for terms unless other capitalization is speciﬁed in the following table or by industry or product guidelines.

| **Item and advice**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | **Examples**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| program or system. A group of related routines often has a collective name such as  *facility*  ,  *feature*  ,  *option*  ,  *support*  , or  *utility*  . Use lowercase for these terms when they refer to integral parts of the system. Use initial uppercase letters for these terms when they can be ordered as separate products. Maintain the original capitalization when a feature that was previously sold  separately becomes an integral part of another product.   |                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
