#### Parentheses

If the parenthetical text is not a complete sentence, do not insert a period inside the parentheses. See more examples in [Parentheses](.) .


You can sort the work items by their state (open, working, or closed.) You can sort the work items by their state (open, working, or closed).

If the parenthetical text is a complete sentence, you can either include the parenthetical sentence in the sentence to which it pertains or in parentheses as a separate sentence. If you include the parenthetical sentence in the sentence to which it pertains, do not insert a period inside the parentheses. If the parenthetical text is a separate sentence, insert the period inside the parentheses.


You cannot include punctuation marks in the name (you are prompted to remove punctuation marks if you include them). You cannot include punctuation marks in the name. (You are prompted to remove punctuation marks if you include them.)

Start of pa ge

#### Quotation marks

For details about using periods with quotation marks, see [Quotation marks with other punctuation](.) . Start of pa ge

### Quotation marks

Use double quotation marks (“ ”) and single quotation marks (‘ ’) correctly. See speciﬁc guidance for [Marketing](.) .

#### Contents

- [Terminology](.)
- [Emphasis](.)
- [Double quotation marks](.)
- [Single quotation marks](.)
- [Quotation marks with other punctuation](.)
- [Typographical considerations](.)

#### Terminology

The term *quotation mark* refers generically to a double quotation mark character or a single quotation mark character. When you refer to quotation marks in text, specify whether you mean *double quotation marks* or *single quotation marks* .

To refer to the position of the characters, use the terms *opening* and *closing* .


Ensure that each set of opening quotation marks has a matching set of closing quotation marks.

Do not use the term *quotes* to refer to quotation marks or to the text between quotation marks. Use the term *quote* only as a verb, and use *quotation* as the noun.


Enclose the value in quotes.

Enclose the value in double quotation marks.


The introduction includes an infamous quote. The introduction includes an infamous quotation.

[Start of page](.)

#### Emphasis

Do not use quotation marks to emphasize words or phrases. Quotation marks can clutter the text. To emphasize words as words, use italic font.


The service processor is also referred to as the 'baseboard management controller.' The service processor is also referred to as the *baseboard management controller.*

To call attention to information that might be overlooked, consider using a note that has a meaningful label. For more information, see Notes .


“Do not” close the lid until the unit is seated.

**Important:** Do not close the lid until the unit is seated.

[Start of page](.)

#### Double quotation marks

Use double quotation marks for the following items:

- Quotations.
- Words that are used in a special sense, but only if no other word clearly expresses the meaning. Do not overuse quotation marks for this purpose. Using a word in a special sense can cause problems for translation.
- Citations that have sentence-style capitalization and do not have any other highlighting.
- Hardware label names.
- Interface elements that have sentence-style capitalization and that need to be distinguished from surrounding text.

For more information and examples, see [Highlighting](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Single quotation marks

Use single quotation marks for the following items:

- Quotation marks inside double quotation marks

After the conference, he explained, “When she said ‘Know your target audience’, I knew we had work to do.”

- Code examples, code syntax, and programming elements that require single quotation marks


&amp;NAME = 'JANE B. DORMANZ'

Execution PARM='CORE=200000,DBRC=N'

- Hexadecimal numbers


X'C1'

X'14'

[Start of page](.)

#### Quotation marks with other punctuation

If a punctuation mark is part of a quotation (or of a programming element that uses quotation marks), place the punctuation mark inside the closing quotation mark; otherwise, place it outside the closing quotation mark. If a sentence ends with a quotation, use only one period, question mark, or exclamation point to end the sentence, placing it inside the closing quotation mark if it is part of the quotation, and outside if it is not.


For more information, see the chapter that is named “Semantic tagging”, which provides examples and a tutorial.


She said, “You meet all the requirements for promotion.”. She said, “You meet all the requirements for promotion.”


I can never remember how to spell “occurred”.  Paul said, “I erased the storage medium.”


Did Paul say, “I erased the storage medium”?


I thought Paul asked, “Who erased the storage medium?”


Did Paul utter the exact phrase “Who erased the storage medium?”? Did Paul utter the exact phrase “Who erased the storage medium?”


Did Paul use the word “medium” or “media”?


If you use the keyword operand **PGMID="PAYCOM"** , you must ...  In the program segment, ensure that the value is X'FF'.


Use the following code in the calendar application:

###### vout("Mon.", "Tues.", "Wed.", "Thurs.", "Fri.")

#### Typographical considerations

You can generate quotation marks directly through the keyboard, by using tagging in an authoring tool, or by using HTML or unicode characters in the source to produce the right characters in the output.

To follow IBM Design Language best practices, use curly quotation marks instead of straight quotation marks where possible. The following table describes the key combinations to use depending on the operating system you’re using.

| **Character**                      | **Unicode representation**   | **Windows**   | **Mac**        | **HTML**        |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------|---------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Opening single quotation mark (‘)  | U+2018                       | Alt+0145      | option+]       | **&amp;lsquo;** |
| Closing single quotation mark (’)  | U+2019                       | Alt+0146      | option+shift+] | **&amp;rsquo;** |
| Opening double quotation marks (“) | U+201C                       | Alt+0147      | option+[       | **&amp;ldquo;** |
| Closing double quotation marks (”) | U+201D                       | Alt+0148      | option+shift+[ | **&amp;rdquo;** |

When writing code samples, code syntax, hexadecimal numbers, or hypertext links, always use straight quotation marks.

| **Character**                       | **Unicode representation**   | **Keyboard key**   |
|-------------------------------------|------------------------------|--------------------|
| Straight single quotation mark (')  | U+0027                       | ' key              |
| Straight double quotation marks (") | U+0022                       | " key              |

Always check the published output to verify that the characters render properly. Some application have settings that automatically replace straight quotation marks with *smart quotes* , which is another name for curly quotation marks. A typographic character that you specify in an authoring tool might not be converted properly when the source ﬁle is published. Checking the output ensures that you can ﬁnd and address any formatting surprises.

#### Related resources


- [IBM Design Language&gt;Punctuation](https:/www.ibm.com/design/language/typography/type-basics/#punctuation)

### Semicolons

Use a semicolon to separate independent clauses or items in a series that has internal punctuation. If a sentence is complex, difﬁcult to read, or longer than 32 words, consider rewriting it, separating it into multiple sentences, or presenting its contents in a vertical list.

#### Semicolons between independent clauses

#### 

Use a semicolon between independent clauses that are not connected by a coordinating conjunction. Coordinating conjunctions are *and* , *but* , *or* , *nor* , *for* , *so* , and *yet* . Use a coordinating conjunction when you need to show the relationship between clauses; use a semicolon when the relationship between clauses is clear.


Remove the lid carefully; place it on a soft surface.

Type the command as shown; the program is case-sensitive.

Use a semicolon between independent clauses that are connected by a conjunctive adverb or a transitional phrase. Conjunctive adverbs include *also* , *besides* , *consequently* , *conversely* , *ﬁnally* , *however* , *instead* , *likewise* , *next* , *otherwise* , *similarly* , *speciﬁcally* , *still* , *subsequently* , *then* , and *therefore* . Transitional phrases include *at the same time* , *for example* , *in addition* , and *on the contrary* .


This product is sold worldwide; however, the US market remains a major focus. Enter a command; for example, type SETUP.

Right-click the selected text; then click **Text Properties** .

#### Semicolons between items in a series

Use a semicolon between items in a series that has internal punctuation.


Save the executable ﬁle, run.exe; the readme ﬁle, rm.txt; and the image for the splash screen, screen.jpg. You can press the yellow, green, or blue button; the off switch; or the mouse button.

### Slashes

Avoid using forward slashes (/) and backslashes (\) in most text and in dates.

#### Contents

- [General text](.)
- [Dates](.)
- [Fractions](.)
- [Mathematical equations](.)
- [Path names](.)
- [Tables](.)
- [Web addresses](.)

#### General text

Follow these guidelines for using slashes in general text:

- In most cases, do not use slashes in text because they can be ambiguous. For example, *1/2* can mean *one half* , *one and two* , *one of two* , and *one or two* . Rewrite the text using *and* , *of* , or *or* .


The meeting has a scheduled tea/coffee break. The meeting has a scheduled tea and coffee break.


You must complete 3/4 tasks.

You must complete three of four tasks.


An emergency contact is often a relative/close friend. An emergency contact is often a relative or close friend.

- Do not use the construction *and/or* , which can be ambiguous and cause problems for translation. Instead, consider whether both conjunctions are needed; if not, use *and* or *or* . If both conjunctions are needed, use the construction *option A, option B, or both* .


Connect your printer and/or scanner to the computer. Connect your printer and scanner to the computer.

Connect your printer or scanner to the computer. Connect your printer, scanner, or both to the computer.

- In a few cases, use a forward slash (/) in terms where the slash construction is an industry standard.


client/server I/O input/output P/N

publish/subscribe read/write

S/N

- Where space is limited, it is acceptable to use a forward slash (/) to mean *per* .


visitors/yr wk/mo in./ft

- Do not insert a space before or after a forward slash or backslash.


input / output input/output

[Start of page](.)

#### Dates

Do not use slashes in dates. For guidelines on how to express dates, see [Dates and times](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Fractions

Whenever possible, use decimal numerals instead of fractions to represent fractional parts of units.


*Avoid* : 1 1/2

*Prefer* : 1.5


*Avoid* : 3 3/4

*Prefer* : 3.75 [Start of page](.)

#### Mathematical equations

Use a forward slash (/) as an operational symbol for division. Do not insert a space before or after the forward slash.


(a + b)/(c + d) = -5

For more information about mathematical equations, see [Mathematical equations](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Path names

When you refer to a subdirectory by using a full path name, such as */usr/bin/samples* , use a forward slash (/) or backslash ( **\** ) according to the convention of the operating system. For information that applies to multiple operating systems, be consistent and describe the convention if necessary.


Windows operating systems use a backslash ( **\** ) to delimit directories in a directory path. AIX operating systems and web addresses use a forward slash (/) as a delimiter. This information uses forward slashes for all delimiters. Depending on your operating system, you might have to enter directory paths differently from what is shown in the examples.

If a path does not ﬁt on one line, end the ﬁrst line after an existing slash, and continue the path on the next line. Do not add a hyphen to indicate a break in a path.


###### C:\Documents and Settings\Administrator\IBM\Lotus\Symphony\appli-cations\eclipse\plugins


**C:\Documents and Settings\Administrator\IBM\Lotus\Symphony\ applications\eclipse\plugins**

#### Tables

#### Web addresses

Follow these guidelines for using slashes in web addresses:

- If the protocol is HTTP, you can typically omit the protocol, colon, and forward slashes (http://); because most browsers default to an HTTP connection. However, some tools convert addresses into live links and require the full address, including the protocol name. If the protocol is not HTTP, always include the protocol in the web address.


ftp.ibm.com [www.ibm.com](http:/www.ibm.com) ftp://ftp.ibm.com [http://www.ibm.com](http:/www.ibm.com)

[https://www.ibm.com/cloud](http:/www.ibm.com/cloud-computing/bluemix)

- Do not include a forward slash at the end of a web address.


[www.ibm.com/](http:/www.ibm.com) [www.ibm.com](http:/www.ibm.com)


[https://www.ibm.com/cloud/](http:/www.ibm.com/cloud-computing/bluemix) [https://www.ibm.com/cloud](http:/www.ibm.com/cloud-computing/bluemix)

- If a web address does not ﬁt on one line, end the ﬁrst line after an existing forward slash (/) or double forward slash (//), and continue the address on the next line. Do not add a hyphen to indicate a break in a path.

[www.ibm.com/software/commerce/net.-](http:/www.ibm.com/software/commerce/net.-) [commerce/action.html](http:/www.ibm.com/software/commerce/net.commerce/action.html)


[www.ibm.com/software/commerce/](http:/www.ibm.com/software/commerce/net.commerce/action.html) [net.commerce/action.html](http:/www.ibm.com/software/commerce/net.commerce/action.html)

[Start of page](.)

### Currency

A currency might be designated in one of three ways:

- The name of the currency in the local language (such as *dollars* )
- A currency symbol (such as $)
- A three letter code (such as USD) from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Standard 4217 - *Currency and funds name and code elements*

When you write about monetary values, ensure that the associated currency is clear.

Symbols such as $, £, and kr are used with multiple national currencies. A country code is sometimes used in an attempt to disambiguate, such as US$, MX$, Nkr or Dkr, but this approach is not standardized. Similarly, if a nation has revalued its currency, the original symbol might be retained or reverted to after a brief migration period.


In general, and especially when you write for a global audience, always use the ISO 4217 currency code, which is unambiguous and independent of the reader’s language or locale. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) . The maintenance agency for these codes also ensures uniqueness over time. The deﬁnitive list is available from the [ISO website  in both XLS and XML formats.](http:/www.iso.org/iso/currency_codes)

Place the currency unit before the numeric amount, with a space.


LKR 100 (100 Sri Lankan rupees)

USD 100 (100 US dollars)

AUD 100 (100 Australian dollars)

GBP 100 (100 UK pounds sterling)

EUR 100 (100 European Union euros)

Do not abbreviate a number to a letter, such as *thousand* to K or *million* to M.


The contract is worth USD 4 M.

The contract is worth USD 4 million. The contract is worth USD 4,000,000.

**Exception:** Using a currency symbol (such as $ or £), a letter as an abbreviation for a currency multiplier (such as K for thousand or M for million), or both is allowed when space is limited (as on some user interfaces or websites, and as in some mobile apps), and when readers can be expected to know or easily determine the meaning of the symbol or abbreviation. In such instances, do not insert a blank between the number and the multiplier.


Sales: £4 K Sales: £4K

#### Local currency symbols

ISO currency codes might not always be appropriate, particularly for domestic use. If your information is not used outside your country or includes scenarios in which the reader is expected to work with local currency symbols, use the appropriate symbol or abbreviation that is commonly used in your country, such as $ (dollar) in Canada and Liberia, or £ (pound) in Gibraltar and the United Kingdom. Note that most information that is written in English is available worldwide and should typically use ISO currency codes with a descriptive label. Always include a currency symbol or abbreviation when you specify a monetary value in general text.


You must provide a deposit of at least 10,000. You must provide a deposit of at least £10,000.

Different cultures express monetary values in different ways. The following examples show format variations in the placement of the currency symbols, designation of negative amounts, decimal and grouping separators, placement of the various symbols, and the presence or absence of spaces between symbols and numbers.

| **Positive format**   | ****Negative format ****   | ****ISO 4217 code ****   | **Example territory**   |
|-----------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|
| Bs 123.456,78         | -Bs 123.456,78             | BOB                      | Bolivia                 |
| $1,234,567.89         | -$1,234,567.89             | CAD                      | Canada English          |
| 1 234 567,89 $        | (1 234 567,89 $)           | CAD                      | Canada French           |
| ¥1,234,567.89         | -¥1,234,567.89             | CNY                      | China                   |
| 1 234 567,89 kr       | -1 234 567,89 kr           | EEK                      | Estonia                 |
| 1 234 567,89 €        | -1 234 567,89 €            | EUR                      | Finland                 |
| € 1.234.567,89        | € 1.234.567,69-            | EUR                      | Greece                  |
| €1,234,567.89         | -€1,234,567.89             | EUR                      | Ireland                 |
| 1.234.567,89 €        | -1.234.567,89 €            | EUR                      | Luxembourg              |
| € 1.234.567,89        | € -1.234.567,89            | EUR                      | Netherlands             |
| 1.234.567,89 €        | -1.234.567,89 €            | EUR                      | Portugal                |
| £1,234,567.89         | -£1,234,567.89             | GBP                      | United Kingdom          |
| 1 234 567,89 Ft       | -1 234 567,89 Ft           | HUF                      | Hungary                 |
| ¥1,234,567            | -¥1,234,567                | JPY                      | Japan                   |
| $U 1.234.567,89       | $U -1.234.567,89           | UYU                      | Uruguay                 |

The use of parentheses to indicate negative values is a conventional format used by some ﬁnancial institutions and banking agencies. This usage does not always match regular currency formatting determined by user locale.

### Dates and times

Express dates and times consistently and in a way that is understandable internationally.

#### Contents

- [General guidance for dates](.)
- [Abbreviations of dates](.)
- [Abbreviations of time](.)
- [Business calendar periods](.)
- [General guidance for times](.)
- [12-hour time notation](.)
- [24-hour time notation](.)
- [Time zones](.)

#### General guidance for dates

Follow these guidelines for formatting dates:

- When technically feasible, localize dates. In product UIs, for example, the date format can often be localized to use the standard date format based on the user's locale preferences.


For static text, such as product documentation, use the following date-and-time format, which is clear regardless of locale:  14 July 2020 10:30 PM

IBM only For more information about how to specify dates in product UIs, see the *Carbon for IBM Products* [Date and time](https:/pages.github.ibm.com/carbon/ibm-products/guidelines/content/date-and-time) guidance.

- To avoid confusion about the meaning of a date, do not use an all-numeric representation. For example, in the US, 12/2/2021 means 2 December 2021; in many other countries, it means 12 February 2021. Specify the day, the month, and the year, in that order. Use a numeral for the day, spell out the name of the month, and use four digits for the year. Insert one space between the day and the month and between the month and the year. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .


The product was manufactured on 12/2/2021. The product was manufactured on 12-2-2021. The product was manufactured on 02.12.2021. The product was manufactured on 2/12/21.

The product was manufactured on December 2, 2021. The product was manufactured on 2 December 2021.

**Exception:** Use of an all-numeric representation is allowed when space is limited, as in a user interface, or when doing so greatly enhances readability. For example, a table that speciﬁes a date in one of its columns might be easier to scan and sort visually when the units (year, month, day) are all numeric. In such cases, use the date format prescribed by ISO 8601 that uses a 4-digit year (YYYY-MM-DD), as documented at [https://www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime](https:/www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime) . Describe the format in the column header or in a legend.

| **Product**   | **Release date (Year-Month-Day)**   |
|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| Product A     | 2021-12-02                          |
| Product B     | 2019-04-09                          |
| Product C     | 2019-09-04                          |

Table 1. Product information

- Do not use a leading zero for a single-digit date, unless you need the zero to align dates in a list or table or to correctly show a date format, such as in a ﬁeld.


The product was manufactured on 01 January 2019. The product was manufactured on 1 January 2019. In the **Date** ﬁeld, type 01jan2019.

- Do not use ordinal numerals (that is, numerals that use the abbreviations st, nd, rd, and th) to specify a date.


The product was manufactured on the 2nd of December, 2021. The product was manufactured on 2nd December, 2021.

The product was manufactured on December 2nd, 2021. The product was manufactured on 2 December 2021.

- If you include the day of the week, use a comma between the day and the date.


The product was manufactured on Thursday 2 December. The product was manufactured on Thursday, 2 December.

- When you refer to a month and year, do not use a comma between the month and the year.


The product was manufactured in June, 2021. The product was manufactured in June 2021.

- When you refer to the names of centuries, use ordinal numerals.


The product was manufactured in the twenty-ﬁrst century. The product was manufactured in the 21st century.

#### Date abbreviations

In static text such as product documentation, avoid abbreviating dates unless space is restricted, such as in a table. If you must abbreviate a date and are not constrained by a required format, follow the general guidelines but abbreviate the month to its ﬁrst three letters. Do not insert a period after the month. Capitalize only the ﬁrst letter for the month. Use 4 digits for the year.


5 Sept 2019

5 Sep 19

5 Sep. 19

5 SEP 19

5 Sep 2019

#### Unit of time abbreviations

In general text, do not abbreviate a unit of time such as *seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months* , or *years* if no numeric value is associated with it. You can abbreviate units of time, and optionally use a slash character to mean “per”, only when space is limited, such as in tables or in detailed diagrams. For example, 10 h/d to mean “10 hours per day”.

The following table lists the unit of time abbreviations that are supported.

| **Unit**   | **Abbreviation**   |
|------------|--------------------|
| second     | s                  |
| minute     | min                |
| hour       | h                  |
| day        | d                  |
| week       | wk                 |
| month      | mo                 |
| year       | yr                 |

Table 2. Supported unit of time abbreviations

The supported unit of time abbreviations are consistent with the SI units for time. SI refers to **The International System of Units**

(abbreviated from the French, le Système International d’Unités). For more information about SI units, see [Units of measurement](.) .

- Write out the units of time when space is available, such as in a table that has room to accommodate them.

| **Experiment**   | **Incorrect time duration**     | **Correct time duration**                     |
|------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|

Table 3. Experiment details with unnecessary abbreviations

- When using unit of time abbreviations, do not add an *s* to indicate that the unit is plural.

The following table shows that **s** is added incorrectly to the hour and minute abbreviations to indicate that they are plural values.

| **Experiment**   | **Team**    | **Lead**   | **Location**   |   **Variable 1** |   **Variable 2** | **Time duration**   |
|------------------|-------------|------------|----------------|------------------|------------------|---------------------|
| Experiment 1     | Red group 3 | Jane Lewis | COL Lab 2      |          0.23432 |          1.23423 | 2 hs 24 mins 30 s   |

Table 4. Experiment details with incorrect plural abbreviations


The following table illustrates how to use time abbreviations in a busy table.

| **Experiment**   | **Team**    | **Lead**   | **Location**   |   **Variable 1** |   **Variable 2** | **Time duration**   |
|------------------|-------------|------------|----------------|------------------|------------------|---------------------|
| Experiment 1     | Red group 3 | Jane Lewis | COL Lab 2      |          0.23432 |          1.23423 | 2 h 24 min 30 s     |

Table 5. Experiment details in a crowded table with correct abbreviations

#### Business calendar periods

To express segments of a business year, follow these conventions:

- When you abbreviate for quarters or halves, start with the numeral, then use uppercase Q for quarter or H for half, with no space between the characters. If you include the year in the segment, insert a space between the letter and the 4-digit year.


The product was released in Q3.

The product was released in 3Q2021. The product was released in H2 2021. The product was released in 3Q.

The product was released in 1H.

The product was released in 2H 2021.

- When you abbreviate for ﬁscal year, show as uppercase FY, then a space, then the 4-digit year.


The product was released in FY21. The product was released in FY 2021.


For more information about time periods for IBM, refer to the [IBM Enterprise Reference Data Manager .](https:/erdmuiapp-prod.wdc1a.cirrus.ibm.com/erdmStandardDetails/70)

#### General guidance for times

Use 12-hour or 24-hour notation as appropriate, but do not mix the two notations in the same information. When times include seconds, use 24-hour notation.

#### 12-hour time notation

Follow these guidelines to format times using 12-hour notation:

- Use colons to separate hours and minutes. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) . Do not insert a space before or after the colon. Use uppercase letters and no periods for the abbreviations AM and PM, and insert a space before these abbreviations.


Lunch will begin at 11.30AM. Lunch will begin at 11.30 A.M. Lunch will begin at 11.30 a.m. Lunch will begin at 11:30 AM.

- Do not use a leading zero for a single-digit hour, unless you need the zero to align times in a list or table or to correctly show a time format, such as in a ﬁeld.


The meeting will start at 02:30 PM. The meeting will start at 2:30 PM.

- Do not use *o'clock* to refer to a whole hour.


The meeting will start at 2 o'clock in the afternoon. The meeting will start at 2 PM.

- Do not use zeros to indicate a time that is exactly on the hour unless, in a list or range of times, one time includes minutes.


The coffee break will be from 2 to 2:30 PM.

The coffee break will be from 2:00 PM to 2:30 PM.

- Use midnight and noon (instead of AM and PM) to indicate those hours.


The program changes at midnight. There is a break from noon to 1 PM.

[Start of page](.)

#### 24-hour time notation

In 24-hour time notation, the day begins at 00:00 (midnight), and the last minute of the day begins at 23:59 (one minute before midnight). Follow these guidelines to format times using 24-hour notation:

- Use colons to separate hours, minutes, and seconds. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) . Do not insert a space before or after the colon.

The maintenance period is from 12:00 to 15:00.

- Use a leading zero for a single-digit hour.

The maintenance period is from 02:00 to 05:00.

- Do not show seconds with whole hours, unless other times include the seconds or the seconds are signiﬁcant.


The job started at 13:00.

The job completed at 13:15:22.

The job started at 13:00:00 and completed at 13:15:22.

- Write hours, minutes, and seconds each with two digits. You can also add fractions of a second after a decimal separator to an appropriate level of precision.

The job completed at 15:37:42.354.

- To refer to midnight, either follow the style that is used in the interface, or use 00:00 when the context is the beginning of the day and use 24:00 when the context is the end of the day.

Event monitoring is scheduled to run for one hour each day at 00:00, 08:00, and 16:00. The event logs are consolidated each day between 23:00 and 24:00.

[Start of page](.)

#### Time zones

If you include the time zone, follow these guidelines:

- On the ﬁrst occurrence, use both the spelled-out form and the abbreviated form of the time zone. Use initial capital letters for the spelled-out form.

The conference will take place on 10 February from 8 AM to 8 PM Eastern Time (ET). You can reach customer service from 7 AM to 9 PM Central European Time (CET).

**Exception:** Using an abbreviated form of a time zone is allowed when space is limited and when readers can be expected to know or easily determine the meaning of the abbreviation, as in a user interface.


14 July 2020, 10:30 PM ET

10 February at 22:30 CET

- Unless necessary, avoid mentioning whether a time zone uses Standard Time or Daylight Saving Time.


The conference will take place on 10 February from 8 AM to 8 PM Eastern Standard Time (EST). The conference will take place on 10 February from 8 AM to 8 PM Eastern Time (ET).


The conference will take place on 10 July from 8 AM to 8 PM Eastern Daylight Time (EDT). The conference will take place on 10 July from 8 AM to 8 PM Eastern Time (ET).

#### Date ranges

To express a range of dates, use one of the following methods:

- Use the words *from* and *through* . Do not use the words *from* and *to* , because the word *to* makes it ambiguous whether the end date is included in the date range. Do not use the word *between* , because that word makes it ambiguous whether the beginning and end dates are included in the date range.

between August 2019 and January 2021 *(This can mean either “after August and before January, that is, in the intervening months” or “after July and before February”)*


from August 2019 through January 2021 *(This can mean only “after July and before February”)*


from 9 October to 12 October 2021 *(This can mean either “from 9 October through 11 October, that is, up until the beginning of 12 October” or “from 9 October through 12 October” )*

from 9 October through 12 October 2021

from 9 through 12 October 2021

- Use an en dash with no space before or after. Always use this method for abbreviated forms. Do not use the words *from* with the en dash.


8 - 15 May 2021

8–15 May 2021


June - September 2021 June–September 2021


from 14Jun2021 - 21Jun2021 14 Jun 2021 - 21 Jun 2021

14 Jun 2021–21 Jun 2021


8-10 and 16-17 November 2021

8-10 November and 16-17 November 2021

8–10 November 2021 and 16–17 November 2021 See guidance for [Dashes](.) and [Ranges](.) .

[Start of page](.)

#### Time ranges

To express a range of times, use one of the following methods:

- Use the words *from* and *to* . Do not use the word *between* , because that word makes it ambiguous whether the beginning and end times are included in the time range. For a time that uses 12-hour format, include *AM* and *PM* in both parts of the range.


between 1:00 and 2:15 PM

from 1:00 to 2:15 PM

from 1:00 PM to 2:15 PM


between 9 October at 1:00 PM and 12 October at 2:15 PM

from 9 October at 1:00 PM to 12 October at 2:15 PM

- Use an en dash with no space before or after. Always use this method for abbreviated forms. Do not use the word *from* with the en dash. For a time that uses 12-hour format, include AM and PM in both parts of the range.


1:00 PM - 2:15 PM

from 1:00 - 2:15 PM


1:00 PM–2:15 PM


9 October 1:00 PM - 12 October 2:15 PM

9 October 1:00 PM–12 October 2:15 PM See guidance for [Dashes](.) and [Ranges](.) .

[Start of page](.)

#### Timestamps

Sometimes, displaying a date and time as an all-numeric timestamp enhances readability. Timestamps should follow ISO 8601, as documented at [https://www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime](https:/www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime) . Do not specify a “T” delimiter between the date and time. Such a timestamp has the form YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss.n..., where seconds and fractions of a second are optional.


2020/12/31 17:45:37

2020-12-31T17:45:37

2020-12-31 18

2020-12-31 17:45

2020-12-31 17:45:37

2020-12-31 17:45:37.309762

[Start of page](.)

#### Durations

For durations where the smaller unit is less than 10, include a leading zero to eliminate any possible confusion. If the duration has only one time unit, don’t include the leading zero.


1 h 2 mins

1 h 02 min


02 seconds

2 seconds

See also [Abbreviations &gt; Units of time](https:/ibmdocs-test.dcs.ibm.com/docs/en/ibm-style?topic=grammar-abbreviations&units-of-time) [Start of page](.)

#### Globalization of dates and times in UIs

Date and time ﬁelds in UIs typically present information in a style that is appropriate to the region in which the UI is used. The Carbon Design System’s [date picker component](https:/www.carbondesignsystem.com/components/date-picker/usage/#time-pickers) , for example, has all of the built-in requirements for globalized date and time ﬁelds.

If it is not possible to globalize the date and time ﬁelds, consider using the date, time, and timestamp formats in the ISO 8601 standard, as documented at [https://www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime](https:/www.w3.org/TR/NOTE-datetime) . However, because these formats are not universally understood, the UI might need to explain them in its online assistance.

[Start of page](.)

### Numbers

Follow these guidelines to correctly express numbers.

#### Contents

- [Abbreviations](.)

- [Alignment in columns](.)
- [Bases (Radices)](.)
- [Comma separators](.)
- [Complements](.)
- [Decimals and decimal separators](.)
- [Digit position in decimals](.)
- [Hyphenation](.)
- [Plurals of numbers as words](.)
- [Proportions](.)
- [Fractions](.)
- [Percentages](.)
- [Ratios](.)
- [Ranges](.)
- [Rounding](.)

#### Abbreviations

Do not abbreviate a multiplier to a letter, such as “thousand” to K or “million” to M. Use letters only as preﬁxes to units of measurement, such as “km” for “kilometers” or “MB” for “megabytes”. For correct usage of multiplier preﬁxes, including k (for x1,000) and K (for x1,024), see [Units of measurement](.) .


The company has 10K employees.

The company has 10 thousand employees. The company has 10,000 employees.


The contract is worth USD 4M.

The contract is worth USD 4 million. The contract is worth USD 4,000,000.


Each turbine can generate 30 MW of power. The power line is 50 km long.

The client system has only 100 KB of memory.

**Exception:** Using an uppercase letter as an abbreviation for a multiplier is allowed when space is limited (as on some user interfaces or websites, and as in some mobile apps), and when readers can be expected to know or easily determine the meaning of the abbreviation. In such instances, do not insert a blank between the number and the multiplier.


100 K visitors/yr. 100K visitors/yr. Sales: $4M

[Start of page](.)

#### Alignment in columns

Align a column of numbers on the decimal separator. Right align integers.

Align times on colons. [Start of page](.)

#### Bases (Radices)

Explicitly identify the base (radix) of a number that is not decimal (that is, not in base 10). For example, identify the following number bases:

- Binary
- Hexadecimal
- Octal

Your authoring tool might automatically handle the representation of number bases. If it does, let the authoring tool determine the representation. If it does not, or if the representation that the authoring tool generates is inappropriate, consider the subject matter and audience to determine how best to indicate these bases.

In general, use programming symbols to show the base and value of a number only when the value must be shown exactly as it is coded. Although the punctuation marks that enclose the value are known as apostrophes in extended binary-coded decimal interchange code (EBCDIC), you can represent them with single straight quotation marks in text.


For the SIZE parameter, code either X'CA' or X'140'. Note the entry B'1010' in the program.

You can represent hexadecimal numbers in several ways. The following formats are most commonly used:


- X'nnnn'. This format was originally used for System z and System i applications but you can also use it for other applications.  The reason code is X'B0'.
- 0xnnnn. This is the most common format for languages such as C++ and Java.

The system returns the value 0x10AF.


- hex nnnn. Consider using this format for less technical users.  The required code point is hex 56.

Whichever format you use in your content, ensure that you use it consistently. Use the abbreviation *hex* only when representing a

speciﬁc hexadecimal number. Do not use it in text (for example, in a phrase such as *The message contains a hex value* ); use the term

*hexadecimal* instead.

Do not use commas or spaces in octal or hexadecimal numbers. For binary values, leave a space between groups of four numbers.


You see the binary number 10011011. You see the binary number 1001 1011.


If you use a decimal number and a number in a different base together, explicitly indicate the base of both numbers.  You can view the data in decimal or hexadecimal format; for example, 33 (decimal) or X'21' (hexadecimal).

#### Comma separators

Use a comma to separate groups of three numerals.


The metric equivalent of 68 750 ft is 20 955 m. The metric equivalent of 68,750 ft is 20,955 m.


The computer cost is USD 10999.99. The computer cost is USD 10,999.99.


The program contains 1115 lines of code The program contains 1,115 lines of code.

Omit the commas when you are instructing the user to enter a value or specifying that the user must enter a value from a range, and including the commas would cause an error.


Enter a value in the range 32,000–485,000. Enter a value in the range 32000–485000.

Do not use commas in numbers that do not represent amounts, such as part numbers or addresses.


Order replacement part number 2,924,563. Order replacement part number 2924563.

For information about separators in binary, octal, and hexadecimal numbers, see Bases (Radices ). [Start of page](.)

#### Complements

Form the name of a complement by adding an apostrophe and the letter *s* ( *’s* ) to the spelled-out number.


The two’s complement of binary 0011 1001 is 1100 0111. The ten’s complement of 235481 is 764519.

#### Decimals and decimal separators

Use a period on the line (.), not a raised dot (·), as a decimal separator unless the comma (,) is a legal requirement in the country for which you are writing.


The clearance is 4·6 cm (1·8 in.).

*Incorrect in most cases:* The clearance is 4,6 cm (1,8 in.).

*Correct in most cases:* The clearance is 4.6 cm (1.8 in.).

Put a 0 in front of the decimal separator when the decimal value is less than 1.


Be sure to maintain a 6 mm (·25 in.) distance. Be sure to maintain a 6 mm (0.25 in.) distance.

#### Digit position in decimals

Refer to the whole-number positions of digits in decimal numerals as follows: the *units position* , *tens position* , *hundreds position* , *thousands position* , and so on. Refer to the fractional positions in decimal numerals as the *tenths position* , *hundredths position* , *thousandths position* , and so on.


#### Hyphenation

Use a hyphen when you spell out numbers 21 through 99, regardless of the part of speech.


twenty-four

three hundred eighty-seven

#### Plurals of numbers as words

For both numerals and numbers that are expressed as words, form the plural by adding *s* alone.


By default, the ﬁeld is ﬁlled with zeros.

The award recipients walked into the auditorium in twos. Binary code contains only 0s and 1s.

The most frequently returned values were 5s, 7s, and 12s.

Several ﬁnancial analysts classify the 1980s and 1990s as a bull market. Of the eight remaining units, six were 517s and two were 918s.

#### Proportions

##### Fractions

Whenever possible, use decimal numbers instead of fractions to represent fractional parts of units.


0.6

5.167

3/5

If the use of a fraction is necessary, use a hyphen between a whole number and a numeric fraction. In this case, do not include a hyphen between the number and a unit of measurement.


5-1/6

When it is appropriate to spell out a fraction, use a hyphen.


three-ﬁfths

ﬁve and one-sixth

##### Percentages

When writing a percentage, always use a numeral (do not write out the number), always use the percent sign (%) (do not write out

*percent* ), and do not leave a space between the numeral and the percent sign.


We debugged ﬁfty % of the modules.

We debugged ﬁfty percent of the modules. We debugged 50 percent of the modules. We debugged 50% of the modules.

1% of users encountered severe errors.

##### Ratios

Always use numerals and a colon (:) to express ratios. Do not insert a space before or after the colon.


Expect to process gadgets and widgets in a ratio of 3:2.

Reclaim space in your data center with 20:1 server consolidation.

#### Ranges

Generally, use an en dash (–) without spaces on each side to indicate a range of numbers. If you list numbers along with other characters, unless the context determines a different order of the characters, list numeric characters ﬁrst, followed by alphabetic characters (uppercase and then lowercase), followed by other characters in ASCII order.


50 - 100

50–100


Permissible characters: 0 - 9 A - Z a - z # &amp; . ^ ~ Permissible characters: 0–9 A–Z a–z # &amp; .^ ~

If the range includes a unit of measurement, include the unit only after the second number, unless there is no space between the unit and the number. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .


16 MB–20 MB

16–20 MB


210 V–240 V AC

210–240 V AC


26mm–45mm (1.02in. - 1.77in.)

26–45 mm (1.02–1.77 in.)


10°–35°C (50° - 95°F)

10°C–35°C (50°F–95°F)


8–80%

8%–80%

For positive numbers, use numerals in ranges, even when either or both of the numbers are less than 10.


two–four 2–4


one–20 1–20

When either or both of the numbers in a range are negative, use the word *to* instead of a hyphen, to avoid confusion between a hyphen and the minus sign in front of a negative number.


-40°C–-60°C

-40°C to -60°C

Do not use words such as *between* and *and* to show a range; it is not clear whether the two numbers are the boundaries of the range or are included in the range. Do not use words such as *from* and *between* with a hyphenated range. Do not use the word *to* except where negative numbers are involved; use an en dash instead.


You need between 16 and 20 MB of free space. You need 16–20 MB of free space.


The acceptable range is 15% to 30%. The acceptable range is 15%–30%.

Do not separate groups of three numerals with a comma when you provide instructions to enter a value or to enter a value from a range, and including the commas would cause an error.


Enter a value between 32,000 and 485,000. Enter a value in the range 32000–485000.

If one or both values in a range include mathematical symbols, use *from* and *to* to express the range, and use parentheses to clarify which value is being modiﬁed. If the range includes a unit of measurement, to avoid ambiguity, include the unit after both expressions in the range.


n - n + 1

from n to n + 1


1 - 2 MB - 1 byte

from 1 MB to (2 MB–1 byte)

If a number range is part of a compound adjective, hyphenate only the number–unit compounds in the range, not the entire compound. You can omit the unit from the ﬁrst of the two compounds in the range.


a 1-character-through-8-character ﬁeld a 1-character through 8-character ﬁeld


a 1-through-8-character ﬁeld a 1-through 8-character ﬁeld

Use the ≥ symbol to express “greater than or equal to” a value. Use the ≤ symbol to express “less than or equal to” a value. In many cases, you can omit the symbol by incorporating a phrase such as “minimum requirement” or “maximum requirement” into the heading or text that precedes the values.


≥16 GB RAM

≤10 KB

a minimum of 16 GB of RAM a maximum of 10 KB


###### Minimum requirements

16 GB RAM

###### Maximum requirements

10 KB

#### Rounding

When you round numbers, use the appropriate number of decimal places for the degree of precision that is required. Be consistent in your method of rounding and how you round numbers that are exactly midway. If the method you use is signiﬁcant, make it clear to your readers.

When you combine numbers, show the result with an appropriate degree of precision.


4.67 × 3.2 = 14.944

4.67 × 3.2 = 14.9

When you convert to a different unit of measurement, express the result with a similar precision to the original measurement.


The computer weighs approximately 15 kg (33.069 lb). The computer weighs approximately 15 kg (33 lb).


The diameter is 89±0.5 mm (3.5±0.02 inches). The diameter is 89.0±0.5 mm (3.50±0.02 inches).

### Numerals versus words

In general, use numerals to represent all numbers, however large or small. For numbers below 10, it is alternatively acceptable to use words instead of numerals. Within a publication, be consistent in your approach.


The upgrade affected 12 servers. The 10th message is important.

The player has number 8 on his shirt.

The number of ﬁles processed averages 5.4 per cycle. (One option) Use the 2nd method.

(Alternative option) Use the second method.

The following tables list when to use words to express numbers. For other guidance about numbers, see [Numbers](.) . For details about how to correctly refer to currencies, see [Currency](.) .

#### Fractions

Fractions represent parts of a whole with a numerator (a cardinal number of parts present; one, two, three) and a denominator (an ordinal number of parts that make up the whole; third, fourth, ﬁfth). They can be written as numerals or words and this depends on the context. Be consistent within your documentation.


Generally, write fractions as words in the main text of a document. Use numerals for fractions in measurements, tables, equations, and other areas of documentation that primarily include numerical data.


Write out the fraction if at the start of a sentence or rewrite so that it doesn’t begin with a fraction.


2/3 of our clients provided feedback.

Two-thirds of our clients provided feedback. We received feedback from 2/3 of our clients.


If written as numerals, fractions should be set in text with a forward slash to separate the numerator and denominator.


For readability and consistency when writing out fractions in running text, they should be hyphenated in noun, adjective, and adverb form, except when the second element is already hyphenated.

| **Numerals**   | **Words**              |
|----------------|------------------------|
| 1/4            | quarter, one-fourth    |
| 1/2            | half, one-half         |
| 2/3            | two-thirds             |
| 5/16           | ﬁve-sixteenths         |
| 1/25           | one twenty-ﬁfth        |
| 1 3/4          | one and three-quarters |

#### When to use words for numbers

| **Situation**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | **Example**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Adjacent numbers**  Use words for the ﬁrst number unless the sentence is easier to understand with a numeral ﬁrst. Always use words for the ﬁrst number if it occurs at the beginning of a sentence.                                                                                                                                                    | Twenty-three 4-person teams participated.  Add 80 three times.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Beginning of a sentence**  In technical documentation, use words if a number occurs at the beginning of a sentence.  In marketing content or situations where character limits apply, you can use a numeral at the start of a sentence.                                                                                                                 | Three alternatives are shown. Seventy-three ﬁles were processed.  One hundred ﬁfty-six errors were found.  Eight-cylinder engines are usually more powerful than 4-cylinder engines.  Ten managers, 2 writers, and 95 programmers  **Exceptions:**  *  *Blog post:*  7 reasons to switch to IBM Cloud.  *  *Drupal release note title*  :  3 steps to take now to stop the security vulnerability in v2. |
| **Distinguishing numbers from letters**  Do not use both a word and numeral to express the same number, such as “ﬁve (5) screws.”  However, if the number might be mistaken for a letter, you can write the numeral followed by the word in parentheses. For example, to distinguish zero from the letter O or one from a lowercase L and an uppercase I. | 0 (zero)  1 (one)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

| **Situation**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | **Example**                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Large numbers**  You can use the words  *million, billion,*  and  *trillion*  in numbers that do not have to be presented as numerals. Use the US deﬁnitions for billion and trillion:  - One billion is one thousand million - One trillion is one million million  Do not abbreviate a number to a letter, such as “thousand” to K or “million” to M. Use letters only as preﬁxes to units of measurement. For correct usage of multiplier preﬁxes, including k (1,000) and K (1,024), see  [Units of measurement](.)  . | The population of Greater London is about 8 million.  Enter a value greater than USD 72.5 billion.  To refer to hard disk drive capacity or communications volume, MB means 1,000,000 bytes. |
| **Numbers under 10**  You can choose whether to use numerals or words for numbers that are less than 10. Whichever approach you choose, use it consistently within a single publication.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | The system has 5 tape drives. The system has ﬁve tape drives.  Use the 2nd method. Use the second method.                                                                                    |

### Mathematical equations

Follow these guidelines when you write mathematical equations and use operational symbols:


Leave a space before and after operational symbols such as the following characters:

+ - ± × ÷ = &lt; &gt;

Do not insert a space if an operator is used to modify a number or another symbol. Do not insert spaces around the forward slash (/) symbol, or between a parenthesis and an enclosed symbol or number.


Operational symbols are substitutes for words and should be written as such, with appropriate punctuation. For example, A + B

&lt; C means *A plus B is less than C* .


Consider putting equations on a separate line if they are difﬁcult to read in the body of the text or if they are referenced, as is equation (1) in these examples:


a + b = c - d (1) x ÷ y = z

(a + b)/(c + d) = -5


In general text, do not use variable names and mathematical symbols as a shorthand for words.


Set *stoppingtime* to *reactiontime* + *brakingtime* .

Set the value of *stoppingtime* to the sum of the values of *reactiontime* and *brakingtime* .


Select all the domains that have &gt;3 members.

Select all the domains that have more than three members.


To indicate multiplication, show the elements side by side. If you must show multiplication explicitly, use the multiplication sign (× - Unicode character U+00D7). Avoid using the letter *x* as a substitute for the multiplication sign, so that screen readers interpret it correctly. You can insert a multiplication sign in several ways:

- As a special character in most editors, including oXygen
- As an HTML character ( **&amp;times;** , **&amp;#215;** , or **&amp;#xd7;** )
- By typing Alt+0215, using the numeric keypad

In a formula or equation, do not use a raised dot to indicate multiplication. In some countries, the raised dot is used as a decimal point.


DIDOCS = (60 · R) + (36 · A) DIDOCS = 60R + 36A

Do not use an asterisk, except in examples from programming languages that use an asterisk as a multiplication sign.


DIDOCS = A * B DIDOCS = AB DIDOCS = A × B


To indicate an exponent, use a superscript. Do not insert spaces around operators in superscripts. If superscripts are not available to you, use two asterisks (**) followed by the exponent.


220

*If superscripts are not available:* 2**20


2(a+b)

*If superscripts are not available:* 2**(a + b)

#### Related resource


[Punctuation and symbols](.)

### Phone numbers

Use national or international formats for telephone numbers as appropriate. Always use designated ﬁctitious phone numbers in examples.

#### Contents


[National](.)


[International](.)


[Fictitious](.)

#### National

If you expect content to be used only in the same country from which a telephone number originates, use the national form of the number. Group the numerals according to the format that is normally used in the area or country.


When you refer to numbers in the US, Canada, and other countries in the North American Numbering Plan (NANP), use hyphens, not parentheses, to separate the groups of numerals.


(958) 555-0123

958-555-0123


Use parentheses for UK area codes to indicate that these digits are omitted when making a local call. Use spaces to separate groups of numerals, as shown in the following examples of national UK numbers:


(020) 7946 0123

(0114) 496 0123

For a telephone number that includes letters, show the corresponding numerals in parentheses after the alphanumeric telephone number.


1-800-IBM-4YOU (1-800-426-4968)

Start of pa ge

#### International


[For an international audience, use the international form of the number, following the guidelines issued by the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) .](https:/www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-E.123-200102-I/en)

Use the format +CC (where CC is the country code) followed by the area code and the telephone line number. The plus sign (+) indicates that the country code is preceded by more numbers that vary from country to country.

Note that the 0 in an area code is often omitted when the number is dialed from outside that country. Do not include the 0 in parentheses to indicate this changing usage. If you must include both national and international forms of a telephone number, show them separately.

Insert spaces between the country code and the area code, and between the area code and the line number. Also, if the line number comprises more than ﬁve digits, insert a space in the number to divide the digits into two groups; grouping the digits enhances memorization, oral presentation, and printing of the telephone number. If possible, make the spaces between the country code and the area code, and the area code and the line number, larger than any space within the line number. However, note that in HTML double spaces are displayed in exactly the same way as single spaces, unless you use the special character **&amp;nbsp;** ( **&amp;#160;** ).


*International US number:* +1 958 555 0123

*International UK number:* +44 114 496 0123 Start of pa ge

#### Fictitious

In examples, be sure not to use telephone numbers that might be someone’s actual number.

The 555 preﬁx is used in the US and other countries in the NANP only for operator-assisted information. You can use this preﬁx in examples. Also, area codes 958 and 959 are not allocated and can be used in examples.

In areas in the UK with 3-digit area codes, you can use line numbers 496 0 *xxx* (where *xxx* is any three digits). In other areas, you can use the unused area code 01632; there are no specially allocated line numbers to use with this area code. For London numbers, you can use 020 7946 0 *xxx* . (Note that the sequence of digits 946 is not the same as the sequence 496 used elsewhere). For ﬁctitious cell (mobile) phone numbers, use 07700 900 *xxx* . Fictitious toll-free (freephone) numbers are 0808 157 0 *xxx* , and premium rate numbers are 0909 879 0 *xxx* .

(The preceding examples, except 1-800-IBM-4YOU, also all use ﬁctitious numbers.)


*Fictitious US number* : 555-4385

*Fictitious UK number:* 07700 900461 Start of pa ge

### Units of measurement

State physical measurements by using both the International System of Units (SI) and the United States customary system (American). Use SI multiplier preﬁxes but be careful when using these preﬁxes with bits and bytes.


**The International System of Units** (SI, abbreviated from the French, le Système International d'Unités): This system is a modern version of the metric system and is the most widely used system of measurement. In the United States, see the [National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) website  for details of the standard SI units and their abbreviations and symbols. Note that the SI spelling of the unit of length, and that is used in most countries, is metre, but the variant meter is used in the US, is used throughout these guidelines, and should be used in all IBM content.](http:/physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units)


**United States customary system** (or the American system): This system is the commonly used system of measurement in the US. It is similar, but not identical, to the British Imperial system. They differ primarily in units of volume.

#### General guidelines

In text, show measurements in SI units followed immediately in American system units within parentheses, and to a similar degree of precision.


Form widths can be in the range 88–476 mm (3.5–18.7 in.) for 8-line-per-inch spacing, or 76–609 mm (3.0–24.0 in.) for 6-line-per-inch spacing.


The dimensions of the control unit are as follows: width 520 mm (20.5 in.), depth 410 mm (17 in.), and height 200 mm (8 in.) However, show unique design measurements in SI or American system units only, as appropriate.


8-line-per-inch spacing 16 mm ﬁlm

19-inch standard rack

Do not use a hyphen if the unit is an abbreviation.


The unit weighs 48.2 kg (106.3 lb). a 12 m (39 ft) cable

an 8 ft clearance

a 1 GB memory module

However, if a numeral precedes the number-abbreviation combination and it is not practical to reword the text, hyphenate the number-abbreviation combination.


3,840 4-KB pages

When you use a number with the spelled-out form of a unit of measurement as an adjective, use a hyphen instead of a space between the number and the unit name, unless the number is expressed as a fraction.


12-meter (39-foot) cable an 8-foot clearance

a 5.25-inch clearance a 5-1/4 inch clearance

You can avoid or minimize using decimals for metric values by using smaller units of measurement. For example, you can show a value that is less than a kilogram by using grams or, if appropriate, milligrams. However, use consistent units of measure. For example, do not mix references to centimeters and millimeters or grams and kilograms; use one or the other throughout the topic or section.


The unit is 442 mm (17.4 in.) wide and 58 cm (22.8 in.) deep. The unit is 442 mm (17.4 in.) wide and 580 mm (22.8 in.) deep.

[Start of page](.)

#### Abbreviations

#### 

The abbreviation for a unit of measurement is both singular and plural. For example, the abbreviation mm means both millimeter (1 mm) and millimeters (10 mm).

Do not abbreviate a unit of measurement in general text if no numeric value is associated with it.


Record the size of the package in mm. Record the size of the package in millimeters.


Download times are reduced from 10 ms to less than a ms. Download times are reduced from 10 ms to less than a millisecond.

Omit periods in abbreviations for units of measurement unless they can be confused with words.


bps, cm, in., kg, lbs, rpm, yd [Start of page](.)

##### Units of time

[For comprehensive information about when and which abbreviations to use for date and time units of measurement, see Dates and times.](.)

The following table lists the unit of time abbreviations that are supported.

| **Unit**   | **Abbreviation**   |
|------------|--------------------|
| second     | s                  |
| minute     | min                |
| hour       | h                  |
| day        | d                  |
| week       | wk                 |
| month      | mo                 |
| year       | yr                 |

Table 1. Supported unit of time abbreviations

The abbreviation **s** for second is an SI base unit for time measurement. Although the abbreviations **min** , **h** , and **d** for *minute* , *hour* , and *day* are are not ofﬁcial SI units, they are accepted as common multiples of the SI unit s.


min (= 60 s)


h (= 3600 s)


d (= 86,400 s)

When using the **d** and **h** abbreviations in particular, be sure that it is clear from the context that these units measure time because the abbreviations for day and hour are also symbols that represent SI preﬁxes:


d for deci


h for hecto [Start of page](.)

##### Feet and inches

Do not use a single quotation mark (') for feet or a double quotation mark (") for inches; instead, use ft for feet and in. for inches, or spell out feet and inches.


The storage unit is 3' 2" long. The storage unit is 3 ft 2 in. long.


Use the tray that is 12" wide.

Use the tray that is 12 inches wide.

[Start of page](.)

#### Multiple dimensions

#### 

When you show two or three dimensions in a single expression, use the multiplication sign (× - Unicode character U+00D7) with a space on each side of it. Avoid using the letter *x* as a substitute for the multiplication sign, so that screen readers interpret it correctly. You can insert a multiplication sign in several ways:


As a special character in most editors, including oXygen


As an HTML character ( **&amp;times;** , **&amp;#215;** , or **&amp;#xd7;** )


By typing Alt+0215, using the numeric keypad

Repeat the unit of measure when you present physical dimensions.


26 mm × 45 mm (1.02 in. × 1.77 in.)

4 in. × 6 in. × 12 in.

[Start of page](.)

#### Tolerances

When you show tolerances, place the plus or minus sign (±) next to the tolerance, without spaces. Show all values to a similar degree of precision.


50±5 V DC

76.0±0.2 mm

[Start of page](.)

#### Dimension lines

When you show a dimension line in artwork, show the measurement in SI units above (or to the left of) the line and in the American system units within parentheses immediately below (or to the right of) the line.


76 mm

&lt;———————————————&gt; (3.0 in.)

Where space is a problem, showing both measurements together is also acceptable.


&lt;———————————————&gt;

76 mm (3.0 in.) [Start of page](.)

#### Degree symbol

In text, use the degree symbol (°) to express angles and temperatures. Do not put a space between the number and the degree symbol. Show temperatures in degrees Celsius followed by degrees Fahrenheit in parentheses. Do not put a space between the degree symbol and C or F.


37 ° C (98.6 ° F)

100°C (212°F)

Open the latch 90°.

If the character set for printing or displaying the information does not include the degree symbol, use degrees for angles and degrees Celsius and degrees Fahrenheit for temperatures.


100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit) Open the latch 90 degrees.

[Start of page](.)

#### SI multiplier preﬁxes

There are 20 SI unit of measurement preﬁxes, from yotta (1,024) to yocto (10-24), used to represent multiplying factors. Be aware [that using SI preﬁxes with bits and bytes can be ambiguous and must be handled carefully to avoid confusion. See Multiplier preﬁxes for bits and bytes.](.)

The following table shows the SI preﬁxes and their associated multipliers:

| **Preﬁx**   | **Abbreviation**   | **Power of 10**   | **Multiplier**                    |
|-------------|--------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------------|
| yocto       | y                  | 10-24             | 0.000,000,000,000,000,000,000,001 |
| zepto       | z                  | 10-21             | 0.000,000,000,000,000,000,001     |
| atto        | a                  | 10-18             | 0.000,000,000,000,000,001         |
| femto       | f                  | 10-15             | 0.000,000,000,000,001             |
| pico        | p                  | 10-12             | 0.000,000,000,001                 |
| nano        | n                  | 10-9              | 0.000,000,001                     |
| micro       | µ                  | 10-6              | 0.000,001                         |
| milli       | m                  | 10-3              | 0.001                             |
| centi       | c                  | 10-2              | 0.01                              |
| deci        | d                  | 10-1              | 0.1                               |
|             |                    | 100               | 1                                 |
| deca        | da                 | 101               | 10                                |
| hecto       | h                  | 102               | 100                               |
| kilo        | k                  | 103               | 1,000                             |
| mega        | M                  | 106               | 1,000,000                         |
| giga        | G                  | 109               | 1,000,000,000                     |
| tera        | T                  | 1012              | 1,000,000,000,000                 |
| peta        | P                  | 1015              | 1,000,000,000,000,000             |
| exa         | E                  | 1018              | 1,000,000,000,000,000,000         |
| zetta       | Z                  | 1021              | 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000     |
| yotta       | Y                  | 1024              | 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 |

Table 2. SI multiplier preﬁxes

Follow these guidelines for using SI multiplier preﬁxes:


Preﬁxes are always used in combination with abbreviations of units of measurement, such as m, g, and Hz. Preﬁxes are never used alone or with units that you spell out. In particular, do not use a letter on its own as a multiplier, such as K to represent “thousand” or M to represent “million”.


The world population is about 7 G.

The world population is about 7,000,000,000.


The unit cost of the system is USD 10 K The unit cost of the system is USD 10,000


2 dhours

12 minutes


Leave a space between the number and the preﬁx, but not between the preﬁx and the unit of measurement.


600MHz

600 MHz


64 µ g

64 µg


Do not use combinations of preﬁxes.


7 dcm

7 mm


Do not use a hyphen if the unit is an abbreviation. However, if a numeral precedes the number-abbreviation combination and it is not practical to reword the text, hyphenate the number-abbreviation combination. For example, it is acceptable to refer to “3,840 4-KB pages.”


a 32-KB cluster a 32 KB cluster


Avoid using multiplier preﬁxes with temperatures measured in °C. If you need to express very large or very small temperature units, express them in kelvin (K).


The core temperature of the sun is about 13 M°C. The core temperature of the sun is about 13 MK.

*Note that 0 K is deﬁned as -273.15°C but at very high temperatures, the discrepancy is negligible.*


Use the same unit of measurement consistently in a list of values, unless this results in a very small or very large number, or a user would expect to see a value speciﬁed in a particular measurement. In any case, be consistent within a set of information.


**ABC:** 1 GB

**RST:** 500 MB

**XYZ:** 2 GB


**ABC:** 1 GB

**RST:** 0.5 GB

**XYZ:** 2 GB


For a unit expressed as an exponential, for example the square or cube of a unit, the multiplying preﬁx is understood to be part of the unit. For example, 1 km2 is one square kilometer (1,000 m x 1,000 m), not 1,000 square meters.

#### Multiplier preﬁxes for bits and bytes

SI preﬁxes represent powers of 10 only. However, SI units are often used in information-technology documentation to represent both powers of 2 and powers of 10 when referring to bits and bytes. In these situations, the only distinction has been to use uppercase K to mean 1,024 and lowercase k to mean 1,000. Therefore, KB means 1,024 bytes, and kB means 1,000 bytes. (In SI, the abbreviation of the preﬁx kilo is always lowercase k.)

The following table shows the preﬁxes and their associated multipliers as used in both situations:

| **Preﬁx**   | **Abbreviation**   | **Power of 2**   | **Power of 2 value**                | **Power of 10**   | **Power of 10 value**               |
|-------------|--------------------|------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------------|
| kilo        | K                  | 210 (1,0241)     | 1,024                               | N/A               | Do not use  *K*  to mean 1,000      |
| kilo        | k                  | N/A              | Do not use  *k*  to mean 1,024      | 103 (1,0001)      | 1,000                               |
| mega        | M                  | 220 (1,0242)     | 1,048,576                           | 106 (1,0002)      | 1,000,000                           |
| giga        | G                  | 230 (1,0243)     | 1,073,741,824                       | 109 (1,0003)      | 1,000,000,000                       |
| tera        | T                  | 240 (1,0244)     | 1,099,511,627,776                   | 1012 (1,0004)     | 1,000,000,000,000                   |
| peta        | P                  | 250 (1,0245)     | 1,125,899,906,842,624               | 1015 (1,0005)     | 1,000,000,000,000,000               |
| exa         | E                  | 260 (1,0246)     | 1,152,921,504,606,846,976           | 1018 (1,0006)     | 1,000,000,000,000,000,0  00         |
| zetta       | Z                  | 270 (1,0247)     | 1,180,591,620,717,411,303,  424     | 1021 (1,0007)     | 1,000,000,000,000,000,0  00,000     |
| yotta       | Y                  | 280 (1,0248)     | 1,208,925,819,614,629,174,  706,176 | 1024 (1,0008)     | 1,000,000,000,000,000,0  00,000,000 |

Table 3. Multiplier preﬁxes for bits and bytes

##### IEC preﬁxes


To help avoid inaccuracy (especially with the larger multipliers) and potential ambiguity, the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) in 2000 adopted a set of preﬁxes speciﬁcally for binary multipliers. (See IEC 60027-2.) Their use is now supported by the [United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)  and incorporated into ISO 80000. They are also required by EU law and in certain contexts in the US.](http:/physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

The binary multiples standardized in IEC 60027-2 are based on the SI preﬁxes and symbols for positive powers of 10, as shown in the following table:

| **IEC preﬁx**   | **EIC preﬁx symbol**   |   **Power of 2** | **SI preﬁx**   | **SI preﬁx symbol**   |   **Power of 10** |
|-----------------|------------------------|------------------|----------------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| kibi            | Ki                     |              210 | kilo           | K                     |               103 |
| mebi            | Mi                     |              220 | mega           | M                     |               106 |
| gibi            | Gi                     |              230 | giga           | G                     |               109 |
| tebi            | Ti                     |              240 | tera           | T                     |              1012 |
| pebi            | Pi                     |              250 | peta           | P                     |              1015 |
| exbi            | Ei                     |              260 | exa            | E                     |              1018 |
| zebi            | Zi                     |              270 | zetta          | Z                     |              1021 |
| yobi            | Yi                     |              280 | yotta          | Y                     |              1024 |

Table 4. IEC preﬁxes

You should generally use these unambiguous IEC preﬁxes when referring to “power of 2” multipliers for bits and bytes unless the product itself (for example, in the interface or ﬁrmware) uses SI preﬁxes for this purpose.

##### Using multiplier preﬁxes


In combination with a preﬁx, use B (uppercase) to mean bytes, and use b (lowercase) to mean bits.


Preﬁxes are never used alone or with units that you spell out.


In general, use the abbreviation KiB, not the spelled-out form.


16 Ki

16 Ki bytes

16 kibibytes

16 KiB


If your audience needs to be told the spelled-out form of abbreviations, include the spelled-out form parenthetically on ﬁrst use only, and use only the abbreviation in all other occurrences.


4 gibibits

4 Gib (gibibits)

24 kibps (kibibits per second) [Start of page](.)

##### Deﬁning abbreviations


Depending on your audience, deﬁne each abbreviation that you use in an information product, and include each abbreviation in the index.


You can provide a deﬁnition parenthetically or in a footnote at ﬁrst occurrence. Avoid using numerals for footnotes; the number might be mistaken for an exponent. For details, see the [Footnotes](.) topic.


A minimum of 64 KiB (where KiB equals 1,024 bytes) is reserved for the nonpageable dynamic area. The computer supports 4 GiB† DIMMs.


† For real and virtual storage, GiB means 1,073,741,824 bytes.  The computer comes with a 1 GB† hard disk drive.

† For hard disk drive capacity, GB means 1,000,000,000 bytes; total accessible capacity can vary by operating environment.


Alternatively, you can deﬁne number abbreviations in the glossary or in general notes.


**MB**

When referring to hard disk drive capacity or communications volume, 1,000,000 bytes.


**MiB**

When referring to processor storage, real and virtual storage, or channel volume, 1,048,576 bytes.


**kibps**

1,024 bits (1 kibibit) per second.


When referring to processor storage, real and virtual storage, or channel volume, KiB means 1,024 bytes, MiB means 1,048,576 bytes, and GiB means 1,073,741,824 bytes.


When referring to hard disk drive capacity or communications volume, MB means 1,000,000 bytes, and GB means 1,000,000,000 bytes. Total user-accessible capacity can vary depending on the operating environment.


In general use and contexts where it is not necessary to be precise, you can deﬁne the abbreviations approximately.


KB equals approximately 1,000 bytes, and MB equals approximately 1,000,000 bytes [Start of page](.)

Apply the following structure and guidelines when you create books.
