#### Sequence of book elements

Place elements in the following order in books and publications that follow the book structure. [Front matter](.)

1. [Front cover](.)
2. [Table of contents](.)
3. [List of ﬁgures](.) (Optional)
4. [List of tables](.) (Optional: Can be combined with the list of ﬁgures)
5. [Preface](.) (Usually titled “About this publication” or “About this information”)
6. [Publication guide diagram](.) (If applicable)
7. [Summary of changes](.) (Optional)
8. [Deﬁnition of symbols](.) (Optional) [Body content](.)

[Back matter](.)

1. [Appendixes](.) , including an appendix titled “Accessibility” (Unless the required accessibility information is included elsewhere)
2. [Hardware warranty](.) (If applicable)
3. [Notices](.)
4. [Glossary](.) (Optional)
5. [Bibliography](.) (Optional)
6. [Index](.)
7. [Back cover](.)

**Note:** The inclusion of optional elements is determined by the organization and type of information.

#### General elements

##### Form numbers

Form numbers are assigned to items, including publications, that can be ordered from IBM. Contact your Controlling Party if you need to have a form number assigned to a deliverable. *Order number* is a synonym for *form number* . They should appear both on the front cover and on the back cover, immediately above the barcode.

**Note:** The form number may be referenced under another name within your authoring tool. For example, DITA tagging refers to form numbers as **&lt;booknumber&gt;** .

##### Page numbers

Use consecutive pagination through an entire book, excluding only the front matter. Use lowercase Roman numerals for pages in the front matter. Do not include page numbers on title pages, copyright pages, and blank pages.

###### Exceptions:

- In a book that contains education material, you can number pages by chapter (known as folio-by-chapter numbering) to distinguish lectures, exercises, or appendixes, and to indicate the sequence of activities. For example, in a book that contains exercises, Exercise 1 might be numbered from page 1-1 to page 1-n, Exercise 2 from page 2-1 to page 2-n, and so on. Do not use folio-by-chapter numbering in the front matter.
- Use folio-by-chapter numbering in situations in which one book is published with several languages in the same book. Because each language can take a different number of pages and the writer creates only one language version of the information, the writer cannot know how many pages are in each translated chapter.

##### Publication dates

#### Front matter

##### 1 Front cover

##### 2 Title page

- Product documentation

- IBM Developer

- Updated the accessibility information to include information about pausing or hiding the animation, in addition to stopping it.

A title page should be used in a book that has a separate cover.

##### Titles

Create titles consistently within a product library. A title must indicate the tasks that users can accomplish by reading the book or indicate other speciﬁc information that the book contains. Include the following elements in each title:

- The product name, including the name of the operating system or systems, if any
- A term or terms that describe the supported tasks or other speciﬁc information that the book contains (for example,

*Administration, Planning and Installing, User’s* , or *Using* )

- Optionally, another term that indicates the type of information (for example, *Guide* or *Reference* )
- In education material, the document type is provided as a separate ﬁeld, such as *Course Exercises Guide* or *Lab Setup Guide*

You can place the task description and any function indication before or after the product name.


IBM TS3500 Tape Library Introduction and Planning Guide\_ DB2 Workload Management Guide and Reference

Installation instructions for IBM Business Process Manager 8.5 Refresh Pack 6

Use the full, ofﬁcial product name in a book title as explained in the [Product and service names](.) topic.

**Note:** Include the version and release in the short title of an online book because they are used to identify the level of the book.

Generally, do not use the version and release in the title of a printed book, but include the version and release on the cover and title page.

Terminology guidance:

- Use the term *guide* to refer to information that describes tasks.
- Use the term *reference* to refer to information that is organized for easy or frequent retrieval.
- Use the term *best practice* with caution, to recommend a procedure to solve a problem or achieve a speciﬁc outcome. Otherwise, it can imply that information in other content types is less valuable. Also, your team or organization becomes obligated to ensure that anything it asserts as a best practice is still supported and correct. Instead, write more descriptive text to guide the user.

Start of pa ge

##### 3 Back of title page

This page includes any edition or special notices.

##### Edition notice

The edition notice is displayed on the back of the title page, or in online books, immediately after the title page.

If you use Digital Content Services tools, you can use an edition notices template ﬁle in the DITATools\oxygenAuthor\samples directory. Do not modify the text in the edition notice, except for options that are available in the template, without consulting your legal department.

**Important:** Unless your documentation library has no other method by which to distinguish one iteration of a publication from another, do not include any edition number or date in edition notices, for example, “Second edition (June 2012)”. Inaccurate or misleading edition numbers cause rejections when IBM documentation is submitted to the Library of Congress for copyright

registration. IBM Intellectual Property and Licensing has agreed that these elements are not required. However, be sure that edition notices show accurate copyright dates, because that information is critical to protecting IBM copyright.

##### Special notices

Hardware products typically require a reference to safety and environmental notices. You can use a boxed notice for this reference. The current template, named bookeditionnotice.dita, is in the DITATools\oxygenAuthor\samples directory.

***Note*** *Before you use this information and the product it supports, read the information in “Safety and environmental notices” on page x and “Notices” on page x.*

##### 4 Table of contents

Use the title “Contents” for the table of contents. Check your stylesheet for your information set to determine how many levels of headings to include in the table of contents for your book.

Generally, select a number of heading levels so that you do not have more than one contents page per 50 pages of text. In a large book, it is sometimes useful to have a partial table of contents for each part or even for each chapter.

Use leader dots in the table of contents.

##### 5 List of ﬁgures

Figures can include an illustration, a chart, a screen capture, or a photograph. Consider the following criteria when you determine whether to include a ﬁgure list:

- Consistency. If other books in the information set use a list of ﬁgures, your book should include one also.
- Number of ﬁgures. If you have a large number of ﬁgures, include a list.
- Placement of ﬁgures. If the ﬁgures in your book are not always placed at the point in text where they are pertinent, include a list.

When you use a ﬁgure list, follow these guidelines:

- Use the title “Figures” for the ﬁgure list.
- Do not repeat the word Figure in any entry in the ﬁgure list.
##### 6 List of tables

Consider the following criteria when you determine whether to include a table list:

- Consistency. If other books in the information set use a list of tables, your book should include one also.
- Number of tables. If you have a large number of tables, include a list.
- Placement of tables. If the tables in your book are not always placed at the point in text where they are pertinent, include a list.

When you use a table list, follow these guidelines:

- Use the title “Tables” for the table list.
- Do not repeat the word Table in any entry in the table list.
##### 7 Preface

Include a preface or an introductory chapter to introduce the book’s content and conventions. You can use the following headings or others; use consistent headings in an information set.

If your information is delivered primarily online or in a format that does not support a preface, consider incorporating one or more of the following elements as topics.

***Title:*** Usually titled **About this publication** or **About this information**

Start the preface with a brief description of the book (not the product). Orient the reader to the purpose and contents of the book. Include information such as supported tasks, level of detail, and what the reader will learn or be able to do as a result of reading the book. Also explain what the book does not contain, if it is likely that readers are expecting something that is not covered, and include where to ﬁnd that information.

***Subtopic*** **: Intended audience**

Describe the intended audience for the book in terms of roles; for example, system administrators or programmers. Provide information about what the reader is assumed to already know. This knowledge might be as general as being familiar with the system, display, keyboard, and printers, or as speciﬁc as being familiar with certain aspects of a product.

***Subtopic*** \_ (Unless covered elsewhere in the front matter)\_ **: Conventions and terminology**

Explain any special style conventions, terminology, notices, or presentation techniques that are used in the book, such as naming conventions for programming languages, or other visual cues to help the reader ﬁnd and recognize information. If you include only conventions and not terminology, or vice versa, change the title of this subdivision accordingly (for example, “Terminology used in this book”). If the book includes icons, special fonts, colors, or other visual cues to help readers ﬁnd and recognize information, explain these conventions or include in a separate section in the front matter, unless they are industry-standard conventions.

###### Subtopic: Prerequisite and related information

Be sure to separate required reading and related information. Include the titles and order numbers of all IBM publications. If only parts of the listed prerequisites are required reading, name the speciﬁc subjects. If the book has a bibliography, refer to the bibliography instead of listing the publications in this subtopic.

***Other subtopics*** *(Optional):* Use headings that reflect the information in the section. Do not include information that is not about the book, such as product or component descriptions.

####### Acknowledgments

Acknowledgments of contributors are not appropriate in most IBM publications. Much of the content that IBM produces comes from the company and not an individual.

**Exceptions:** It is acceptable and expected to include contributors' names on white papers. Authors' names are also often indicated in IBM Redbooks publications and in articles published on the IBM Developer website. You can include the authors' information, such as job titles and contact details. Check the stylesheet for your information set to determine whether to include acknowledgment information.

##### 8 Publication guide diagram

Some IBM books provide a publication guide diagram, which shows the interrelationships of the books in a library and how they relate to user tasks. The diagram also indicates the sequence in which the publications should be read.

##### 9 Summary of changes

The front matter can include a summary of the changes that occurred between publications. Often, statements about changes to the book are presented with the statements about changes to the product. If publishing previous summaries of changes is useful to customers, place the summaries of changes in reverse order, starting with the most recent. Do not include revision bars.

When a book contains a summary of changes to the product, place it after the preface. Do not place a description of changes to the product in the preface.

##### 10 Deﬁnition of symbols

Some IBM manuals list symbols that are used in diagrams in a separate element of the front matter. If the symbols only appear in one chapter, deﬁne them in the introductory text of the chapter in which they occur. Otherwise, include deﬁnitions in the “Conventions and terminology” section of the preface.

#### Body content

#### 

##### Divisions

Some books divide content into sections, chapters, or parts. Do not use the word section in the titles of parts or chapters of a book.

If a publication is divided into separate volumes, treat each volume as a separate book, and include all required book elements in each volume.

##### Parts and part titles

Divide a book into parts if a logical grouping of related chapters makes the information in the book easier to understand and retrieve. For example, an application programming guide and reference could have guidance information as Part 1 and reference information as Part 2.

Do not divide a book into parts if the main text is one part and the appendixes and back matter are the only other parts.

A part title consists of the word Part, an Arabic numeral followed by a period, and descriptive wording. Like other headings, the part title should follow sentence-style capitalization rules.

##### Chapter titles

A chapter title consists of the word Chapter, an Arabic numeral followed by a period, and descriptive wording. Like other headings, the chapter title should follow sentence-style capitalization rules. Chapter numbers simplify cross-references and make it easier for the reader to ﬁnd headings.

**Exception:** In a book that contains education material, the ﬁrst word of a chapter title can be *Unit* or *Module* if it is an instructional lecture, or *Exercise* if it is an activity for students to practice what they learned.

You can subdivide a unit or module into *Topic* or *Lesson\_headings* , or an exercise into *Part* or *Section headings* , if two or more subdivisions are used.


In each case, use of the ﬁrst word must be consistent for all content within an education curriculum.  Chapter 4. Using the IBM Storage Provider for VMware VASA


Part 2. Database conﬁguration

Follow the *Chicago Manual of Style* practice of numbering chapters consecutively; do not begin with Chapter 1 in each part. Follow this practice in both a modular book (a book that can be divided into portions for ﬁling in other books) and a nonmodular book (one that is not divided).

If you divide a book into parts, you can present the appendixes and back matter in either of the following ways:


Present the appendixes as a separate part (titled “Part n. Appendixes”) and the glossary, bibliography, and index in another part (titled “Part n+1. Glossary, Bibliography, Index”).


Present the appendixes and back matter in one part (titled “Part n. Appendixes, Glossary, Bibliography, Index”). This method is preferable if there is only one appendix.

##### Headers and footers

Headers and footers help readers easily locate their place in the book. As the names imply, headers are displayed at the top of a page, and footers are displayed at the bottom.

**Headers:** The use of headers is optional. Use headers to help readers ﬁnd information quickly. If you use headers, follow these guidelines:


Do not duplicate the chapter title.


Use header text that is most helpful to the reader. When there is more than one heading level on a page, use the most meaningful text as the header.


Do not use headers when the header changes on every page.


Indicate the content that is described on the page. The wording of the header must correspond to the text heading, but does not have to be identical.


Use headers throughout a book, not just in speciﬁc chapters.

If your authoring tool supports the process, omit headers from these pages:


Part title pages


Chapter title pages


Any page that displays the equivalent of a chapter title, such as the ﬁrst page of the table of contents, preface, appendix, notices, glossary, and bibliography.

However, you can use a header on a page that contains only an illustration or a table. The material in the illustration or table should pertain to the topic of the header.

**Footers** : Footers are required and are usually generated for the copyright notice, the book title, and the chapter title by your authoring tool. If they are not, use the following format:


The footer for the copyright notice must be displayed on any page that includes the equivalent of a chapter title, such as the ﬁrst page of the table of contents, preface, appendix, notices, glossary, and bibliography.


The footer for the book title must be displayed on the left page following the equivalent of a chapter title.


The footer for the chapter title must be displayed on the right page following the equivalent of a chapter title.

**Exception:** Footer requirements might vary for online and education books, which might no longer distinguish between left and right pages.

#### Back matter

##### 11 Appendixes

An appendix consists of material that supports the information in the book but that is not required for the user to accomplish tasks or to understand the material in the body of the book. In education material, an appendix includes any content that is not directly covered in class. Appendixes can be placed after the last chapter in the book, in the order in which they are referred to in the body. If you divide a book into parts, place the appendixes and back matter in a separate part (titled “Part\_ n.\_ Appendixes”) to include all appendixes, the glossary, the bibliography, and the index.

When a book has only one appendix, the title is “Appendix”, followed by a period and descriptive wording. When a book has more than one appendix, each appendix title is “Appendix”, followed by a capital letter (starting with A), a period, and descriptive wording.


Appendix A. Performance considerations Appendix B. Conversion tables

**Exception:** If the Notices section is an appendix instead of a separate division, it must be the last appendix. [Start of page](.)

##### 12 Hardware warranty

Consult your organization for the current and required hardware warranty for your book. [Start of page](.)

##### 13 Notices

Legal notices protect IBM assets. Consult your legal department for the current and required notices for your book. [Start of page](.)

##### 14 Glossary


Producing a glossary is mandatory for all products. However, including a glossary in your book is optional. For details, see [Glossaries](.) and [IBM Content: Terminology &gt;Glossaries .](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/en/technical-content?topic=standards-terminology&glossaries)

[Start of page](.)

##### 15 Bibliography

A bibliography is not required, but it is recommended for a book that contains a long list of related publications. Related publications include publications that are cited in the text of the book as containing more information about speciﬁc topics and publications that,

although they are not cited in the text, deal with the same subject as the book. List titles of prerequisite publications in the preface or introductory chapter, regardless of whether they are cited in the bibliography.

Do not use a short bibliography at the end of each chapter unless the information is modular and the chapters are included in other publications.

You can design the bibliography to associate short titles (which are used in the text) with the full titles (and IBM form numbers, where applicable) of the publications.

M Carey, et al., *Developing Quality Technical Information: A Handbook for Writers and Editors* , SC26-4195, 3rd edition: IBM Press, 2014. **Short title:** DQTI

You can provide an annotation with each title to explain the relationship of the cited publication to the book in which it is cited. In the annotation, avoid value judgments such as “useful”, “good”, and “indispensable”.

You can format an annotation in either of the following ways. Use the same format for all citations in the bibliography.

- The title in the ﬁrst sentence of the annotation

*IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator Reference Guide* , SC23-6562-00, contains the information that you need to develop solutions using components that are part of the IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator. This book is intended for those responsible for the development, installation, and administration of solutions with the IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator.

- The title on a separate line that precedes the annotation

*IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator Reference Guide,* SC23-6562-00

This book contains the information that you need to develop solutions using components that are part of the IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator. This book is intended for those responsible for the development, installation, and administration of solutions with the IBM Tivoli Directory Integrator.

##### 16 Index

##### 17 Back cover

For information about adding content to the back cover and delivery formats, see *Creating a DITA bookmap for DCS* .

The country of origin statement is a legal requirement for hardcopy material that will be delivered to clients. If material is available only via download, then the country of origin statement is not required. Refer to your product offering team to conﬁrm the requirement for your documentation.

The default country of origin statement is “Printed in USA”. IBM internal printers and vendor printers outside the USA change “Printed in USA” as appropriate; therefore, this is taken care of by the printers as part of the manufacturing process.

Non-US manufacturing reviewers ensure that the country of origin conforms to the IBM speciﬁcations. In cases where books are printed only in a non-US location, it is acceptable to edit the default text (for example, “Printed in Ireland” if a book is printed only in that country.)

It is not necessary to delete the country of origin for online material or PDF ﬁles. Do not create one version with the country of origin and another without it.

### Examples

Use a consistent approach for examples throughout your information, whether they are inline examples or stand-alone example sections.

#### Contents


[Inline examples](.)


[Stand-alone examples](.)

#### Inline examples

To introduce an inline example, always use the text *for example* or *such as* . Never use the phrase *for instance* or the Latin abbreviations *e.g.* or *i.e.*

If the example is an independent clause, use the text *for example* and one of the following approaches:


Use a semicolon before *for example* , and use a comma after *for example* .


Enter a command, for example, type **SETUP** . Enter a command; for example, type **SETUP** .


Start a new sentence with *For example* , and use a comma after *For example* .


You can insert a line break, for example, you can use the **&lt;br/&gt;** element. You can insert a line break. For example, you can use the **&lt;br/&gt;** element.

If the example is not an independent clause, use one of the following approaches:


Use a comma before and after *for example* .


Specify a platform; for example, z/OS. Specify a platform, for example, z/OS.


Use the text *such as* , but do not include a comma after *such as* .


Specify a platform, such as, z/OS. Specify a platform, such as z/OS.


Rewrite the phrase as an independent clause, and follow the guidance for independent clauses.


Specify a platform. For example, z/OS. Specify a platform. For example, specify z/OS.

If the example is an inline list or series, use one of the following approaches:


Use a comma before and after *for example* .


Specify a font, for example, Arial, Courier, or Helvetica.


Use the text *such as* , but do not include a comma after *such as* .  Specify a font, such as Arial, Courier, or Helvetica.


Rewrite the sentence to include an independent clause, and follow the guidance for independent clauses.  Specify a font; for example, specify Arial, Courier, or Helvetica.

[Start of page](.)

#### Stand-alone examples

Use a consistent approach for stand-alone examples within an information set. For example, if examples are indented, ensure that the indentation is consistent.

If examples are included in separate headed sections, ensure that the subheadings are consistent. Where possible, use standard tagging to ensure consistency.


**Example**

**SELECT FLOOR( 3.5),**

**FLOOR(3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.5)**

###### FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1a

If text is used to introduce a stand-alone example, use a complete sentence to introduce the example. Do not start a sentence before an example and continue the sentence after the example. End the sentence with a colon unless other sentences intervene between the introductory sentence and the example; in that case, end each sentence with a period.


The following example uses the FLOOR function, which returns the largest integer value that is less than or equal to the argument:

**SELECT FLOOR( 3.5),**

**FLOOR(3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.5)**

**FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1**

### Figures

Use ﬁgures to clarify or complement information. Figures include nontextual visual elements such as graphics, drawings, photographs, icons, illustrations, and screen captures.

#### Contents


[Captions](.)


[Numbering](.)


[References](.)


[Placement](.)


[Callouts](.)


[Screen captures](.)


[Maps](.)


[Alternative text](.)

#### Captions

Place the ﬁgure caption below the ﬁgure. A ﬁgure caption can include a ﬁgure number and text. Use sentence style [capitalization](.) for captions. Depending on the context, you might choose to omit the ﬁgure number or the text. When you use captions in your information, use them consistently for all ﬁgures.

Figure captions are required in the following situations:


When you must refer to the ﬁgures by a caption, such as in a table of contents or in a link


When the ﬁgures are complex and require explanation


When the ﬁgures are not self-explanatory or are not explained in the surrounding text Otherwise, ﬁgure captions are optional.

**Format recommendation:** Some authoring tools apply a default format to ﬁgure captions. If you apply the format manually, use italic font and insert a period between the ﬁgure number and the text. See speciﬁc guidance for [Mobile](.) .

Use one of the following types of text in ﬁgure captions:


Fragment: If you can describe a ﬁgure briefly and clearly, use a fragment (less than a complete sentence). Apply sentence-style capitalization. Do not start the fragment with a deﬁnite or indeﬁnite article. Do not insert a period (.) at the end.


*Figure 22. The functions of the assembler. Figure 22. Functions of the assembler*


Complete sentence: If you must provide a more detailed explanation in the caption, use one or more complete sentences. Apply sentence-style capitalization and punctuation.


*Figure 22. The assembler converts the source program into an object program.*


Combined fragment and complete sentence: If a ﬁgure requires a very detailed explanation, begin the caption text with a fragment and then continue with one or more sentences. Use sentence-style capitalization. Insert a period after the fragment and after each sentence.


*Figure 22. Functions of the assembler. The assembler converts the source program into an object program.*

In the caption text, do not include the word *ﬁgure* , *table* , *chart* , or any other word that is redundant within the caption.


*Figure 6. Illustration of component relationships Figure 6. Component relationships ﬁgure*

*Figure 6. Component relationships*

If a ﬁgure is long and prints on more than one page, repeat the caption on successive pages.

Each section of the ﬁgure should contain some designation to indicate that it spans more than one page. The preferred method is to include *(Part x of y)* at the end of the ﬁgure number. However, you might have to use another method, such as *(continued)* , depending on the tool that you are using.

Use a colon to separate a caption and subcaption.


*Figure 4. Scenario 1: The Department A client Figure 5. Scenario 2: The Department B client*

[Start of page](.)

#### Numbering

Make sure the numbers you use for ﬁgures are consecutive and consistent throughout your documentation, including ﬁgures in the appendixes. Your environment and tools might number ﬁgures differently. While it’s not obligatory to specify numbers for ﬁgures, use the convention that best matches the documentation style. See speciﬁc guidance for [Numbers](.) .

Always consider the [IBM Accessibility](https:/www.ibm.com/able) content requirement for [Figure and table captions](https:/www.ibm.com/able/toolkit/design/content/#figure-and-table-captions) . If your users are printing hard copies of a PDF ﬁle, including numbers is recommended to help with manual navigation between ﬁgures.

If a ﬁgure must be split into two or more parts, qualify the ﬁgure number as shown in the following example.


*Figure 7 (Part 1 of 3). Use of IF statements Figure 7 (Part 2 of 3). Use of IF statements Figure 7 (Part 3 of 3). Use of IF statements*

The separate parts of such ﬁgures must have the same caption text. If different caption text is necessary, create the parts as separate ﬁgures.

If your authoring tool numbers ﬁgures by starting with *Figure 1* in each separate web-based topic, consider not numbering your ﬁgures. If your documentation for ﬁgures uses links or cross-references, use those instead of numbers.

[Start of page](.)

#### References

When you refer to ﬁgures in text, use correct [capitalization](.) and appropriate placement.

Use regular text instead of an inline link when a reference is near a ﬁgure. Always introduce a ﬁgure with a sentence that immediately precedes it. If you present the same type of information in two or more consecutive ﬁgures, you do not have to introduce each speciﬁc ﬁgure, but you must introduce the group of ﬁgures.

Use a period or a colon after the introduction to a ﬁgure. Either punctuation mark is correct if it follows a complete sentence. Choose the punctuation mark that best suits the context. For example, you might use a colon if the introduction immediately leads in to the item that follows. Use a period if the introduction is more descriptive or is interrupted by an intervening sentence. In your information set, be consistent with the punctuation marks that you apply for the context.


You can modify any of the properties that are included in the following ﬁgure:

Figure 10 shows results from the ﬁrst test and ﬁgure 11 shows results from the second test. The results in both ﬁgures are accurate to two decimal points.

In text references, when a reference is not near a ﬁgure, include the word *ﬁgure* . (Italic is used here for emphasis; do not use italic in your text references.)

If a document has both ﬁgures and tables and they are labeled as such, include the page numbers or hypertext links in cross-references to them in the text. Do this only when it is not possible to use regular text to refer to the ﬁgure or table. This retrievability aid helps the reader to distinguish between *ﬁgure x* and *table x* references. If your text formatter cannot provide the page numbers or hypertext links in cross-references to ﬁgures and tables, consider captioning them all as ﬁgures and numbering them in a single sequence.

It is not necessary to use a cross-reference to a ﬁgure in text if the ﬁgure is not referred to, or if it is referred to in such a way that the ﬁgure can be identiﬁed without a number.

Enclose a subheading for a ﬁgure caption in parentheses and add it to the end of the caption text.


*Figure 7. Run times for test programs (in microseconds) Figure 8. Real storage requirements (KB equals 1,024 bytes)*

If parts of a ﬁgure are labeled, use sentence-style capitalization for the labels.


Client code

iSeries or zSeries server [Start of page](.)

#### Placement

Place a ﬁgure as close as possible to the principal reference to it.


If the reference and the ﬁgure are in the same topic, implement one of these solutions:

- When the reference is close to the ﬁgure, use a text reference. For example, write “For a complete list of requirements, see the following ﬁgure.”
- When the reference is not close to the ﬁgure, create a link to the ﬁgure. For example, write “For a complete list of requirements, see *Process steps* .”

If the ﬁgure is on a separate page or in a separate topic, use a link to the page or topic that contains the ﬁgure. [Start of page](.)

#### Callouts

When you include ﬁgures in information, you can include brief words or symbols that are connected by lines or arrows to parts of a ﬁgure. These *callouts* provide immediate information about parts of the ﬁgure. Use sentence-style capitalization for callouts.

If you number callouts, start with the callout in the upper-left corner of the ﬁgure and number the callouts clockwise. If the callouts are in a row, number them from left to right. If the callouts are in a column, number them from top to bottom.


*Example of callouts*


When you number ﬁgures that indicate steps in a procedure, display the steps in the sequence in which they are performed. To avoid confusion with the steps in a procedure, you can use letters to identify the callouts.

#### Screen captures

Copying user interface elements in a form that readers can use as visual reference can help provide orientation, reduce confusion, and increase retrievability. The decision to include screen captures can be complex, and you might want to consult your translation coordinator, information architect, management, and other interested parties as you consider the issues that are involved.

Do not translate or mirror screen captures. Capture the images from the national language versions of your product. Follow all international design guidelines for graphics, including guidelines that relate to cultural issues, acceptable graphic ﬁle formats, and expansion guidelines to ensure that the amount of space required for text is available.

Screen captures can be useful and successful when they achieve one or more of these objectives:


Illustrate a user interface that is complex or difﬁcult to explain in text


Help the user ﬁnd a small element in a complex user interface


Provide accessibility alternatives


Show the results of a series of steps or user actions


Orient readers who are reading the publication without the user interface in front of them Screen captures can be less successful in these situations:


Too many are used; for example, they are used to document the interface, as opposed to documenting the tasks that users want to do.


They are used inconsistently, for example, by providing screen captures for some complex processes and no screen captures for others.


Simple user interfaces are displayed that provide no additional help for the user.


Inappropriate borders, highlighting, or other added design elements inhibit quick identiﬁcation.


Poor-quality captures are used.

Consider these issues when you create screen captures:


The ease of creating translated screen captures


The accuracy of screen captures


Maintenance in future releases

Think about potential legal considerations for content that might be the intellectual property of another company. For example, [before including screen captures of UIs from third-party products, you must obtain the required permission. See Republishing existing  content.](.)

When you decide to include screen captures, follow these guidelines:


Use captures of windows and other user interface elements sparingly.


Include the cursor, mouse pointer, or menus only when their presence is signiﬁcant.


Capture just the part of the screen or window that users must focus on.


Show the user interface elements exactly as they are displayed for most users for quick recognition.


Keep your captures in proportion to each other.


Annotate screen captures where it helps the reader ﬁnd a user interface element.


Note the user interface actions that are required for each capture and any system prerequisites that are required to duplicate the data. Share these detailed instructions with translators and language testers.

#### Maps

Because national boundaries are contested in some areas, if you include a geographic map that outlines country borders, include a reference to the source of the map. Otherwise, include the following disclaimer:

###### This map might not reflect actual political or geographic boundaries.

#### Alternative text

LLM helper A graphic image must never be the only way of presenting important information. Describe in text the information that is expressed in the graphic. Unless the graphic is purely decorative, a graphic image requires a description in the alt attribute of the image element. For complex graphics that are described in the surrounding text, include a short summary in the alt value ( **alt="Bar graph of sales for 2024."** ).

If the graphic is decorative and conveys no information, the alt value can be null ( **alt=""** ).

*Tip for writers working with DITA in Oxygen* : To add the **alt=""** attribute to an element, you must change editor modes in Oxygen from Author to Text, and then add the attribute. For example, **&lt;image href="images/my-file.svg alt="" /&gt;** . When you try to add an alt attribute with no value in Author mode, the attribute is not saved.


For information about creating alternative text, see [Alternative text for visuals  at the IBM Accessibility site.](https:/www.ibm.com/able/toolkit/design/content/#alternative-text-for-visuals)

### Glossaries

A glossary includes terms that are new to the intended audience and terms that are used in a way that is speciﬁc to the product.

In content, do not highlight a term in italic font because it is included in the glossary; only apply italic font if the term is deﬁned immediately in that context.


When you create a glossary, follow these general guidelines. Sorting and formatting are applied automatically if you generate a glossary from the [IBM Terminology export site .](https:/ibm.biz/glossaries)

| **Item**      | **Guideline**                          |
|---------------|----------------------------------------|
| Abbreviations | Include abbreviations in the glossary. |

| **Item**        | **Guideline**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Capitalization  | Do not capitalize a term in the glossary unless it is a proper noun.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Indexing        | Do not index the glossary.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Title           | Use “Glossary of terms and abbreviations” or “Glossary”.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

### Headings

Organize text in a logical way within a hierarchy of headings.

#### Contents


[Dividing  information](.)


[Capitalization](.)


[Highlighting](.)


[Numbering](.)


[Punctuation](.)


[Wording](.)

#### Dividing information

Follow these general rules for subdividing text and creating headings:


Divide content only when two or more subsections are required. In other words, do not create subsection A unless the content also requires a subsection B.


Do not place one heading directly after another. Ensure that each heading is followed by text, or consider whether one heading can be removed. If the text that separates the headings is trivial, one of the headings is likely unnecessary.

#### Capitalization

For guidance on how to capitalize headings, see [Capitalization: Headings, titles, and banners](.) .

#### Highlighting


Ensure that the typographic style is consistent for each heading level in your content. When possible, use semantic tagging and style sheets to apply consistent highlighting automatically. For example, in DITA, use **&lt;title&gt;** elements rather than simulating subheadings with **&lt;p&gt;** and **&lt;b&gt;** tags.


Apply IBM Style highlighting guidelines to all elements in a heading unless your authoring tool does not allow it or the highlighting would make the heading inconsistent with other parts of your information. For example, use bold monospace to highlight a command name in a heading.


Mapping assets by using the cf map-route command Mapping assets by using the **cf map-route** command

#### Numbering


Generally, do not number headings, other than chapter titles. However, you can use numbering to aid retrievability, to indicate a sequence, or when it is required by the guidelines for a particular type of content.


In a book that contains education material, you can number the headings of *Unit* , *Module* , or *Exercise* chapters and the next highest level of headings within them, but do not number the headings of further subdivisions. Make the numbering style consistent within an education curriculum.

|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

#### Punctuation


Do not end a heading with a period or colon.


Separate a heading from a subheading by using a colon. Do not use dashes or parentheses for this purpose. Begin a subheading after a colon with a capital letter, regardless of whether the heading uses sentence-style or headline-style [capitalization](.) .


Conﬁguring Maximo database properties - WebSphere Application Server Conﬁguring Maximo database properties (WebSphere Application Server) Conﬁguring Maximo database properties: WebSphere Application Server Plug and receptacle types: By model

Plug and receptacle types: By country or region


Consider whether a heading requires a subheading or can be written as a single heading.


*Subheading:* Conﬁguring Maximo database properties: WebSphere Application Server

*Single heading:* Conﬁguring Maximo database properties for WebSphere Application Server [Start of page](.)

#### Wording

#### 


Make headings brief, descriptive, grammatically parallel, and, if possible, task oriented.


For a task procedure heading, use a gerund or imperative verb form. Use a gerund for a high-level task such as installing, administering, or troubleshooting. Use either a gerund or an imperative verb form for the subtasks of a high-level task. A gerund implies that a task is not necessarily mandatory, but rather that the task applies only if it is what the reader wants to do (for example, “Deleting obsolete entries”). The imperative voice is more prescriptive and implies that a step is mandatory (for example, “Ensure that prerequisite software is installed”). The imperative voice is also preferable for subtask headings that are used to create a list of steps in what is a larger procedure, such as a series of installation steps.

Examples that use a gerund:


Creating a data load activity Building an API response

Setting the active build conﬁguration Examples that use an imperative verb form:


Ensure that prerequisite software is installed Clean up your environment


For conceptual and reference information, use noun phrases for headings.


Track types Query language

Platform and application integration


If a heading is about a single item, use the singular form. If a heading is about a group of items, use the plural form.


Unpacking the system

Uninstalling an app *(When only one app can be uninstalled at a time, even if this procedure can be repeated to uninstall more apps)*


Deleting ﬁles *(When several ﬁles can be selected, then deleted by a single action)*


If the subject is a functional overview, end the heading with words such as *Introduction* or *Overview* rather than contriving a pseudo-task-oriented heading.


Learning about the installation process Installation overview


Understanding text analytics Overview of text analytics


Put important words ﬁrst in headings. In titles, include keywords as early as possible to improve search engine optimization. Writing keywords ﬁrst also makes information easier to scan and keeps important information visible when titles are truncated to accommodate smaller screens.


The business process management system Business process management


Interoperability of transparent cloud tiering with other features Transparent cloud tier support


Use “question-style” headings sparingly and only when appropriate. For example, a heading that uses a question is probably not appropriate for a topic that describes a task or procedure, that provides reference information, or that explains concepts. However, it might be appropriate for the following types of information:


Tutorials

What is a client program?


How-to documents How do I ...?


Video titles

When should you install a client?

Do not use closed-ended questions (questions that can be answered with “yes” or “no”) in headings. See speciﬁc guidance for [Marketing](.) .

[Start of page](.)

### Highlighting

Use highlighting such as italics, bold or underline to distinguish between and emphasize elements in text. If you are referring to an element that should be highlighted in bold, italics, or monospace but your writing tool does not support rich text, you can use double quotation marks or asterisks for emphasis.

The following tables list the highlighting conventions for IBM content. The ﬁrst table is organized by element, and the second table is organized by the highlighting style to use.

#### Contents


[Highlighting  by element](.)


[Highlighting  by style](.)

You might have to make judgment calls about some highlighting situations such as matching the style of existing information or following product style conventions. Do not highlight any element that is not shown in these tables.


Do not use color as the only way to convey meaning; information that is conveyed by color should also be evident when it’s rendered without color. Make sure that there is sufﬁcient contrast between text and the page background, and that the contrast is maintained when the page is rendered without color. For more information, see the [Accessibility Center Documentation Checklist .](https:/www.ibm.com/able/guidelines/ci162/accessibility_checklist.html)

For information that is written only for the web, you can use bold instead of italic.

**Tagging consideration:** Always use the semantic tagging of your authoring tool to produce the correct output. This practice ensures that entities are highlighted consistently and improves translation. For example, to highlight a user interface control in DITA, use the element, not the **&lt;b&gt;** element.

### Lists

Use a vertical list to visually organize a long series at the end of a sentence or a series of parallel sentences or paragraphs. Lists can make information easier to read and to translate, if they are not too long. Avoid in-sentence enumerations in technical information. Do not overuse lists; text that consists of a series of vertical lists that are loosely tied together with short introductory sentences can look more like an outline than a ﬁnished work.

**Tagging considerations:** Always use the semantic tagging of your authoring tool to produce the correct output for lists. For example, to create a parameter list in DITA, use the **&lt;parml&gt;** tag, not the **&lt;dl&gt;** tag or **&lt;ol&gt;** tag.

#### Unordered lists

#### 

Use an unordered (bulleted) list when the sequence of list items is not signiﬁcant. In an unordered list, arrange list items in a logical way. If there is no better method for arranging them, put them in alphabetical order. If you group items in a way that is not obvious, briefly explain how you grouped them. Where applicable, list the products of your own company ﬁrst, for example in lists of hardware or software.


When you conﬁgure the computer, you can use the program to set the following items:

- Date and time
- Passwords
- Drive startup sequence

Avoid nesting bulleted lists beyond two levels, and never nest more than three levels; restructure the information instead.

When you create nested bulleted lists, make sure that the bullet symbol for the ﬁrst level is different from the bullet symbol for the second level.


The following choices are on the menu:

- DPI Settings
    - Set Write Access Managers
    - Set Trap Receivers

#### Ordered lists

Use an ordered (numbered) list when the sequence is signiﬁcant, for example, when you write procedures or rank items. If the items in a list represent rules or other types of information that you want to refer to, you can refer to them by number. For example, in a list of rules, the item numbered 1 is implied to be Rule 1. For guidelines about writing procedural steps, see [Procedures](.) .


Write comment statements according to the following rules:

1. Use an asterisk in the ﬁrst column.
2. Do not exceed 80 characters.
3. Do not place a comment statement between an instruction and its continuation line.

Avoid nesting numbered lists, including procedural lists, beyond two levels, and never nest more than three levels; restructure the information instead.

When you create nested numbered lists, use the following numbering scheme unless your authoring tool uses a different scheme.

- Begin each ﬁrst-level item with an Arabic numeral, followed by a period.
- Begin each second-level item with a lowercase letter, followed by a period.
- If a third-level item is required, begin the item using a numbering scheme that is distinct from that of the ﬁrst and second levels.

The following example shows a nested numbered list:

1. Remove the cover.
2. Install the adapter:
    1. Insert the adapter into the slot.
    2. Connect the adapter cable to the connector on the system board.
3. Install the cover.

#### Deﬁnition lists

Use a deﬁnition list to describe terms or explain concepts. Avoid using an unordered list with bold highlighting, as shown in the following incorrect example; use a deﬁnition list instead.


The following access levels are associated with resources:


**All** grants the highest level of access. You can delete and perform all operations on resources.


**Create** grants privileges to view, edit, and add resources.


**Modify** grants privileges to view and edit resources.


**Read-only** limits privileges to only viewing resources.


**None** provides no privileges. You cannot view or perform any other operations on resources.

Follow these guidelines for the terms in the list:


Use bold font.


Capitalize the ﬁrst letter unless it requires lowercase because it is a command or variable name such as *prodname* , for example.


Visually separate the term from its deﬁnition. Follow these guidelines for the deﬁnitions in the list:


Capitalize the ﬁrst letter unless it requires lowercase.


Add a period at the end.

Apply one of these writing styles to the deﬁnition list. Be consistent; do not mix these styles in the same list.


The deﬁnition is a complete sentence that describes but does not include the term.


The following access levels are associated with resources:

###### All

You can delete, view, edit, and add resources.

###### Create

You can view, edit, and add resources.

###### Modify

You can view and edit resources.

###### Read-only

You can only view resources.

###### None

You cannot view or perform any other operations on resources.


The deﬁnition is a fragment that describes but does not include the term. The fragment can begin with a noun phrase or with a verb. This style is common in glossaries.


The batch job processing option contains the following components:

###### Batch job

The job that allocates data sets and builds and conﬁgures a runtime environment.

###### Batch parameter member

The member that includes all the conﬁguration values for the products that you can conﬁgure in the runtime environment.

###### RTE utility

A utility that creates the batch parameter member for a runtime environment.


The following access levels are associated with resources:

###### All

Grants privileges to delete and perform all operations on resources. All is the highest level of access.

###### Create

Grants privileges to view, edit, and add resources.

###### Modify

Grants privileges to view and edit resources.

###### Read-only

Limits privileges to only viewing resources.

###### None

Provides no privileges. You cannot view or perform any other operations on resources.

#### Capitalization in lists


Capitalize the ﬁrst word of each item in a vertical list.  The routine makes the following conversions:


An EBCDIC value to a real number


A real number to an EBCDIC value


An EBCDIC value to an integer


An integer to an EBCDIC value  Run the routines in this order:

1. Initialization routine
2. Processing routine

#### Wording of list items

Use list items that are grammatically parallel. For example, do not mix passive voice with active voice or declarative sentences with imperative sentences.


When the 4123 stops, perform these tasks:

1. Measure the amount of oil in the casing.
2. The new ﬁlter should be inserted.
3. You must inspect the bearings.

When the 4123 stops, perform these tasks:

1. Measure the amount of oil in the casing.
2. Insert the new ﬁlter.
3. Inspect the bearings.

XYZ Manager has the following features:


A graphical user interface.


It is compatible with ABC Manager.


It can be used on many types of systems.  XYZ Manager has the following features:


It has a graphical user interface.


It is compatible with ABC Manager.


It can be used on many types of systems.

#### Length of lists

Use at least two list items in an ordered list. You can have one item in an unordered list to match the format of other unordered lists in the same area.

Long lists of items can be overwhelming. Try to keep lists to a maximum of nine items. If a list exceeds this limit, consider using more than one list. Longer lists of reference information in alphabetical order can be acceptable because readers browse reference lists to select the data that they need rather than reading them from beginning to end.

#### Alphabetization and sorting methods of lists

General guidance:


Use letter-by-letter sort order, to keep related terms together. Ignore punctuation, spaces, and capitalization.


Numbers should be listed before letters. Within a group of related terms:


Uppercase should be listed before lowercase.  AC, ac


A two-word version should be listed before a hyphenated version, which in turn should be listed before a one-word version.


off line, off-line, offline


Unless you use a tool that imposes a different sort sequence, sort punctuation marks and special characters by using the following [Unicode sort sequence :](https:/en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Unicode_characters)

(space or null) ! " # $ % &amp; ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; &lt; = &gt; ? @ [ \ ] ^ \_ ` { | } ~ ¢ ° ÷ ≤ ≥


When ordering or listing names in your documentation, alphabetize by the person’s surname (last name or family name). Seek help from a local contact for regional naming conventions before trying to index any but the most straightforward examples.

To manually sort lists of items that have no other obvious sorting criteria, use letter-by-letter alphabetization. This approach is used in most dictionaries, including *Merriam-Webster* . The sorting of indexes and glossaries is usually controlled by the authoring tool, not by the writer. In most authoring tools, index entries are sorted using the word-by-word method.

When you alphabetize items in a list, do not use the word-by-word method, where a space precedes A in an alphabetical sequence. Use the letter-by-letter method, which ignores spaces. The following table shows the difference between the methods:

|------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FOR statement                      | form                                   |
| form                               | format                                 |
| format                             | FORMAT statement                       |
| FORMAT statement                   | forms control                          |
| forms control                      | FOR statement                          |

If an item includes a hyphen, slash, or apostrophe, ignore the punctuation and treat the item as a single word.


*Letter-by-letter alphabetization with hyphens*


END-IF


ENDING


END-INVOKE

When you list punctuation marks and special characters with alphabetic characters, numeric characters, or both, sort them the same way you sort indexes. Sort by special characters (sorted by Unicode sequence) ﬁrst, followed by numeric entries (sorted in ascending order), followed by alphabetic entries. If your product requires that you use a different sorting sequence, be consistent in the use of that sorting sequence throughout your product information. For numbers, you might also want to create a spelled-out version if you think that users might look for the word that way.

#### Punctuation in lists

Write lists so that all or none of the items start with complete sentences. If list items comprise only complete sentences, include a period after each sentence. Except in deﬁnition lists, do not include any end punctuation if list items comprise only sentence fragments.

If a list contains list items that start with sentence fragments, and one or more of the fragments are followed by complete sentences, include periods after all sentence fragments and sentences.

### Messages

A message is any communication that is passed from the application to a customer or to another application.

Customers see messages usually when something goes wrong or the system is processing an operation. Their perception of the software or hardware is strongly influenced by how well the message conveys the information or helps them to solve a problem.

Poorly written and incomplete messages are costly to IBM:


Poor messages cause customers to call IBM Support. If the IBM Support team resolves customer issues, the process is time consuming and expensive.


Poor messages reflect badly on IBM products. Consumable software and hardware products require that all parts of the product, including user interface (UI) text, embedded assistance, help center topics, *and messages* are clear, accurate, complete, and helpful.

Your organization decides whether and how to create and publish product messages. This guidance focuses on the quality of the message content, not on the process you use to generate messages. However, the guidance applies to all messages, whether they are displayed in an application user interface, in a command line, or in a log ﬁle.

#### Contents


[Message types](.)


[Error messages](.)


[Warning  messages](.)


[Informational messages](.)


[Success messages](.)


[General guidance for writing  all message types](.)


[Describing  messages in documentation](.)


[Related links](.)

#### Message types

The following types of messages are shown to customers:


[Error](.)


[Informational](.)


[Success](.)


[Warning](.)

##### Error messages

Inform users of an error or critical failure and optionally block the user from proceeding until the issue has been resolved. For example, an error message might be:

###### ABCISJ234E: The user ID is not valid.

Error messages typically consist of an optional message identiﬁer and a short description of the problem. Good messages describe the cause of the problem and provide instructions for resolving or working around the problem.

Follow these guidelines when writing error messages:


Focus on the problem, not the error, and describe the problem concisely.


An error occurred.

An exception was thrown. An error was encountered. The page was not created.


If possible, tell users why the problem occurred, and how to ﬁx or diagnose the problem.


The service cannot be started. The application server might not be running or your session expired. Ensure that the application server is running. If your session expired, log in, and start the service.


If your audience is programmers, you can use programming language terms when appropriate.

For example, you can write, **An exception occurred** , as long as you also describe in detail the method that threw the exception and, if available, the handler that caught the exception.


An error was generated by exception handling.

The save function returned an error to the createDocument method.

[Start of page](.)

##### Warning messages

Inform users that they are taking actions that might have unwanted or unexpected consequences or to alert them to a condition that might cause problems in the future. For example, a warning message might be:

###### ABCRTE033W: The parser could not parse all documents. Some documents will be skipped.

[Start of page](.)

##### Informational messages

Provide information to users that might not be tied to their current action or task. If there is no action that the customer needs to take, include the statement, **No action is required.** For example, an informational message might be:


###### ABCSTM066I: The index is processing updates from the server. Do not add more documents until  after the update is completed.


**ABCADM156I: The source files for the images in the document were deleted when the document was deleted. No action is required.**

##### Success messages

Conﬁrm that a task was completed as expected.

Avoid expressions of excessive enthusiasm, which are often indicated by exclamation points. Such expressions can be viewed as insincere or convey a tone of unnecessary excitement.


Congratulations! The server was successfully installed! The server was installed successfully.

Consider your audience. A single exclamation point might be appropriate in messages that are shown to new customers who are performing basic tasks, for example.


You did it! You created your ﬁrst account! Success! Your account was created.

[Start of page](.)

#### General guidance for writing all message types


Use full, concise sentences, with direct language. Messages should be kept short, but that doesn’t mean they need to sound robotic. Do not omit words or articles.


Run install.sh on the AIX server

Run the install.sh command on the AIX server.


Use accurate and consistent spelling and capitalization for product and component names.


ObjectStore, Object store, or Object Store object store


Use correct and legally approved product names.


WAS

WebSphere Application Server


Avoid using exaggerated adjectives, such as *catastrophic* , *fatal* , or *illegal* , in the error description.Focus on the problem and not on how bad it is.


A catastrophic error occurred with the database.

The database ﬁles are corrupted. The database can no longer be updated… [add more info to tell users what to do]


Avoid using jargon, and target your messages to the right audience. For example, the following message is suitable for administrators:

###### The {0} template was not found in the target object store.

The following version of the same message is suitable for nonadminstrators:

###### The {0} template does not exist.


Use casual expressions with care.

People see error and warning messages when something has gone wrong or they are being asked to wait or to repeat an action. An overly casual tone can give the impression that IBM is complacent or insensitive to the inconvenience that the error has caused. While such expressions can appear friendlier, terms that seem fashionable today can become outdated quickly and seem trite tomorrow. Even a trendy expression will likely irritate people if they are forced to encounter it repeatedly while trying to complete a task.


D'oh Oops Sorry! Whoops

Oh snap! The connection to the database was lost. Make sure your application server is running and then try again.


Avoid terms of politeness, such as *please* and *thank you* . These terms are inappropriate or offensive in some cultural contexts.


Avoid wording that blames the customer.


You failed to create a page because you don’t have the right access role. Check your access role. You must have the **admin** role to create a page.

Use passive voice if it helps you avoid assigning blame.


You entered the wrong user ID.

The user ID is not valid. Enter a different user ID. An incorrect value was entered.


Avoid telling users to call IBM Support.

When possible, include instructions to help customers resolve or work around problems themselves. If you tell customers to check something, tell them how and why. For example, if you ask customers to refer to log ﬁles, tell them how to access the log ﬁles. Otherwise, provide links to documentation, community channels, or forums where customers can ﬁnd a solution before they call IBM.


Use stock phrases for commonly repeated text:  Contact the system administrator.


Don’t expose more information than is necessary.

Avoid sharing information that attackers could use to hack an application or gain unauthorized access to other IT systems. For example, unless it’s required to fully explain the problem or describe a solution, do not refer to the application’s source code language and version, or mention speciﬁc host names, IP addresses, database names, or ﬁle names.

If you document messages or edit messages that are exported directly from the product, consider reviewing the content to check for and remove unnecessary details that could be misused by bad actors.


You can say that an issue was ﬁxed in an earlier version, but never promise a future code ﬁx.


Use the appropriate terms to express quantities. Use “large” and “small” to refer to size, dimensions, or mass. Use “high” and “low” to refer to levels or numerical values.


The number of items to delete must be *larger* than zero. The number of items to delete must be *higher* than zero.


The program requires a *low* amount of memory. The program requires a *small* amount of memory.


Represent variable values in messages consistently and clearly.

If you are documenting messages outside of the product, use descriptive text to represent variables where possible. Highlight the variable by using italic font. If you use angle brackets or underscores, the variables can be misinterpreted to be code snippets, which are not always translated.


The document cannot be created. The maximum limit of maximum\_number\_of\_documents documents was reached. Consider deleting documents or upgrading your plan.


The document cannot be created. The maximum limit of **&lt;maximum\_number\_of\_documents&gt;** documents was reached. Consider deleting documents or upgrading your plan.


The document cannot be created. The maximum limit of *maximum number of documents* documents was reached. Consider deleting documents or upgrading your plan.

If you are authoring messages as part of the product (in a properties ﬁles, for example), your development team determines the syntax to use to represent variables. For example, you might be asked to use **%d** to represent a number variable that will be replaced at run time.


The document cannot be created. The maximum limit of %d documents was reached. Consider deleting documents or upgrading your plan.

[Start of page](.)

#### Describing messages in documentation

In product documentation, you can explain to customers when a message might be displayed. Use the following format to do so.


If the document cannot be deleted, a message is issued.

If the document cannot be deleted, a message is returned.


If the document cannot be deleted, an error message will occur. If the document cannot be deleted, a message is displayed.

[Start of page](.)
