### Notes

Do not overuse notes because they can lose their signiﬁcance. IBM uses speciﬁc terms to alert customers of potential damage to hardware and software, or to physical risk and danger.

#### Contents


[Standard notes](.)


[Attention notices](.)


[CAUTION notices](.)


[DANGER notices](.)

#### Standard notes

To call attention to important hints, tips, guidance, restrictions, or advice that might be overlooked, use a meaningful label that describes the nature of the content. Consider labels such as **Exception** , **Fast path** , **Important** , **Remember** , **Requirement** , **Restriction** , and **Tip** . Avoid using **Recommendation** .

The label and the colon that follows the label must be bold. See speciﬁc guidance for [Mobile](.) .


**Exception:** This function is not available in this version.

**Fast path:** Instead of creating a new conﬁguration ﬁle, you can copy one of the sample ﬁles in the samples folder and modify it.

**Important:** Ensure that you select the correct service document before you commit your changes.

**Note:** Hyphens and dashes can be easily mistaken for each other, but they are different. **Remember:** Memory requirements are affected by the size and complexity of your database system. **Requirement:** You must have SYSADM authority.

**Restriction:** You cannot create a new subscription until you successfully complete this task.

**Tip:** For a faster installation, accept the default settings.

If you use an IBM authoring tool, create notes by using the appropriate semantic tags and allow the transform to control the format.

Do not interrupt a paragraph with a note. A note must not be inline; it must stand alone. Do not indent note text, and do not use notes where they distort the appearance of the surrounding text.

If two or more notes are together, use a plural label on a separate line and arrange the notes in the appropriate type of list.


###### Requirements:

- No assumed value is applied for the function attribute; you must specify a value.
- You must clear the temporary storage area before you can build a new query.

**Tips:**

1. Before you begin the conﬁguration process, determine all of the required conﬁguration values.
2. After you complete the conﬁguration process, run some test queries to verify that you conﬁgured the system correctly.

If a note consists of more than one paragraph, consider reorganizing the information to make the note a subsection with a heading, rather than a note with a label. When a note is longer than one paragraph, differentiating the note from the general text is difﬁcult.

[Start of page](.)

#### Attention notices

Use an Attention notice to indicate the possibility of damage to a program, device, system, or data. Create the **Attention** label, followed by a colon, in bold. Place the text of the notice on the same line as the label. Treat the notice as a separate paragraph, with space above and below it.


**Attention:** If the exporting and importing databases use different code-page values, the exported data corrupts the importing database.

In a procedure, place the notice *before* the step to which it applies.


To repair the array board:

1. Raise the main panel.
2. Remove the six bolts.
3. Unlatch the array board retainers.

**Attention:** Do not touch the plastic locating pins in the cover. You might bend or break them.

1. Remove the array board carefully.

Do not use the word *warning* in an Attention notice, either as the label or within the notice text. In some countries, the word *warning* is reserved for safety notices, which pertain to possible physical harm to people. In IBM publications, safety notices are either CAUTION or DANGER notices.

#### CAUTION notices

Use a CAUTION notice to call attention to a situation that is potentially hazardous to people because of a condition that exists or can develop from an unsafe practice. For example, you might need a CAUTION notice to notify readers to use special care when they lift a piece of heavy equipment.

IBM only Consult your local Safety department before you use a CAUTION notice.

Create the **CAUTION** label on a line by itself. Set the label in all uppercase letters, followed by a colon, in bold. Ensure that the text of the notice is also bold. If your authoring tool does not display the text in bold, apply bold manually. Treat the notice as a separate paragraph, with space above and below it. In a procedure, place the notice *before* the step to which it applies.


To replace the server:

1. Use a screwdriver to remove the four screws.
2. Remove the back cover.

**CAUTION:**

###### Do not remove or install this unit without using the provided lift tool.

1. Use the lift tool to lift the server out of the rack.

#### DANGER notices

Use a DANGER notice to call attention to a situation that is potentially lethal or extremely hazardous to people. For example, after a computer side panel is removed, exposed high-voltage wires might be lethal.

Use the DANGER notice with discretion. Limit its use to situations where irreparable injury or loss of life might occur unless extreme care is used.

IBM only Consult your local Safety department before you use a DANGER notice.

Create the **DANGER** label on a line by itself. Set the label in all uppercase letters, followed by a colon, in bold. Enclose the text of the notice in a box and ensure that the text of the notice is also bold. If your authoring tool does not display the text in bold, apply bold manually. Treat the notice as a separate paragraph, with a space above and below it. In a procedure, place the notice *before* the step to which it applies.


To restart the unit:

1. Remove the four corner bolts.
2. Lift the protective cover.

**DANGER:**

**Electrical voltage and current from power, telephone, and communication cables are hazardous. To avoid a shock hazard, never turn on any equipment when there is evidence of ﬁre, water, or structural damage.**

### Paragraphs

Group sentences that support an idea into paragraphs to break up the text on a page and make it easier for readers to consume the information.

Separate one paragraph from another with an empty new line. Omit paragraph indentation, setting the ﬁrst line flush left.


In this ﬁrst lab, you initiate your Soleil virtual machine and review the IBM Cloud Pak for Data user interface.

In this ﬁrst lab, you initiate your Soleil virtual machine and review the IBM Cloud Pak for Data user interface.

[Start of page](.)

### Procedures

Follow these general guidelines for writing numbered procedure steps.

#### Contents


[Organizing  the steps in a procedure](.)


[Prerequisite information](.)


[Introducing  the procedure](.)


[Writing  steps](.)


[Indicating  optional and conditional steps](.)


[Handling  nonsequential actions](.)


[Ending  the procedure](.)

#### Organizing the steps in a procedure

When you write a tutorial or procedure, think about the user's high-level goal and take time to organize the information in a way that makes the task easier to complete.

Avoid writing excessively long procedures. Break up long procedures into smaller sets of steps. For example, a user goal might be to share a resource with colleagues. To reach the goal, the user might need to grant the colleague access to the resource, and then share the resource, two tasks that involve many steps. Separate the information into two short, clear procedures.

A task that lists steps that link to smaller sets of steps is sometimes called a supertask. If space is limited, such as in a presentation, ensure that the entire supertask or summary can be viewed at one time so that it is easier for users to understand the overall goal.

LLM helper When you break a long procedure or tutorial into smaller chunks, include a summary at the start of the procedure or tutorial. In the summary, explain the overall goal or list the sets of steps that are required to complete the procedure or tutorial.


You must complete the following sets of steps to install in an active-active conﬁguration:

1. [Install the orchestration manager operator on cluster 1](.) .
2. Update the custom resource for cluster 1.
3. Add cluster details to the custom resource for cluster 1.

Each step in the list is a link to a subtask. For example, step 1 goes to the following subtask:

##### Installing the orchestration manager operator

1. Lorem ipsum

#### Prerequisite information

Add any information that must be known or conditions that must be met before users can start the procedure.

You can add prerequisite information in a separate section with a heading such as **Prerequisites** or **Before you begin** . Or you can group the information with the introduction to the procedure.

The following examples cover different scenarios:


The exercises that are described in this course must be completed in a lab environment. For more information about how to create the lab environment, see the Appendix .

Correct example You must be an administrator of the project where you plan to deploy the service.

You cannot delete a skill until after you remove it from all of the assistants that use the skill. For more information, see Removing skills .

Don’t describe a step that is part of the main procedure, such as logging in to an application, in the prerequisite section. The exception is an initial step that is complex and required before multiple procedures. In such cases, you can separate the step out into its own procedure and link to it from the prerequisite section.

#### Introducing the procedure

Use one of the following approaches to introduce a procedure:

- A heading such as “Procedure”

*Heading*

###### Installing XYZ Manager

XYZ Manager provides an installation wizard that you use to install XYZ Manager on Linux, UNIX, and Windows systems.

###### Procedure

1. To start the XYZ Manager installation wizard, click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.
3. A lead-in sentence

If you use a sentence to introduce a procedure, use a colon at the end of the lead-in sentence unless another sentence intervenes between the lead-in sentence and the procedure. If a sentence intervenes, use a period to end both the lead-in sentence and the intervening sentence.


*Sentence*

###### Installing XYZ Manager

XYZ Manager provides an installation wizard that you use to install XYZ Manager on Linux, UNIX, and Windows systems. To install XYZ Manager, complete the following steps:

1. To start the XYZ Manager installation wizard, click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.

*Sentence followed by another sentence*

###### Installing XYZ Manager

XYZ Manager provides an installation wizard that you use to install XYZ Manager on Linux, UNIX, and Windows systems. To install XYZ Manager, complete the following steps. This procedure installs the program in the default location.

1. To start the XYZ Manager installation wizard, click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.
3. A lead-in inﬁnitive phrase (one that starts with *To* )

If you use an inﬁnitive phrase to introduce a procedure, use a colon at the end of the phrase.

**Translation consideration:** To avoid translation problems, consider using a lead-in sentence instead of an inﬁnitive phrase. Ensure that you use only one method of introducing a procedure consistently throughout your information.


*Inﬁnitive phrase*

###### Installing XYZ Manager

XYZ Manager provides an installation wizard that you use to install XYZ Manager on Linux, UNIX, and Windows systems. To install XYZ Manager:

1. To start the XYZ Manager installation wizard, click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.
3. A combination of a heading such as “Procedure” and a lead-in sentence or inﬁnitive phrase

*Heading and inﬁnitive phrase*

###### Installing XYZ Manager

XYZ Manager provides an installation wizard that you use to install XYZ Manager on Linux, UNIX, and Windows systems. Alternatively, you can install XYZ Manager by using a response ﬁle.

###### Procedure

To install XYZ Manager by using the installation wizard:

1. To start the XYZ Manager installation wizard, click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.

Use a colon at the end of a sentence that introduces a subprocedure (equivalent to a nested ordered list) unless another sentence intervenes between the lead-in wording and the subprocedure. If a sentence intervenes, use a period to end both the lead-in sentence and the intervening sentence.


*Sentence*

1. Conﬁgure the multicast IP addresses:
    1. In the **Start address** ﬁeld, type the ...
    2. In the **Pool size** ﬁeld, type the ...

*Sentence followed by another sentence*

1. Connect the cables. The connectors are color coded.
    1. Connect the keyboard cable to the keyboard connector.
    2. Connect the mouse cable to the mouse connector.

#### Writing steps

Write one step for each signiﬁcant user action, but avoid being too granular. For all but novice computer users, use arrows to show a sequence of menu selections.


*Incorrect example*

1. Click **File** .
2. Click **Print** .

*Correct example*

1. Click **File &gt; Print** .

If you tell the user to press Enter to complete the action, do so as part of the step, not in a separate step.


*Incorrect example*

1. Type yes.
2. Press Enter.

*Correct example*

1. Enter yes.

If an ellipsis, colon, or other punctuation is part of an interface element label, do not include that punctuation in the description of the action.


*Incorrect example*

1. Click **Print** ...
2. Enter a value in the **Threshold:** ﬁeld.

*Correct example*

1. Click **Print** .
2. Enter a value in the **Threshold** ﬁeld.

Avoid writing excessively long procedures. Try to break up long procedures into smaller tasks. Procedural steps should have no more than two levels; restructure the information instead. If space is limited, such as in a video or presentation, ensure that an entire supertask procedure can be viewed at one time so that it is easier for users to understand the overall task. See speciﬁc guidance for [videos](.) .


*Incorrect example*

1. Remove the drive:
    1. Prepare the drawer:
        1. Open the release levers on the left and right side of the drawer.
        2. Slide the drawer out until it is fully extended.
    2. Raise the DDM handle to release the drive that you want to replace.
    3. Lift the drive out of the drawer.

*Correct example*

1. Remove the drive:
    1. Open the release levers on the left and right side of the drawer.
    2. Slide the drawer out until it is fully extended.
    3. Raise the DDM handle to release the drive that you want to replace.
    4. Lift the drive out of the drawer.

If a procedure consists of only one step, present it as a sentence or short paragraph, and do not number it.

Do not use *please* in any instructions. Terms of politeness are superfluous, convey the wrong tone for technical material, and are not regarded the same way in all cultures.

Use imperative mood in the ﬁrst sentence of each step.

If it is necessary to provide an explanation, do so in the same step, after the imperative sentence, not in a new step. If possible, avoid describing the result of each step:

- If the context is clear, omit any locational information.
- If the context is not clear, in the next step, orient the user to the location where that step is performed.

*Results are presented as a step*

1. Click **Install program** .
2. The Installation window lists the available features. Select a feature.

*If the context is clear*

1. Click **Install program** .
2. Select a feature.

*If the context is not clear*

1. Click **Install program** .
2. In the Installation window, select a feature.

*If the context is not clear*

1. Click **Install program** . The Installation window lists the available features.
2. Select a feature.

If you orient the user to the location where the action is performed or explain the purpose of the action, do so before describing the action.


1. Select a feature from the list in the Installation window.
1. In the Installation window, select a feature from the list.


3. Click **Replace** to overwrite the previous version.

3. To overwrite the previous version, click **Replace** .

If the procedure includes snippets of code as examples, place the code (or link to the code, if the code is in a separate topic) in the step that it applies to. If the example of code applies to the whole task, place the code or link after the last step. Label the link to the code so that the purpose of the code is clear to users, for example, “Code for an SQL table”.

[Start of page](.)

#### Indicating optional and conditional steps

If a step is optional, begin the step with the word *Optional* . If your authoring tool provides a semantic element to generate the word

*Optional* , use that element.


1. Optional: Click **Set password** . In the **Password** ﬁeld, type a password.

If a step is conditional, state the condition or begin the step with an *if* clause.


1. Master repository only: In the **IP address** ﬁeld, type the IP address.
1. If data options are on the menu, click the option that is appropriate for your environment. [Start of page](.)

#### Handling nonsequential actions

Do not use sequential steps to describe actions that are not sequential. When a procedure has mutually exclusive alternatives or any kind of branching condition, do not present the alternatives as sequential steps. Describe the branching condition in a single step, using a sublist or subprocedures to present the alternatives. Do not insert the word *or* between alternatives.


*Incorrect example*

1. If you did not set a password, go to step 3.
2. If you did set a password, type the password and click **Continue** .
3. ...

*Incorrect example*

1. If you did not set a password, go to step 3, or
2. If you did set a password, type the password and click **Continue** .	3. ...

*Incorrect example*

1. If you did not set a password, go to step 2, or if you did set a password, type the password and click **Continue** .
2. ...

*Correct example*

1. Choose the appropriate method to log in to the system:
    - If you did not set a password, go to step 3.
    - If you have set a password, type the password and click **Continue** .
2. ...

*Incorrect example*

1. Click **Conﬁgure** .
2. To add a subnet, click **Add** and type the address.
3. To delete a subnet, select the subnet and click **Delete** .
4. To perform an action on all subnets, click **All Subnets** .

*Correct example*

1. Click **Conﬁgure** to do any of the following tasks:
    - To add a subnet, click **Add** and type the address.
    - To delete a subnet, select the subnet and click **Delete** .

- To perform an action on all subnets, click **All Subnets** .
1. ...

#### Ending the procedure

Do not include actions that are outside the scope of the procedure. Do not continue with steps for another procedure. If a subsequent procedure is necessary, direct the user to it after the ﬁnal step in a cross-reference or, in online documentation, in a link.


*Incorrect example*

To set a password:

1. Click **Set password** .
2. In the **Password** ﬁeld, type the password and click **OK** .
3. To delete the password, click **Delete password** .

*Correct example*

To set a password:

.	1. Click **Set password** .

1. In the **Password** ﬁeld, type the password and click **OK** .

Deleting passwords
Otherwise, direct the user to other procedures in a paragraph that follows the procedure, or provide a link. Avoid using a statement at the end of a procedure that only informs the user that the procedure is complete.
*Incorrect example*
To install the adapter:
    1. Remove the cover.
    2. ...
    3. ...
    4. Replace the cover. The adapter is now installed. You must now conﬁgure the adapter. See “Conﬁguring adapters”.
*Correct example*
To install the adapter:
    1. Remove the cover.
    2. ...
    3. ...
    4. Replace the cover.
After you install the adapter, you must conﬁgure it.**Parent topic:** Installing and conﬁguring adapters**Previous topic:** Planning to install adapters**Next topic:** Conﬁguring adapters
*Correct example*
To install the adapter:
    1. Remove the cover.
    2. ...
    3. ...
    4. Replace the cover.
After you install the adapter, you must conﬁgure it. See “Conﬁguring adapters” for instructions.

### Tables

### 

Often, text that is difﬁcult to understand in paragraph form becomes clear in a table format. Tables help highlight relationships among similar pieces of information and are easily scanned for quick reference.

#### Contents


[Text](.)


[Empty or not applicable cells](.)


[Formatting](.)


[Accessibility considerations](.)


[Headings](.)


[Captions](.)


[Numbering](.)


[References](.)


[Placement](.)

#### Text

Follow these guidelines for text in tables:


Use grammatically parallel text for all cells in a column.


Follow standard punctuation rules. For details, see [Punctuation and symbols](.) .


Use [sentence-style capitalization](.) for these table elements:

- Cell contents
- Column headings
- Row labels
- Table captions

Follow IBM Style highlighting conventions. For details, see [Highlighting](.) .


If you repeat a word or phrase in all cells in a column, consider rewording the column heading to include that word or phrase and eliminate the repetition.

##### Empty or not applicable cells

Cells with missing information and those with zero or null values can be treated in several ways:


Use “0” in situations where a numeric value of zero is appropriate, such as a sum that equals zero, or a cell showing zero occurrences of an attribute that is being counted.


Do not use a zero when the data is unknown or not applicable.


Use a blank ("") in situations where an empty string is appropriate for an alphanumeric cell value, (e.g., a last name ﬁeld for “Cher” or “Bono”). Industry-standard screen readers are able to correctly interpret blank cells.


A blank or en dash can be used to indicate that data is missing, not applicable, or null.


En dashes are preferred over “N/A” in situations that are not applicable, both to conserve cell space and to reduce the need for localization.


To indicate that something is included, covered, or applicable, use a character such as a checkmark in table cells. A checkmark is preferred over a letter X, since an X may be interpretted to mean either applicable or not applicable. Center-align the character in each cell. If all body cells in a column have center-aligned content such as checkmarks, center-align the column heading for consistency, even if other column headings are left-aligned. In the sentence that introduces the table, explain the convention that you are using.


In the following table, the checkmark indicates devices that each model supports.

|   **Model** | **Device A**   | **Device B**   | **Device C**   |
|-------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
|        1234 | ✓              |                |                |
|        3456 | ✓              | ✓              |                |
|        5678 | ✓              |                | ✓              |


Arrange the items in the ﬁrst column of the table in a logical way, for example, largest to smallest or vice versa. If there is no logical order, put the items in alphabetical order.


Do not put more than one type of information into a single column.


| **Parameter**   | **Range (Default)**   |
|-----------------|-----------------------|
| util_heap       | 16 - 2147483647 (16)  |
| util_burd       | 10 - 100 (50)         |
| x_heap          | 12 - 750 (500)        |
| x_burd          | 1 - 20 (1)            |

| **Parameter**   | **Range**       |   **Default** |
|-----------------|-----------------|---------------|
| util_heap       | 16 - 2147483647 |            16 |
| util_burd       | 10 - 100        |            50 |
| x_heap          | 12 - 750        |           500 |
| x_burd          | 1 - 20          |             1 |


If you use table footnotes, place the deﬁnition as close to the table as possible so they are easily retrievable. Use a note list and superscript numbers, rather than letters, to indicate table results. However, if superscript is not available, include in the table an explicit phrase such as “See note 1.”


| **1 Gbps Ethernet (iSCSi)**   | **10 Gbps Ethernet-Copper (iSCSi)**   | **12 Gbps SAS**   | **16 Gbps FC**   | **10 Gbps Ethernet-Optical (iSCSi/FCoE)**   |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------|-------------------|------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| 8 ports1                      | 4 ports (standard)                    | 8 ports1          | 8 ports1         | 8 ports1                                    |

1 With optional adapter card feature, one of which is allowed per Storwize V5000 control enclosure.

| **Model**          | **Height**        | **Depth**         | **Width**         |
|--------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Tower              | 440 mm (17.3 in.) | 747 mm (29.4 in.) | 218 mm (8.6 in.)  |
| 5U rack (see note) | 218 mm (8.6 in.)  | 696 mm (27.4 in.) | 424 mm (16.7 in.) |

#### Formatting

Follow these guidelines for formatting tables:


Top-align and left-align the text in all table body cells. This alignment helps to clarify the row and column boundaries.

**Exception:** Center-align characters such as a checkmark that indicates that something is included, covered, or applicable. Center-align the contents of spanned cells if such alignment improves legibility and understanding.


*Table 2. 2S4U feature comparisons*

| **Description**            | **POWER9**                              | **POWER8**                              |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Processor                  | 2 P9 SCM sockets                        | 2 P8 DCM sockets                        |
| Pluggable processor module | Yes                                     | Yes                                     |
| Max N-way                  | 24                                      | 24                                      |
| L3 cache                   | 10 MB/core                              | 8 MB/core                               |
| Threads                    | 8 MB/core                               | 8 MB/core                               |
| LPAR max                   | 480                                     | 480                                     |
| Capacity on demand         | Available (not offered in entry server) | Available (not offered in entry server) |


Bottom-align and left-align the text in all column headings.

**Exception:** If all body cells in a column have center-aligned content such as checkmarks, center-align the column heading for consistency, even if other column headings are left-aligned.


Avoid putting too much information into a single table, and avoid creating a table that requires horizontal scrolling when it is viewed online. If possible, break large amounts of information into separate tables.


If space is limited or information must be absorbed quickly, such as in a presentation or video, avoid using a long or complex table. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .


Avoid scaling text in tables to smaller than 80%, or 8-point type.


Use column widths that are proportional to the amount of information that the cells contain.


Use a consistent format for all tables in the information unit. For example, if some tables do not have horizontal rules, do not use horizontal rules in any tables in the information unit.

##### Accessibility considerations


For more complete accessibility requirements for tables, see other resources such as [IBM Accessibility.](https:/www.ibm.com/able)


Use data tables, which are tables with column and row headers. Column and row headers enable screen readers to provide information about the relationship of data cells in a table to some visually impaired users.


Do not use tabs, forward slashes, or spaces to arrange tabular information.


Some formats, such as simple text-based documents, do not support the ability to deﬁne column and row headers. When a document format does not support the ability to deﬁne column and row headers, do not use data tables.


If a table contains spanned cells, you must include a table summary to make your table accessible. [Start of page](.)

#### Headings

Follow these guidelines for table headings:


Ensure that column headings are tagged in accordance with accessibility requirements. The speciﬁc tags that you must use [depend on the tool that you use. For detailed information about how to tag column headings for accessibility, see IBM Accessibility.](https:/www.ibm.com/able)


Use [sentence-style capitalization](.) for column headings.


Bottom-align and left-align the text in all column headings.

**Exception:** If all body cells in a column have center-aligned content such as checkmarks, center-align the column heading for consistency, even if other column headings are left-aligned.

|           3 | Logs all error messages and messages before and after each step of an operation   |

#### Captions

You can use a caption to describe the contents of the table and, if necessary, the organization of the table. Place the caption above the table. A table caption can include a table number and text. Depending on the context, you might choose to omit the table number or the text. When you use captions in your information, use them consistently for all tables.

Table captions are required in the following situations:


When you must refer to the tables by a caption, such as in a table of contents or in a link


When the tables are complex and require explanation


When the tables are not self-explanatory or are not explained in the surrounding text Otherwise, table captions are optional.

**Format recommendation:** Some authoring tools apply a default format to table captions. If you apply the format manually, use italic font and insert a period between the table number and the text. See speciﬁc guidance for [Mobile](.) .

Use one of the following types of text in table captions:


Fragment: If you can describe a table briefly and clearly, use a fragment (less than a complete sentence).

- Apply sentence-style capitalization.
- Do not start the fragment with a deﬁnite or indeﬁnite article. Do not insert a period (.) at the end.

*Table 22. The functions of the assembler. Table 22. Functions of the assembler*


Complete sentence: If you must provide a more detailed explanation in the caption, use one or more complete sentences.


Apply [sentence-style capitalization](.) , and [punctuation](.) .

*Table 22. The assembler converts the source program into an object program.*


Combined fragment and complete sentence: If a table requires a very detailed explanation, begin the caption text with a fragment and then continue with one or more sentences.

- Use [sentence-style capitalization](.) .
- Insert a period after the fragment and after each sentence.

If the organization of the table requires more explanation than can ﬁt in the caption, explain it in the text. If the organization of the table is obvious, do not explain it.


*Table 22. Functions of the assembler. The assembler converts the source program into an object program.*

In the caption text, do not include the word *table* , *chart* , or any other word that is redundant within the caption, except as it is used to precede the number.


*Table 2. System requirements table Table 2. System requirements*

If a table is long and prints on more than one page, repeat the caption on successive pages.

Each section of the table should contain some designation to indicate that it spans more than one page. The preferred method is to include “ *(Part x of y)* ” at the end of the table number. However, you might have to use another method, such as “ *(continued)* ”, depending on the tool that you are using.

Use a colon to separate a caption and subcaption.


*Table 4. Scenario 1: The Department A client Table 5. Scenario 2: The Department B client*

[Start of page](.)

#### Numbering

Make sure the numbers you use for tables are consecutive and consistent throughout your content, including any tables in the appendixes. Your environment and tools might number tables differently. While it’s not obligatory to specify numbers for tables, use [the convention that best matches the documentation style. Always consider the IBM accessibility content requirement to properly title tables. If your users are printing hard copies of a PDF ﬁle, including numbers is recommended to help with manual navigation](https:/www.ibm.com/able/toolkit/design/content/text-meaning/#table-captions) between tables.

For example, if your authoring tool numbers tables by starting with *Table 1* in each separate web-based topic, consider not numbering your captions. If your documentation for tables uses links or cross-references, then use those instead of numbering.

If a table must be split into two or more parts, qualify the table number as shown in the following example.


*Table 7 (Part 1 of 3). Message logging by level Table 7 (Part 2 of 3). Message logging by level Table 7 (Part 3 of 3). Message logging by level*

The separate parts of such tables must have the same caption text. If different caption text is necessary, create the parts as separate tables.

For more information about numbering in headings, see [Headings](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### References

When you refer to tables in text, use correct [capitalization](.) and appropriate placement.

Use regular text instead of an inline link when a reference is near a table. Always introduce a table with a sentence that immediately precedes it. If you present the same type of information in two or more consecutive tables, you do not have to introduce each speciﬁc table, but you must introduce the group of tables.

Use a period or a colon after the introduction to a table. Either punctuation mark is correct if it follows a complete sentence. Choose the punctuation mark that best suits the context. For example, you might use a colon if the introduction immediately leads in to the item that follows. Use a period if the introduction is more descriptive or is interrupted by an intervening sentence. In your information set, be consistent with the punctuation marks that you apply for the context.


You can modify any of the properties that are included in the following table:

Table 10 shows results from the ﬁrst test and table 11 shows results from the second test. The results in both tables are accurate to two decimal places.

For more information about punctuation, see the [punctuation](.) topic.

In text references, when a reference is not near a table, use the word *table* . (Italic is used here for emphasis; do not use italic in your text references.)

If a document has both ﬁgures and tables and they are labeled as such, include the page numbers or hypertext links in cross-references to them in the text. Do this only when it is not possible to use regular text to refer to the ﬁgure or table. This retrievability aid helps the reader to distinguish between *ﬁgure x* and *table x* references. If your text formatter cannot provide the page numbers or hypertext links in cross-references to ﬁgures and tables, consider captioning them all as ﬁgures and numbering them in a single sequence.

It is not necessary to use a cross-reference to a table in text if the table is not referred to, or if it is referred to in such a way that the table can be identiﬁed without a number.

Enclose a subheading for a table caption in parentheses and add it to the end of the caption text.


*Table 7. Run times for test programs (in microseconds) Table 8. Real storage requirements (KB equals 1,024 bytes)*

[Start of page](.)

#### Placement

Place a table as close as possible to the principal reference to it.


If the reference and the table are in the same topic, implement one of these solutions:

- When the reference is close to the table, use a text reference. For example, write “For a complete list of requirements, see the following table.”
- When the reference is not close to the table, create a link to the table. For example, write “For a complete list of requirements, see *Process steps* .”

If the table is on a separate page or in a separate topic, use a link to the page or topic that contains the table. [Start of page](.)

### Type size

In all documentation, ensure that the text meets accessibility requirements.

In printed documentation and legal notices, use a type size that corresponds to a minimum of 8 points.

The ISO/IEC 26514:2008 speciﬁcation, *Systems and software engineering - Requirements for designers and developers of user documentation* , states that printed text, including text in illustrations, should be no smaller than 2.75 mm for capital letters when measured on the printed page. For reference, 2.75 mm converts to approximately 8 points.

Some legal jurisdictions do not accept into evidence legal notices with text that is smaller than 8 points.

### Citations and references

The following guidelines apply to citations for publications and other materials, regardless of the medium that is used to distribute them, including standard IBM publications, IBM Documentation, special IBM publications, and publications of other organizations or individuals.

#### Contents


[General guidelines](.)


[Online information](.)


[IBM Documentation](.)

[Quotations](.)


[Videos, podcasts, and other online multimedia](.)

#### General guidelines

Follow these general guidelines for citing one publication (such as a book, article, or web page) in another publication:


When you refer to a publication that is listed in the preface or bibliography, follow these guidelines in the document:

- Use a short title that distinctly identiﬁes the publication.
- Use an italic font for the title unless the title is also a link, in which case use normal link highlighting. Do not include the document number.

For more information, see the *DQTI* book.

For syntax details, see the *Programming Reference* .


If your publication does not have a preface or bibliography, follow these guidelines:

- Use the full title of the publication.
- Use an italic font for the title unless the title is also a link, in which case use normal link highlighting.
- Provide the document number (without the sufﬁx) in a regular font.

Use commas to separate the document number from the title and from subsequent text.

For information about 9370 conﬁgurations, see *Introducing the IBM 9370 System* , GA24-4031, and *Planning for your System* , GA24-4032.


For more information, see the *Reference Guide for Db2 12 for z/OS* .


Include a deﬁnite article and an identifying noun when they are needed for clarity. For example, you can add the words *the* and

*book* to a title.


If you refer to a smaller piece of work within a larger container such as a chapter within a book or an article in a magazine, use italic font for the larger container and double quotation marks for the smaller piece.


If you are unable to ﬁnd a speciﬁc type of reference in IBM Style, see the *Chicago Manual of Style* for further direction. It is important to remain consistent within the documentation created for the brand.


When you refer to multiple publications that share a common element in their titles, do not shorten those references by omitting the common element.


See the *Db2 Administration Tool Installation and User’s Guides* .

See the *Db2 Administration Tool Installation Guide* and the *Db2 Administration Tool User’s Guide* .


When you punctuate a title in a cross-reference, follow these guidelines:


When a library name appears at the beginning of the title, end that portion of the title with a colon:  See *Information Development Guideline: Indexing* , ZZ27-1987.


When the complete name of a product appears at the beginning of the title, end that portion of the title with a colon:


See *IBM TCP/IP for MVS: Messages and Codes* , SC31-7132.


When the name of a product is shortened, do not use punctuation between it and the rest of the title:  See the *Db2 Command Reference* .


When you refer to information within the same document, follow these rules:

- Give a reason for the cross-reference. Unless the reason is clear from the context, tell readers why you are referring to another section, or tell them what they can expect to ﬁnd.


For detailed information about …, see chapter 12. To learn how to …, see chapter 4.

- Use a brief cross-reference when the reason for the cross-reference is obvious from the context.


Follow the rules for database names (see chapter 3). Notice the placement of controls on the console (ﬁgure 2).


Do not send the reader back and forth needlessly. If the cross-referenced information is essential, consider reproducing it instead of referring to it. But be careful to ensure that reproduced information will not become obsolete if the original is updated.


Refer to a part, chapter, or appendix by its number or letter. For a reference within the same chapter or to a subdivision of another section of the book, provide the heading title and a page reference.


For detailed information about error codes, see appendix B. For software requirements, see “Requirements” on page 5.


If the name of the chapter helps the reader, add the title.


For more information about these topics, see chapter 9, “Programming techniques”.


Use page numbers in cross-references only if your authoring tool can track them and change them as chapters expand or contract.


Special programming considerations are described in “Input/output coding” on page 37.


Use lowercase on the words *appendix, bibliography, chapter, contents, ﬁgure, glossary, note, part, preface, table,* and *volume*

when these words are used in a cross-reference or when referred to generically.


Hexadecimal conversion codes are in appendix C. For an illustration of these relationships, see ﬁgure 6.

Deﬁnitions for unique terms are included in the glossary.

An exception is allowed for tools that autmoatically insert these words in uppercase letters as the link label for a hypertext link. For example, when authoring in DITA, a DITA XREF element that links to a table with a title inserts the word *Table* as the link label.


When you refer to ﬁgures or tables, do not include captions.


See ﬁgure 6, “Data structures”, on page 26. See ﬁgure 6 on page 26.


Do not abbreviate *chapter, part,* or *volume* in cross-references or elsewhere.


In online publications, section headings and page numbers can change in a revision. When you must refer to speciﬁc information in another publication, link directly to the referenced location. Do not capitalize generic uses of part, chapter, volume, or other subdivision names. Include the title of the publication.


When referencing a section in another piece of content, include any existing section number with the heading if the content is in a large PDF or print format to help readers locate the information easily. In most other cases, referencing just the section heading is sufﬁcient. Be aware that section numbers and headings might change, and if the reference isn’t dynamically updated, you’ll need to revise it manually.

If you also intend to include section titles or page numbers, consider whether they might change. Consider also linking the main body of work in the event that the location of the reference contained within it changes.

When citing a quotation, you can edit words and pronouns in order to be more inclusive. Use brackets to indicate that the quotation has been edited. For example:

Original: “Treat each case as an individual case, and give every man an opportunity to earn just as much money as he is capable of earning.” – Thomas J. Watson

Edited: “Treat each case as an individual case, and give every [person] an opportunity to earn just as much money as [they are] capable of earning.” – Thomas J. Watson

#### Online information

Link to and cite only reliable, authoritative sites. Do not link to sites, such as blogs or wikis, where the information can be edited by unreliable or irresponsible contributors. You can link to blogs and wikis that are owned and maintained by IBM, but consider the cost of maintaining such links and the risk of broken links as such sites change or information is updated. Wikipedia is well moderated and is generally safe to link to. However, before linking to Wikipedia, consider whether the article has problems that are flagged within it; whether it is simply factual or expresses opinions; whether the information is outdated; or even whether the web page has a history of multiple changes.

If you choose to cite a blog from IBM, use one of the following formats:


Richelle Newby, [New to data governance? Five best practices to get started, Journey to AI (blog), 9 September 2020.](https:/www.ibm.com/blogs/journey-to-ai/2020/09/new-to-data-governance-five-best-practices-to-get-started)


1 Richelle Newby, [New to data governance? Five best practices to get started, Journey to AI (blog), 9 September 2020.](https:/www.ibm.com/blogs/journey-to-ai/2020/09/new-to-data-governance-five-best-practices-to-get-started)


If you endorse or incorporate social media in content, ensure that you follow the policies in the [IBM Social Computing  Guidelines . These guidelines are reviewed and updated periodically to reflect emerging technologies and online social tools. For detailed guidance about linking to social media, see .](https:/w3.ibm.com/hr/web/empdata/social_computing_guidelines)

When you consider using a deep link, be aware of the risk that the website you are linking to might be changed or removed in the future. A deep link is a link to a speciﬁc page or image on a website instead of to the main or home page of a website. When you use a deep link, you assume responsibility for maintaining that link.

When referring to online documentation, including standard IBM publications, IBM Documentation, special IBM publications, and publications of other organizations or individuals, follow these guidelines:


Conﬁrm that the reference is a reliable source of information.


Ensure that use of the reference does not read as an endorsement when none is intended.


Verify that the reference is current and available.


Ensure that readers know what they can expect to ﬁnd in the referred-to information.

#### IBM Documentation

If you refer to product information in IBM Documentation (formerly known as IBM Knowledge Center), follow these guidelines:


Write the name IBM Documentation with initial uppercase D, with no preceding article, and always preceded by “IBM”.


Write the name IBM Documentation in plain font (no italic font, no double quotation marks).


You can also use IBM Docs to refer to IBM Documentation, following the same guidelines.


Link or refer to speciﬁc content and omit unnecessary references to the container of the information. For example, consider whether you can link directly to a topic and whether you must tell the user where that topic is located.


If you refer to a smaller piece within IBM Documentation for printed material, use double quotation marks.


Use a general term to refer to the type of content in IBM Documentation, such as “online product information”, “technical content”, or “publication”.


Do not refer to a subset of information in IBM Documentation as a “knowledge center” or an “information center”.

*Online information*


For more information, go to IBM Documentation and see [IBM Spectrum Conductor documentation . For more information, see](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/spectrum-conductor)


Detailed information is available in the [IBM Cognos Analytics  page in IBM Documentation. Detailed information is available in](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/cognos-analytics/11.1.0)


All online product information is now available in the [Documentation Center . All online product information is now available in](https:/www.ibm.com/docs)


For speciﬁc product publications, see [IBM Documentation .](https:/www.ibm.com/docs)


Online product technical content is available in [IBM Documentation . For API command details, see the Db2 documentation in](https:/www.ibm.com/docs)

If you cannot directly link to content, such as in printed material, then use double quotation marks.

*Printed material*


For more information, see “IBM Spectrum Conductor documentation” ( [https://www.ibm.com/docs/spectrum-conductor](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/spectrum-conductor) ). Detailed information is available in “IBM Cognos Analytics” ( [https://www.ibm.com/docs/cognos-analytics/11.1.0](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/cognos-analytics/11.1.0) ).

All online product documentation is now available in IBM Documentation ( [https://www.ibm.com/docs](https:/www.ibm.com/docs) ).

#### Special IBM publications

In addition to the guidelines in [General guidelines](.) , more guidelines apply when you refer to “special” IBM publications. To refer to IBM white papers, IBM case studies, and IBM developerWorks publications, follow the general guidelines above.

##### IBM Redbooks publications

IBM Redbooks content is developed and published by the IBM Digital Services Group, Technical Content Services (TCS). When you refer to an IBM Redbooks publication or associated materials such as IBM Redpapers, IBM Redguides, and IBM WebDocs, follow these guidelines:


Use the full title of the document.


Use an italic font for the title.


Provide the document number (without the sufﬁx) in a regular font (not an italic font).


Make a general reference to a Redbooks publication only when it might serve as an extra reference for solution-based information that might be of value to the client, but that does not describe an interface.


Do not make a general reference to a Redbooks publication from an area of a product publication that describes an interface. Such a reference can cause legal problems. The information that Redbooks publications contain, regardless of any disclaimers, might be considered product speciﬁcations or might contain other information that does not apply to the client’s environment. If clients apply incorrect information to their environments, legal problems might result.


If you must refer to a Redbooks publication from an area of a product publication that describes an interface, provide a speciﬁc reference to directly relevant information. In addition, ensure that a technical reviewer approves the cited information before you reference or link to it.


The term *Redbooks* is a registered trademark of IBM. Always spell the Redbooks name in the plural form, never in the singular form, and never in lowercase. For the initial reference, you must write “IBM Redbooks® publication” and include both “IBM” and the registered trademark symbol ®. For subsequent references, write “Redbooks publication”.

##### IBM Conﬁdential publications

You can refer to an IBM Conﬁdential publication from a nonconﬁdential publication only if you speciﬁcally state that the publication is conﬁdential and that it is available only with the approval of its owner or controller. However, product speciﬁcations must not refer to IBM Conﬁdential publications. You can refer to IBM Conﬁdential publications in other IBM Conﬁdential publications without stating the conditions of availability.

##### IBM Press publications

Do not copy content from IBM Press publications unless you have permission from the publisher. IBM does not own the copyright to IBM Press publications, the publisher does. Treat an IBM Press publication as an external resource.

##### Licensed publications

Avoid referring to a licensed publication (one that can be used only by clients who have signed a license agreement, acknowledging ownership by IBM and agreeing to the terms and conditions of the agreement) from a nonlicensed publication, because the licensed publication is unlikely to be available to all readers.

[Start of page](.)

#### Publications of other organizations or individuals

You can list or refer to publications of other organizations or individuals in an IBM publication only when such citations are essential to the intended use of the information. IBM avoids such citations because customers might infer that IBM endorses the cited publications, even if that is not the intent. In an annotated bibliography, avoid terms that convey value judgments such as “useful”, “good”, and “indispensable”.

In instances where IBM uses information from a non-IBM owned website for commercial purposes such as the marketing of IBM products or services, it must abide by the terms of use as stated on the non-IBM owned website. This might include restrictions on reproducing content in any manner (including citation) without express permission from the website owner. Read and abide by the terms of use for any non-IBM owned site.

Before you quote more than one sentence of text from non-IBM publications, obtain approval from your legal department or product IP attorney.

As in any other book citation, present titles of standards, such as ISO and ANSI standards, in an italic font. Citations for periodicals should include some or all of the following:


Full name(s) of author or authors


Title and subtitle of article or column inside double quotation marks


Title of periodical in italic font


Issue information (volume, issue number, date, etc.)


Page reference (where appropriate)


Online periodical citations should include a URL


Joseph Boyden. “The Lessons Not Learned from the Gulf Coast Oil Spill: It’s been a Year Since the BP Disaster, and Nobody has Learned Anything.” *Macleans* , May 2, 2011. [https://www.macleans.ca/news/world/spilling-over/](https:/www.macleans.ca/news/world/spilling-over)


Tom Simonite. “Watson Won *Jeopardy* , but Is It Smart Enough to Spin Big Blue’s AI Into Green?” *Wired,* July 21, 2017. [https://www.wired.com/story /ibm-watson-won-jeopardy -but-is-it-smart-enough-to-spin-big-blues-ai-into-green/](https:/www.wired.com/story/ibm-watson-won-jeopardy-but-is-it-smart-enough-to-spin-big-blues-ai-into-green)

*Online information*

*Printed material*

Unless you are limited by a contract, you can list or refer to publications of other companies in technical reports and in information that is not available to customers. You can also list or refer to these publications in academic papers, conference papers, and other works that are not sponsored by IBM and are understood to reflect the opinions of the individual rather than IBM as a company.

When citing publications in a video, follow the guidelines for a publication without a preface or bibliography, with one exception: provide the document number in only the transcript, not in the audio or captions. Also, two or three short citations at the end of a video are acceptable. If you need more, mention in the audio that more citations are available in the transcript. #### Quotations

When you include a standalone quotation in web pages, presentations, or other published content, follow this guidance:


Use short quotations, aiming for fewer than 165 characters.


Always include an attribution.


If the person who is quoted is not known globally, include the person’s title and company or institution afﬁliation, if applicable.


“Progress, not perfection.” – Rob Thomas, Senior Vice President, IBM Software

#### Videos, podcasts, and other online multimedia

Citations for such recorded media usually include some or all of the following information:


Name of the person primarily responsible for the content of the recording, for example composer, writer, or speaker.


The title in quotation marks or italics.


Recording company or publisher’s name, if applicable.


Identifying number, if applicable.


Type of medium, for example DVD, podcast, or YouTube.


Copyright, production, or performance date.


Entries for recorded material found online should also include a URL.

### Footnotes

Avoid using footnotes. Use a footnote only when information must be presented but including the information would disrupt the text.

Use a superscript numeral, a number written above and to the right of another character, to denote a footnote. Number footnotes consecutively throughout a chapter or topic so that the ﬁrst footnote in each chapter or topic is a superscript 1.


ﬁrst footnote1 second footnote2 third footnote3

If, because of the subject matter, a superscript numeral might be mistaken for a mathematical symbol, use a dagger symbol. Do not use an asterisk because it might be mistaken for another symbol such as the multiplication sign.


asterisk* dagger†

Place a footnote symbol at the end of the sentence or at the end of the clause to which the footnote applies. If a footnote explains a particular word or abbreviation, place the footnote symbol immediately after the word, abbreviation, or other item to which the footnote applies.


Sometimes an entire sentence requires a footnote.1 Sometimes, if it is appropriate,2 a footnote follows a clause. Sometimes a particular term3 requires a footnote.

If you use a footnote to cite information from another source, use the following guidelines:


Use a superscript number in the text to indicate the citation.


If the cited reference is used somewhere else in the document, reuse the same footnote number.


If there are several citations, list the references at the end of the document or in the bibliography of a book.


If citing a reference in a slide presentation, add the citation to the bottom of the slide. If there are several citations, you can also list them again on the last slide. If the reference cited is to online material, link directly to the reference in the slide. See the [Citations and references  topic for more information about linking strategies.](https:/ibmdocs-test.dcs.ibm.com/docs/en/ibm-style?topic=references-citations)


Use a superscript number and the following format in the list:


1“ *This is the title of the source,* ” Author, company/publication/website name, date, (written-out link, if applicable)


Optionally create inline links to the citations in the body of the document and in the list of citations.

In a table, use a superscript numeral or dagger symbol. Place the footnote deﬁnition within or as close to the table as possible so they are easily retrievable.


*Table 1. Device speciﬁcations*

| **Model**                | **Height**        | **Depth**         | **Width**         |
|--------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Tower                    | 440 mm (17.3 in.) | 747 mm (29.4 in.) | 218 mm (8.6 in.)  |
| 5U1 rack                 | 218 mm (8.6 in.)  | 696 mm (27.4 in.) | 424 mm (16.7 in.) |
| 1 A unit (U) is 4.45 cm. |                   |                   |                   |

| **1 Gbps Ethernet (iSCSi)**                    | **10 Gbps Ethernet-Copper (iSCSi)**   | **12 Gbps SAS**                                | **16 Gbps FC**                                 | **10 Gbps Ethernet-Optical (iSCSi/FCoE)**      |
|------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| 8 ports (with optional  adapter card feature1) | 4 ports (standard)                    | 8 ports (with optional  adapter card feature1) | 8 ports (with optional  adapter card feature1) | 8 ports (with optional  adapter card feature1) |

1 One optional I/O adapter card feature is allowed per Storwize V5000 control enclosure.

In online information, link the symbol for the footnote to the footnote text. Also, provide a link from the footnote text back to the symbol, and use the same character for both links..

### Geographic locations

When you refer to a geographic location, use the correct terminology and capitalization, use abbreviations appropriately, and ensure that the context of the location is clear.

#### Contents


[Correct terminology](.)


[Abbreviations](.)


[Capitalization](.)


[Context](.)


[IBM regions](.)

#### Correct terminology

When you refer to a geographic location, ensure that you use the correct terminology.


Use current terminology. Many cities and countries have changed names, and some references to regions are outdated. Use the most recent and appropriate terms.


Bombay, Ceylon, Far East, Turkey

Mumbai, Sri Lanka, East Asia, Türkiye or Turkiye (the umlaut is optional)


Use correct geographical terms. For example, do not use “state” to refer to a province or territory. Do not use “country” for a region that is not a country.


IBM only **Important:** Do not refer to Taiwan, Hong Kong, or Macao as countries. Do not use the term “Republic of China” or “R.O.C.” in references to Taiwan. Any instances of these terms in a product or documentation can stop shipment of the product. For more information, see the IBM Globalization guidelines for [References to Taiwan, Hong  Kong, or Macao .](http:/w3-03.ibm.com/globalization/page/1806)


Many laws are regulated at the state level in Canada. Many laws are regulated at the provincial level in Canada.


Conference attendance increased for countries such as Africa and Argentina. Conference attendance increased for African countries and Argentina.


Use neutral and unambiguous geographical terms. Some terms have a different meaning, or no meaning, in different geographies.


*Ambiguous:* Asian

*Unambiguous:* Southeast Asian


*Ambiguous:* East Coast lab

*Unambiguous:* lab in Boston, Massachusetts [Start of page](.)

#### Abbreviations

Many geographic regions, such as states, provinces, and countries, have abbreviations that might not be familiar to international audiences. For geographic abbreviations in general text, apply the standard [Abbreviations](.) guidance. That is, do not use an abbreviation that is unnecessary or unclear.


Portland ME (not to be confused with Portland OR) is the most populous city in Maine. Portland, Maine (not to be confused with Portland, Oregon) is the most populous city in Maine.


In 2005, GD surpassed HEN and SC to become the most populous province.

In 2005, Guangdong surpassed Henan and Sichuan to become the most populous province.

You can use an abbreviation for a geographic location if it is internationally recognized or if it is spelled out at the ﬁrst instance in text.


Many writers are unaware of the spelling variants between US and UK English.

Economic policy is geared towards creating steady growth and more jobs in the European Union (EU). The capital of the United States is Washington, DC.


For geographic abbreviations in formats other than general text, such as in postal addresses or bibliographies, follow the standard for that format. For example, you can ﬁnd information about how to address mail correctly from many national postal services, such as the [United States Postal Service  or](http:/pe.usps.gov/text/pub28/28c2_001.htm#ep526236)

[Start of page](.)

#### Capitalization

#### 


Capitalize places and names that appear on maps, such as continents, countries, cities, and bodies of water. Also capitalize adjectives or nouns that are formed from these terms.


Ireland, Irish Liverpool, Liverpudlian Atlantic Ocean


Capitalize regional terms that are accepted as places, but do not appear on maps. In general, use lowercase for the adjectives that are formed from these terms.


West Coast, westerner, western the South, southern

Paciﬁc Northwest, northwestern


Use lowercase for compass points when they refer to simple directions or locations. Also use lowercase for adjectives that are formed from these terms.


north wind southern climate eastern part of town sets in the west

[Start of page](.)

#### Context

Ensure that a reference to a geographic location provides enough context to make the location clear to the audience. The amount of context that is required for a geographic reference depends on several factors:


**Overall context:** If the context of a location is clear or explicitly stated, no further context is required. For example, if a report on sales in European capitals includes data for Paris, you can assume the audience understands it’s Paris, France and not Paris, Texas.


**Familiarity:** If the intended audience is familiar with a location, no further context is required. Determining familiarity requires judgment and knowledge of the audience; however, many locations are recognized internationally. For example, most countries, many well-known US states, and many large cities, such as Beijing, New York, or Rome, do not require further identiﬁcation. If you are unsure whether the audience knows a location, provide more context.


**Differentiation:** If a location could be confused with or needs to be contrasted with another location, provide further context.


The cycle tour includes stops in both Paris and London.

The cycle tour includes stops in both Paris and London in Ontario, Canada.


Many buildings in the Venice Canal Historic District are architecturally signiﬁcant.

Many buildings in the Venice Canal Historic District of Los Angeles are architecturally signiﬁcant.

Follow these guidelines to provide more context:


Provide the minimum amount of context to make the location clear. A reference does not need to include all geographic designators, only the ones that are signiﬁcant to the information and the audience.


*Extra context:* IBM headquarters are in Armonk, Westchester County, New York, United States.

*Enough context:* IBM headquarters are in Armonk, New York.


*Extra context:* The research grant was awarded to the University of Newcastle, New South Wales, Australia.

*Enough context:* The research grant was awarded to the University of Newcastle, Australia.


If several locations are mentioned, provide more context for only those that require it.


The conference included delegates from Benin, Africa and from Brazil.

The council assigns emission ratings to metropolitan areas such as Mexico City and Linfen, China. The company located its data centers in Tokyo and in Birmingham, England.


The extra context does not have to be the same format for each location.


Focus groups were conducted in Prague; Lake Bluff, Illinois; and La Paz, Bolivia.

The Cascadia fault line extends from Vancouver Island, Canada to Northern California.

[Start of page](.)

#### IBM regions

Capitalize these terms in all usages. Abbreviations can be used as indicated after ﬁrst reference or if for internal communication only and without IBM in front of each abbreviation. Do not use these abbreviations in technical documentation.


IBM Americas—includes the United States, Canada and Latin America IBM Europe/the Middle East/Africa—abbreviate as EMEA

IBM Asia Paciﬁc—abbreviate as APAC IBM Japan

### Names and titles

This topic provides general guidance to establish consistency in using personal names and titles associated with personal names.

#### Professional titles

When referring to an individual in combination with their job title, use headline-style capitalization, regardless of the order in which the title is used.

Examples:


Arvind Krishna, President and Chief Executive Ofﬁcer, IBM IBM President and Chief Executive Ofﬁcer Arvind Krishna IBM President and CEO Arvind Krishna

the President and Chief Executive Ofﬁcer of IBM, Arvind Krishna

When using a job title or role without also referring to the person who holds that position, use sentence-style case. Examples:


The chief ﬁnancial ofﬁcer of NewCo, Inc., is expected to announce 2Q earnings today.

Chief ﬁnancial ofﬁcers throughout the manufacturing sector are expected to announce 2Q earnings today.

When you write about a titled professional, use the full name on the ﬁrst occurrence, and the title and last name in all subsequent occurrences.


Dr. Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Dr. Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Dr. Curie won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.


If the person prefers to omit their title in subsequent mentions or elects not to use it at all, use their preferred form of address.  Dr. Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

#### Full name

The full name is the name by which a person wants to be identiﬁed. Usually, this name comprises one given name and one surname, but it might also include one or more middle names, a sufﬁx (such as “Jr.”), or an honoriﬁc (such as “Dr.”). Use “full name” as a ﬁeld label only when the full name is to be entered in a single ﬁeld. If the given name and surname are to be entered in separate ﬁelds, use the labels “given name” and “surname” for those ﬁelds.


Full name:

Full name:

Given name: 	Surname:

#### General guidelines

This topic provides general guidance and might not reflect the practice for speciﬁc products. If you have any questions about product names or versions, contact your product manager, release manager, or naming representative.

In the product user interface of any IBM digital offering, do not mark IBM trademarks. However, include a trademark attribution statement in the legal notice section within the offering and in the related product documentation, marketing, and sales information.

The following guidelines summarize the corporate guidance about using IBM trademarked terms and referring to product names in published content.


The ﬁrst reference to an IBM product name in each topic or book must be preceded by “IBM” and must include the designated trademark symbols ® or ™ as appropriate. Do not use a trademark symbol in a topic title unless the trademark does not occur in the body of the topic. The trademarking tool in ID Workbench implements this approach as its default behavior.


*First occurrence* : The MVS operating system

*First occurrence* : The IBM® MVS™ operating system


Always use the name or trademark of a product as an adjective qualifying a noun that is a generic description of the product or service.


With IMS™, you can ...

With an IMS™ subsystem, you can ...


WebSphere® includes over 150 products. WebSphere® software includes over 150 products.


Do not change the form or representation of the product name, including its capitalization or punctuation.


Websphere WebSphere


Use only approved names in social media, even when space is limited. Do not use unapproved shortened names or abbreviations. If in doubt, consult your naming and branding coordinator, or your local IP legal attorney.


Products are often known by internal “code” names during development. Do not use code names in external content; always use approved product names.


Warrior

IBM MQ Appliance


Do not use *’s* to show the possessive form of brand names or product names.


Use Rational Software Architect’s views to model systems or applications.

Use the views in Rational Software Architect to model systems or applications.


If a product has changed its name, seek advice from product management or your legal representative about how to refer to it. In general, refer to a product by its current name. However, if you refer to a speciﬁc release, use the name that was current for that release. Depending on the context, you might add “formerly known as ...” or “now known as ...”.


IBM Integration Bus (formerly known as WebSphere Message Broker) is based on an enterprise service bus ... The following updates were made to WebSphere Message Broker 8.0 (now known as IBM Integration Bus).


[For complete corporate guidance about using IBM trademarked terms and referring to product names, see IBM Copyright and trademark information .](http:/www.ibm.com/legal/us/en/copytrade.shtml)

#### Full ofﬁcial names and approved short names

The full ofﬁcial name generally contains all qualiﬁers, including the “IBM” company designation, brand name (if used), operating system designation, and version or design-level designation. For details, see the sections that follow.

Typically, approved short names consist of the full ofﬁcial name minus “IBM” and any platform and version identiﬁers. IBM does not maintain a corporate-wide list of approved short names. To determine a product’s approved short names, contact the branding or naming representative for your department or division. Do not use abbreviations or the initials of names unless they are speciﬁcally approved.

#### Topic-based information


Use the full ofﬁcial name for the ﬁrst reference to a product in each topic.


Use an approved short name for subsequent references within each topic.

#### Book-based information


Use the full ofﬁcial name at the ﬁrst occurrence in the introductory chapter.


Use an approved short form in subsequent references throughout the remainder of the book.

#### Topic and chapter titles

If the ﬁrst reference to a product is in a topic or chapter title, use an approved short form in the title, and use the full ofﬁcial name in the ﬁrst sentence of the topic or chapter.

#### Abbreviations

Do not abbreviate *IBM* to *I* in any product names.


IRAM

IBM Rational Asset Manager


IEM

IBM Endpoint Manager

Do not abbreviate product, brand, or service names in any publications unless the abbreviations are approved by branding and legal representatives. Abbreviating a company or product name dilutes the strength of a brand or trademark.

Write out product names in full on the ﬁrst and most prominent mention. Subsequently, use a generic reference to the product, or use a short name that is approved by branding and legal representatives. Contact your branding coordinator to conﬁrm that a product or name has an approved short name.

Do not abbreviate product names in user interfaces unless there is a critical lack of space, and only if you receive approval to do so from the legal representative for the product.


IWS

IBM Workload Scheduler (IWS is permitted in the UI)


RAD

Rational Application Developer


WAS

WebSphere Application Server *or* the application server [Start of page](.)

#### Software product names

Most full ofﬁcial software product names adhere to the following format: IBM + *Offering Name* [+ for *Operating System* ] + *version number*

For more information about version number identiﬁers, see [Product versions](.) .


IBM DB2 Database Partitioning Feature for Linux, UNIX, and Windows IBM Producer Lifecycle and Credential Management 9.0.1

IBM Platform Symphony 7.1

Do not capitalize the word *software* when it follows the word *IBM* or the brand name. The only exception is when a design-related requirement calls for initial capital letters or all uppercase.


IBM WebSphere Software IBM WebSphere software

To ensure consistency, contact the appropriate branding and naming representative or the sponsor of the name to determine the conventions that you should use.


IBM only Contacts are listed at the [Product Pages .](https:/w3.ibm.com/systems/productpages)

#### Service names

Most full ofﬁcial service names adhere to the following format: IBM + *a Generic Descriptor* + Services


IBM Emerging Server Technology Services IBM Data Security Services

IBM SmoothStart Services

Use the full ofﬁcial name for the ﬁrst reference to a product in a publication other than marketing and sales content or an advertising headline.

[Start of page](.)

#### Terms that include “as a service”

When writing about a kind of service that includes “as a service” in the term, do not hyphenate the words. Do not capitalize the words unless the term is part of an ofﬁcial product name, in which case, Service would be capitalized. When abbreviating “as a service” in a term to *X* aaS, where *X* is a type of service, the S is uppercase.

For product names that include “as a Service”, only use “aaS” if the product has that in its legal short name.


Example terms


database-as-a-service Identity as a Service

S-a-a-S

database as a service = DBaaS desktop as a service = DaaS identity as a service = IDaaS infrastructure as a service = IaaS platform as a service = PaaS software as a service = SaaS


Example product names


IBM Backup as a Service (BaaS)

IBM Cyber Recovery as a Service (has no acronym) IBM Digital Workplace as a Service (DWaaS)

IBM Workplace Analytics as a Service (has no acronym) [Start of page](.)

#### Advertising headlines and marketing and sales content

Version and release identiﬁers should generally not be used in names in advertising headlines or other marketing and sales content unless the purpose of the advertisement is to announce a new model, version, or release. In this case, to ensure clear communication, announcement text can indicate the version and release information before the full product name.


Version 3 release 1 of CICS Transaction Server for z/OS includes the following improvements: *xx, yy,* and *zz* . [Start of page](.)

#### Generic names in text

In some cases, generic names can be used in text that describes the product. After the ﬁrst reference to a product or service in a document, use a generic name for most or all subsequent references. In general, use the same generic name throughout the content. Choose a generic name that is not ambiguous in the context. Consider explaining all the generic names in the preface or introduction.


The server The compiler The processor The service

In service information, when you write about an IBM hardware device, consider using its IBM machine-type number, such as 3179 or 8775, as the name; the numbers do not require translation by service representatives in non-English-speaking countries.

[Start of page](.)

#### Related resources


[IBM Copyright and trademark information](http:/www.ibm.com/legal/us/en/copytrade.shtml)


IBM only [IBM Corporate naming guidelines](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/brand-naming-guidelines)

### Product versions

**Important note** : This topic provides general guidance and might not reflect the practice for speciﬁc products. If you have any questions about product names or versions, contact your product manager, release manager, or naming representative.

When you refer to the full product name, you can mirror the capitalization that is used in the product interface and packaging.
