#### Version, release, and modiﬁcation identiﬁers

Identiﬁers provide important information for customers and are an extension of the software product name. At the ﬁrst occurrence in text, it is preferable to spell out the full ofﬁcial name of the product and the version, release, and modiﬁcation level.

First occurrence in text:


IBM® MQ 9.2 contains the following updates...

In references to an ofﬁcial product name, do not use the words *Version* or *Release* or the abbreviations *V* or *R* . In running text, it is acceptable to use the word *version* , lowercase, to make a generic reference to a product name that has already been mentioned.

Always verify that the format that you use is acceptable to the naming representative for your product.

IBM only For full version number guidance, see the [IBM Naming  Guidelines](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/brand-naming-guidelines/products-services#ProductVersioning) . For IBM Support guidelines for referring to version, release, modiﬁcation level, and ﬁx pack numbers, see [IBM Software product versioning  explained](https:/www.ibm.com/support/pages/ibm-software-product-versioning-explained) .

To identify a product version, such as to clarify when a feature was added or a defect was ﬁxed, include the speciﬁc version, release, modiﬁcation level, and ﬁx pack number (if applicable) in which the change was made. Do not include a trailing x in the number to represent all ﬁx packs for a modiﬁcation, all modiﬁcations for a release, or all releases for a version because doing so is redundant.


This feature does not apply if you are working with Version 5.1.1.1. This update applies to WebSphere Message Broker 6.1.x.

This update applies to WebSphere Message Broker 6.1.

This feature was introduced with WebSphere Message Broker 6.1.3. If you are working with IBM Notes 9.2...

When the product name has already been mentioned:


This feature does not apply if you are working with version 5.1.1.1.

See speciﬁc guidance for [Advertising  headlines and marketing  and sales content](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Book edition notices


In edition notices, it is acceptable to use the word *Version* . Spell out *Version* by using an uppercase *V* .  Version 8.1.1

For more information about referring to versions in books, see the “Title page” section of the [Books](.) topic.

[Start of page](.)

#### References to multiple releases

If you have to refer to more than one release (for example 5.1, 5.1.1, 5.2, and 5.2.1 but not 6.1), do not use a convention such as 5.x or 5.n. Instead, write out the information completely. If the product name changes but the numbering scheme continues, use both product names.


This update applies to all releases of version 5.

This function can be used with DB2 Universal Database 5 (all releases). This change affects 7.1, 7.1.1, and 7.2.

This change affects iSeries Access for Windows 5.4 and System i Access for Windows 5.5.

[Start of page](.)

#### Migration and upgrades

When you write information about migrating or upgrading to the latest version from more than one previous version, order the previous versions so that the most recent version comes ﬁrst.


Use this command to create new components in version 6.1, based on existing components in version 5.1, 4.2, or 4.1. [Start of page](.)

#### References to earlier or later versions

To state a requirement that includes earlier or later versions of a product, use the phrases *or earlier* to indicate earlier versions and *or later* to indicate subsequent versions.


To use the transformers, you need DB2 Universal Database 5.1 or later. This memo applies to IBM Mobile Connect 3.2 or earlier.

Install DB2 Database for Linux, UNIX, and Windows 9.7 or later.

[Start of page](.)

#### Operating systems as part of product names

Most software product names include the name of an operating system. This is the standard format: IBM + *offering name* + for *operating system version number.release number*

Unless it is part of the approved, ofﬁcial product name, do not include extra punctuation, such as a comma, in the name.


IBM® XL C/C++ for Linux, 16.1.1 IBM® XL C/C++ for Linux 16.1.1

For more information about referring to product names, see [Product and service names](.) . [Start of page](.)

#### Industry practice

It is common practice in the software industry to refer to the ﬁrst release of the ﬁrst version of a program as 1.1. There is no longer a legal concern that it implies a commitment to produce a second version or release.


IBM WebSphere Studio for Multiplatforms 3.1 [Start of page](.)

#### Advertising headlines and marketing and sales content

In general, do not use version and release identiﬁers in names in advertising headlines or other marketing and sales content unless the purpose of the advertisement is to announce a new model, version, or release. In this case, to ensure clear communication, announcement text can indicate the version and release information before the full product name.


Version 3 release 1 of CICS Transaction Server for z/OS includes the following improvements: *xx* , *yy* , and *zz* . For more information about writing for marketing content, see [Marketing](.) .

[Start of page](.)

### Code and command examples

Where necessary for clarity, use examples to help show how to write code and use commands. Present code and command examples clearly and consistently.

Follow these guidelines for code and command examples:


Use examples to support text, not replace it. Do not expect users to extrapolate instructions from examples.


Use a monospaced font to show examples. To emphasize a new or changed line, you can use a bold monospaced font. To make it easier for users to follow the flow of an example, consider using indentation.


The following code example demonstrates how to begin a nested work area. The name of the creating class identiﬁes the nested work area.

###### public class SimpleSampleBeanImpl implements SessionBean {

**public String [] test() {**

**...**

**String invoker = userWorkArea.getName();**

###### try {

**userWorkArea.set("key", "value");**

**}**

###### catch (NotOriginator e) {

**}**

**// Begin a nested work area. By using the name of the creating**

**// class as the name of the work area, you can avoid explicitly**

**// setting the name of the creating class in the work area.**

**userWorkArea.begin("SimpleSampleBean");**

**...**

**}**

**}**


To introduce a multiline example, use one of the following approaches:


A complete sentence. If the example is immediately after the introductory sentence, end the sentence with a colon. If other sentences intervene between the introductory sentence and the example, end each sentence with a period.


A short, simple sentence fragment, such as “For example”. End the fragment with a colon.


Do not start a sentence before an example and continue the sentence after the example.  The following example:

**SELECT FLOOR( 3.5),**

**FLOOR(3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.5)**

**FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1**

results in these values:

**03. 03. -04. -04.**

Instead, write one or more complete introductory sentences. The introduction can describe the example input and its result or not.


The following example uses the **FLOOR** function, which returns the largest integer value that is less than or equal to the argument:


The following example uses the **FLOOR** function. The function returns the largest integer value that is less than or equal to the argument.


For example:

**SELECT FLOOR( 3.5), FLOOR(3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.1),**

**FLOOR(-3.5)**

**FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1**


Use a separate complete sentence to describe the results.  The results of the query are as follows:

**03. 03. -04. -04.**


If you use an inline example, ensure that it is part of a complete sentence, not just a sentence fragment.


For example, **db2 ping hostdb 5 times** .

For example, enter **db2 ping hostdb 5 times** . For example, **Floor(3.5)** returns 3.


Even if the example is at the end of a sentence, end the example with a period. Consider putting the example on a separate line in the following cases:


If the period at the end of the sentence might be mistaken for part of the example


If the example contains a period that might not be recognized as part of the example


If it is likely that the example will be copied and pasted and the period might be incorrectly included or omitted In Prolog, queries end with a period, as shown in the following example:

###### ?- animal(cat).


Use a consistent approach for captioning examples. You might choose to show large examples as ﬁgures, with appropriate captions, and embed small examples within the text, without captions. If you use captions, use informative ones that help the reader to identify the examples in the table of contents.


If you indent examples, use a consistent approach.


If a user must enter code or a command on one line but the example does not ﬁt on one line in your output, explain that in introductory text.


Enter the following command on one line:

###### start very long command that has lots and lots of parameters and must be entered without any carriage returns or continuation characters


If the example is from software that uses continuation characters, show the example exactly as it is displayed in the program.


Enter the command as follows:

###### start very long command that has lots and lots of parameters \ and must be entered with the backslash continuation character


Avoid overly long examples. It is harder to maintain an understanding of an example that must be broken up, such as across several screens in a video or slides in a presentation. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .


Use ellipses to omit parts of code snippets that do not contribute to the example you want to illustrate. To omit one or more lines of code, add an ellipsis to its own line.


Specify your custom stop words in a comma-separated list, as shown in the following example:

**{**

**"a", "an", "the", "what", "when", ...**

**]**

**}**

### Command line data entry

### 

Use speciﬁc terminology when you tell users to provide data. Highlight that data in a monospaced font, and explain clearly how to provide that data.

In documentation for only Windows operating systems, use *command prompt* . In documentation for other operating systems or for both Windows and other operating systems, use *command line* .


*Windows operating systems:* At the command prompt, enter the name of the ﬁle.

*Other or mixed operating systems:* On the command line, enter the name of the ﬁle.

To instruct users to provide data on the command line or at the command prompt, use *type* or *enter* . If users can provide data in several ways or can use a method other than a keyboard to provide data, such as voice-activated software, consider using *specify* .


On the command line, type your password.

At the command prompt, enter your password. When prompted, specify your user ID.


Use a monospaced font for the data that users provide.  Correct example:

Enter the following text:

**/Y,N/**


Spell and capitalize data the same way that the user must provide it.  Type **/REPLY 02,0/** .

If the data includes a variable, show the variable in an italic monospaced font. Explain immediately afterward what the variable

represents. Use an italic monospaced font for the variable in the explanation. Optionally, use the word *where* , with a lowercase *w* , to introduce the explanations.


Incorrect example:

Type the following text:

###### filename REPLACE


where **filename** speciﬁes the name of the replacement ﬁle.  Correct example:

Type the following text:

***filename*** **REPLACE**

where ***filename*** speciﬁes the name of the replacement ﬁle.

To explain multiple items, consider creating a vertical list for better readability by using the following guidelines:


Unless you are limited by your authoring tool, use a simple list or deﬁnition list, as shown in the examples. If your authoring tool prevents you from using these types of lists, use a different but clear and consistent format.


If you introduce a list with the word **where** , use a colon after **where** . Use a consistent style for descriptions in lists.


If you use a deﬁnition list, start all descriptions with a full sentence, or start all descriptions with a sentence fragment. If you use sentence fragments, start each one with the third-person form of a verb, or start each one with a noun phrase. Start each description with an uppercase letter.


Correct example:

Type the following ﬁle names:

**input\_filename, output\_filename, error\_filename**

where:

**input\_filename**

Speciﬁes the name of the input ﬁle.

**output\_filename**

Speciﬁes the name of the output ﬁle.

**error\_filename**

Speciﬁes the name of the ﬁle to which any errors are written.


Correct example:

Type the following ﬁle names:

**input\_filename, output\_filename, error\_filename input\_filename**

The name of the input ﬁle.

**output\_filename**

The name of the output ﬁle.

**error\_filename**

The name of the ﬁle to which any errors are written.


If you use a simple list, start all descriptions with a sentence fragment that starts with the third-person form of a verb and a lowercase letter.


Correct example:

Type the following ﬁle names:

**input\_filename, output\_filename, error\_filename**


**input\_filename** is the name of the input ﬁle.


**output\_filename** is the name of the output ﬁle.


**error\_filename** is the name of the ﬁle to which any errors are written.

If users might mistake the punctuation for part of the data to enter, rewrite the sentence.


Type the following characters: **/\*%$** . Correct example:

Type the following characters:

**/\*%$**

### Command syntax

To specify simple command syntax, such as in task topics, use text. To specify complex syntax, such as in reference topics, use syntax diagrams (also referred to as *railroad diagrams* ) if your authoring tool supports them; otherwise, use text.

#### Contents


[Using  text to specify command syntax](.)


[Using  diagrams to specify command syntax](.)

#### Using text to specify command syntax

Follow these guidelines to specify syntax by using text:


If necessary, explain the syntax conventions in your documentation. For example, in a book, include the explanation of syntax conventions in the preface or in an introductory chapter.


Use a monospaced font for a command name. If a parameter or option is a variable value, use an italic monospaced font; otherwise, use a monospaced font. If it is likely that a user will paste a variable value from the documentation into a location that does not support an italic font, such as a command line or script, you can enclose the variable in angle brackets. Angle

brackets can make it easier for users to identify variables that must be replaced where an italic font is not supported. Apply the italic font to both the angle brackets and the variable.


To ensure that the daemon is synchronized, enter **lssrc -ls xntpd** .  Type the following command:

**db2dclgn -d** ***sample*** **-t** ***employee\_resume*** **-l cobol -a replace**


In your script, include the following command:

**db2 BACKUP DATABASE** ***&lt;database\_alias&gt;*** **USER** ***&lt;username&gt;*** **USING** ***&lt;password&gt;*** **TO** ***&lt;backup\_directory&gt;***


For a non-numeric variable, use a short, descriptive term, such as *ﬁlename* . For a numeric variable, use one of the following options:


A short, descriptive word, such as **max**


A single letter, such as **n**


Multiple letters, such as **nnnn** , if it helps users to understand the number of digits that they must specify

When you use words to represent variables, consider using complete words or phrases to help communicate the meaning of the variable to the audience.

If you can specify the same variable multiple times, use two consecutive letter or number sufﬁxes with the name, as in **max1** , **max2** or **n1** , **n2** , and use an ellipsis to indicate that more variables can follow.


Enter the following command:

###### LOAD filename1, filename2, ...

If you must use a multiple-word variable name, remove the spaces between the words, or connect the words with underscores, for example, **database\_name** . Base your decision on clarity and the convention for the technology that you are documenting, if applicable.


Use vertical bars to separate alternative values.


Use the **set monitor** command to turn the monitor on or off:

**set monitor on|off**


Enclose optional items in square brackets.  Enter the following command:

###### copy filename[filetype]


Underline default parameter values.


Use the **set monitor** command to turn the monitor on or off. If you do not specify on or off, off is selected automatically.

**set monitor on|** off


Use braces to enclose a choice of values.  The syntax is as follows:

**docker exec -it Db2wh manage\_hadr {-start\_as {primary|standby}|-stop|-status|-enable\_acr**

**[ssl]|-update\_db}**

Explain the meanings of items in the syntax immediately after showing the syntax:


Be consistent in explaining both the parameters and options or explaining just the options.


*Explains both the parameters and options*

Enter the following command:

###### connect -u username -p password

**-u username** speciﬁes the name of a user with administrator authority and **-p password** speciﬁes the associated password.


*Explains only the options*

Enter the following command:

###### connect -u username -p password

**username** is the name of a user with administrator authority and **password** is the associated password.


Optionally, use the word **where** , with a lowercase **w** , to introduce the explanations.  Enter the following command:

###### connect -u username -p password

where **username** is the name of a user with administrator authority and **password** is the associated password.


To explain multiple items, consider creating a vertical list for better readability by using the following guidelines:


Unless you are limited by your authoring tool, use a simple list or deﬁnition list for a main list, and use an unordered list or deﬁnition list for a nested list, as shown in the examples. If your authoring tool prevents you from using these types of lists, use a different but clear and consistent format.


If you introduce a list with the word *where* , use a colon after *where* .


Use a consistent style for descriptions:


If you use a deﬁnition list, start all descriptions with either a full sentence or a sentence fragment. If you use sentence fragments, start each one either with the third-person form of a verb or with a noun phrase. Start each description with an uppercase letter.


If you use a simple list or unordered list, start all descriptions with a sentence fragment that starts with the third-person form or a verb and a lowercase letter.


*Deﬁnition list that is prefaced by where and uses sentence fragments that start with the third-person form of a verb*

To test the performance of your queries, enter the following command:

**db2batch -d dbname -f input\_filename -r output\_filename**

where:

**-d** ***dbname***

Speciﬁes the database against which to run the queries.

**-f** ***input\_filename***

Speciﬁes the input ﬁle containing your queries.

**-r** ***output\_filename***


Speciﬁes the ﬁle to which the results of the command are written. *Deﬁnition list that uses sentence fragments that contain noun phrases* To test the performance of your queries, enter the following command:

**db2batch -d dbname -f input\_filename -r output\_filename**

**-d** ***dbname***

The database against which to run the queries.

**-f** ***input\_filename***

The input ﬁle containing your queries.

**-r** ***output\_filename***

The ﬁle to which the results of the command are written.


*Simple list*

To test the performance of your queries, enter the following command:

**db2batch -d dbname -f input\_filename -r output\_filename**


**-d dbname** speciﬁes the database against which to run the queries.


**-f input\_filename** speciﬁes the input ﬁle containing your queries.


**-r output\_filename** speciﬁes the ﬁle to which the results of the command are written.

*Simple list, prefaced by where, that contains a nested unordered list*

To test your program, enter the following command:

**run -p program\_name -t trc\_level**

where:


**-p program\_name** indicates the name of the program.


**-t trc\_level** indicates the degree to which code execution is traced.


1 indicates ...

Unless your authoring tool imposes a different standard, use a bold monospaced font for parameters and a monospaced font for options, except for variable values. Use an italic monospaced font for variables. If you use angle brackets in the syntax, include the angle brackets in the variable description.


Optionally, use text to indicate whether an item is required, is optional, is the default, or can be speciﬁed multiple times. Use consistent wording.


###### copy filename[filetype]

#### Using diagrams to specify command syntax

Syntax diagrams visually represent command syntax. An example of a syntax diagram follows.


**Important** : Syntax diagrams are inaccessible to users of screen readers. Both the dotted decimal format and Backus-Naur Form (BNF) are alternative formats that are accessible by screen readers.


[IBM only To learn how to create DITA-sourced syntax diagrams, see Tutorial: Creating  Syntax Diagrams for Programming  Languages](https:/ibmdocs-test.dcs.ibm.com/docs/en/dcs-doc?topic=tutorials-tutorial-creating-syntax-diagrams-programming-languages) [. Because syntax diagrams are inaccessible to users of screen readers, you must also provide an alternative accessible format. Th](https:/ibmdocs-test.dcs.ibm.com/docs/en/dcs-doc?topic=tutorials-tutorial-creating-syntax-diagrams-programming-languages) e IDWB tools automatically create an alternative accessible format.

If space is limited or information must be absorbed quickly, such as in a video or presentation, show only basic syntax and use text, not syntax diagrams. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) .

Follow these guidelines to specify syntax by using a syntax diagram:


Explain the syntax conventions in your documentation. For example, in a book, include the explanation of syntax conventions in the preface or in an introductory chapter. In topic-based information, provide a topic about command-syntax conventions.


Use the following basic components in the syntax diagram. If your authoring tool supports syntax diagrams, see the tool documentation for detailed information about how to create these components.


Use two right-facing arrowheads and a dash (&gt;&gt;-) to indicate the beginning of a syntax diagram. Use a dash, a right-facing arrowhead, and a left-facing arrowhead (-&gt;&lt;) to indicate the end of a syntax diagram. If you cannot show all the syntax on a single line, use a dash and a right-facing arrowhead (-&gt;) to indicate that the syntax is continued on the next line. Use a right-facing arrowhead and a dash (&gt;-) to indicate that the syntax is continued from the previous line.


Put required items on the main path. The following diagram shows that the **DETACH** command name is required.



Put optional items below the main path. The following diagram shows that the **SHOW DETAILS** parameter is optional.



Put choices in a stack. If users must choose at least one of the items, put the ﬁrst item in the stack on the main path. The following diagram shows that users must choose between the **on** and **off **parameters.


If users do not have to choose any of the items in a stack, put the entire stack below the main path. The following diagram shows that users can specify a parameter such as **BACKUP** , **ROLLFORWARD** , and others or can specify none of the parameters.


If one of the items in a stack is the default, put it above the main path. The following diagram shows that **verbose** is the default parameter.



Use a monospaced font for a command name and for parameters and options that are not variable values. For variable values, use an italic monospaced font.

For a non-numeric variable, use a short, descriptive term, such as **filename** . For a numeric variable, use one of the following options:


A short, descriptive word, such as **max**


A single letter, such as **n**


Multiple letters, such as **nnnn** , if it helps users to understand the number of digits that they must specify

If there are variations on the same type of variable, you can follow the word or letter with a number, such as **max1** , **max2** , and so on or **n1** , **n2** , and so on.

If you must use a multiple-word variable name, remove the spaces between the words, or connect the words with underscores, for example, **database\_name** . Base your decision on clarity and the convention for the technology that you are documenting, if applicable.

The following diagram shows that users must provide a database name and can optionally specify an alias name.



Indicate that users can specify an item more than once or can specify more than one item by using an arrow above the main path that returns to the left. The following diagram shows that users can specify a ﬁle name, pipe name, device name, or the other options multiple times. The separator for multiple or repeated values, if required, is shown on the arrow. In the example, each name must be separated by a comma.


Explain the parameters and their options after the syntax diagram, as follows:


In general, describe the parameters and their options in the same order in which you display the parameters and their options in the syntax diagram. However, if the order of parameters is not signiﬁcant for the command and the parameters are numerous, alphabetize the descriptions to improve retrievability.


Use a deﬁnition list to specify the parameters and options and their descriptions, unless there are multiple options for a parameter. If a user can specify multiple options for a parameter, specify those options and their descriptions in a nested deﬁnition list or nested unordered list.


Unless your authoring tool imposes a different standard, use a bold monospaced font for parameters and a monospaced font for options, except for variable values. Use an italic monospaced font for variables.


Use a consistent style for descriptions in a particular list:

### Commands

#### Capitalization

If the command language is case-sensitive, show the commands, parameters, and options as they must be entered from the console, terminal, or keyboard. If the command language is not case-sensitive, show the commands, parameters, and options in lowercase. If you write information for multiple operating systems and the command language is case-sensitive on one operating system but not on the others, show the commands, parameters, and options in the case-sensitive form.

#### Commands, parameters, and options in general text

In general text, use a bold monospaced font for a command. If a parameter or option is a variable value, use an italic monospaced font; otherwise, use a bold monospaced font for the parameter and a monospaced font for the option.


Use the **BROWSE** command. Use the **Copy** command.

To copy the ﬁle, specify the **copy** command with the **ﬁlename** parameter.

Generally, when you specify the name of a command, parameter, or option in text, specify the word *command* , *parameter* , or *option* after the name. Command, parameter, and option names are not translated; without the identifying noun, users might be confused about what the name represents.

Exceptions to the guideline are as follows:


If you are specifying a sequence of commands, parameters, or options, you can specify the identifying noun after only the last item in the sequence.


You can omit the identifying noun in a column of commands, parameters, or options if the column heading includes the identifying noun.


You can omit the identifying noun in a list of commands, parameters, or options if the introduction to the list includes the identifying noun.

Alternatively, refer to a command, parameter, or option by using a lowercase descriptive phrase, such as one that includes an adjective and a noun.


You can use **db2trc** to record information about operations.

You can use the **db2trc** command to record information about operations. You can use the trace facility to record information about operations.

You can use the **db2iauto** , **db2icrt** , **db2idrop** , **db2ilist** , and **db2imgr** commands.

Do not use a command name as a verb. Using command names as verbs can cause problems for translation.


**REORG** the database.

To reorganize the database, use the **REORG** command.


IMPORT the data.

To import the data, use the **IMPORT** command.

#### Commands, parameters, and options in instructions

To instruct users to enter commands, use a verb such as *run* , *type* , *enter* , or *issue* . Use one term consistently throughout your information.

To refer to the area where you enter commands, in documentation for only Windows operating systems, use *command prompt* . In documentation for other operating systems or for both Windows and other operating systems, use *command line* .

When you tell users to run, type, enter, or issue a command on a command line or at a command prompt, use a monospaced font for the command name.

If a parameter or option is a variable value, use an italic monospaced font; otherwise, use a monospaced font. If it is likely that a user will paste a variable value from the documentation into a location that does not support an italic font, such as a command line or script, you can enclose the variable in angle brackets. Angle brackets can make it easier for users to identify variables that must be replaced where an italic font is not supported. Apply the italic font to both the angle brackets and the variable.

### Files and directories

Use correct capitalization, highlighting, punctuation, and grammatical constructions when you refer to ﬁle names, ﬁle name extensions, ﬁle types, and directory names. A ﬁle type is a word or uppercase abbreviation that indicates the kind of ﬁle, such as PDF. A ﬁle name extension is the portion of a ﬁle name that follows the dot, such as *exe* in **install.exe** .

Follow these guidelines:


Use lowercase for ﬁle names and directory names for operating systems and application programs that are not case-sensitive. For a case-sensitive operating system or application program, use the capitalization that is used in the operating system or application program. Highlight ﬁle names, ﬁle name extensions, and directory names in a monospaced font.

For information that applies to multiple operating systems, be consistent and describe the convention if necessary.


Windows operating systems use a backslash (\) to delimit directories in a directory path.

AIX operating systems and web addresses use a forward slash (/) as a delimiter. This information uses forward slashes for all delimiters. Depending on your operating system, you might have to enter directory paths differently from what is shown in the examples.


When you know that your audience uses an operating systems such as AIX, Linux, or Apple macOS, you can use a tilde ( **~** ) to represent the user’s home directory in a ﬁle path. For example, for a ﬁle named **myfile.json** that is stored in the

**/Users/jdoe/Documents** directory, you can specify the ﬁle path as follows:


**~/Documents/myfile.json**


If a path does not ﬁt on one line, end the ﬁrst line after an existing forward slash or backslash, and continue the path on the next line. Do not add a hyphen to indicate a break in a path.

#### Variables

For a non-numeric variable, use a short, descriptive term in an italic monospace font, such as ***filename*** . For a numeric variable, use one of the following options:


A short, descriptive word in an italic monospace font, such as ***max***


A single letter in an italic monospace font, such as ***n***


Multiple letters in an italic monospace font, such as ***nnnn*** , if it helps users to understand the number of digits that they must specify

When you use words to represent variables, consider using complete words or phrases to help communicate the meaning of the variable to the audience.

If there are variations on the same type of variable, you can follow the word or letter with a number, such as ***max1*** , ***max2*** , and so on, or ***n1*** , ***n2*** , and so on.

If you must use a multiple-word variable name, remove the spaces between the words, or connect the words with underscores, for example, ***databaseName*** or ***database\_name*** . Base your decision on clarity and the convention for the technology that you are documenting, if applicable.

If it is likely that a user will paste a variable value from the documentation into a location that does not support an italic font, you can enclose the variable in angle brackets. Angle brackets can make it easier for users to identify variables that must be replaced where an italic font is not supported. Apply the italic font to both the angle brackets and the variable.

#### Location of interface elements

**Accessibility and globalization requirement:** People who have limited vision, or who use interfaces that are translated into a bidirectional language, might not understand information if it is conveyed only by location. When you refer to the location of an element in a graphical user interface, do not use only sensory words, such as *top* , *bottom* , *right* , or *left* . In addition to sensory words, refer to the element by its label or tooltip. Although in English and some other languages, *above* and *below* are commonly understood to refer to content prior to or after a point in the content, alternatives are available:


*top* : *beginning* or *start* ; often can be removed

Select an action from the menu bar on the header.


*bottom* : *end*


Scroll to the bottom of the page. Scroll to the end of the page.


*below* : *that follows* or *following* ; often can be removed


Select an option from the list below the table.

Select an option from the **Data types** list, following the table.


*right* (location) or *left* : can be removed or supplemented with the UI label


The list of tables is displayed in the upper-right corner of the window.

The tables are displayed in the Table List pane in the upper-right corner of the window.

For more information about creating accessible content, see the [Accessibility](.) topic. [Start of page](.)

The omission of the punctuation would result in confusion over the meaning of the interface element.

Use one of the following approaches when you refer to an interface element:


For some interface elements, as shown in the table in this topic, use the label, title, descriptive name, or name that is indicated by the tooltip, followed by the type of the interface element.


In the **User** ﬁeld, type the administrator ID that you created when you conﬁgured the server. From the **Resolution** list, select a resolution.


For other interface elements, as shown in the table in this topic, use only the label, title, descriptive name, or name that is indicated by the tooltip. However, if an interface contains elements with the same label or very similar labels, include the element type to ensure clarity.


Click the **Enable content** radio button. [If there is an element with the same name or a similar name.] Click **Enable content** . [In all other situations]


For all elements, if users clearly know which element to use, use only the type of the element, or tell users to perform the action without using the label, title, descriptive name, name that is indicated by the tooltip, or type.


*Examples that show only the type of the element*

In the ﬁeld, type the administrator ID that you created when you conﬁgured the server. From the list, select a resolution.


*Examples that tell the user to perform a task, without referring to the interface elements*

Type the administrator ID that you created when you conﬁgured the server. Specify a resolution.

If the settings are correct, conﬁgure the device.

Some elements, such as checkboxes and radio buttons, have a visual state that indicates when the element is selected. People might be confused if they are told to select an element that is already selected, or to clear an element that is not selected. If you are aware of the state of the element, for example during an installation process, use the standard verbs as shown in the “Usage and highlighting for user interface elements” table. If you are unaware of the state of the element, use the wording “Ensure that” at the start of the instruction, and provide the required state at the end of the instruction.


*Unknown visual state for a checkbox:* Ensure that the **Full report** checkbox is not selected.

*Unknown visual state for a radio button:* Ensure that **List view** is selected.

*Known visual state for a checkbox:* Clear the **Full report** checkbox.

*Known visual state for a radio button:* Click **List view** .

In most cases, avoid describing the result of an action. If you think that the context is clear, do not provide locational information. If the context isn’t clear, and you must orient the user to the location where that step is performed, provide locational information at the start of the sentence.


*Incorrect example*

1. Click **Fonts** . The **Fonts** list is displayed.
2. Select **Times New Roman** .

*If the context is clear*

1. Click **Fonts** .
2. Select **Times New Roman** .

*If the context isn’t clear*

1. Click **Fonts** .
2. From the **Fonts** list, select **Times New Roman** .

For group elements such as windows, menus, lists, and group boxes, you can use the verb form “is displayed” to describe the presence of the element on the screen. For windows and wizards, you can use “opens” to describe the immediate result of a user action. Do not use “appears” or the active verb “displays”.


Click **Help** . The help ﬁle appears in a separate browser window. Click **Help** . The help ﬁle opens in a separate browser window.

Do not use a label as a generic noun or verb.


Type your **Password** . Specify a **Resolution** .

If the settings are correct, **Conﬁgure** the device.

LLM helper For graphical items such as push buttons or icons, if users would beneﬁt from seeing the graphic, include it after the label or tooltip name. If the graphical item does not have a label or name, provide a generic description.


On the toolbar, click the **Permanent Pen** icon .  Click the ellipsis button .

Avoid using food names, such as *hamburger menu* , *kebab icon* , and *toast notiﬁcation* to refer to interface elements. Instead, refer to the element’s function or use the tooltip, if available.


- *Where the element opens a menu and has no tooltip*

Click the hamburger menu. Click the main menu icon.


- *Where the element opens a menu and its tooltip is “Node options”*

Click the kebab icon.

Click the **Node options** icon.


- *Where the element is a non-modal, time-based notiﬁcation*

A toast notiﬁcation shows a success message. A success message is displayed briefly.

#### Tagging considerations


Always use the semantic tagging of your authoring tool to produce the correct output. This practice ensures that entities are highlighted consistently and improves translation. For example, to highlight a user interface control in DITA, use the **&lt;uicontrol&gt;** tag, not the **&lt;b&gt;** tag. If you author in DITA, consult the [DITA highlighting  table  to determine the appropriate semantic tagging.](https:/ibmdocs-test.dcs.ibm.com/docs/en/dcs-doc?topic=modules-highlighting-education-module)

### Web, IP, and email addresses

Use this guidance to refer to web addresses, use addresses in examples, format and punctuate web addresses, and link to websites.

#### Contents

Web addresses


IPv4 addresses


IPv6 addresses


Email addresses


[Formatting  and punctuating  web addresses](.)


[Linking  strategies](.)

#### Deﬁnitions

The following deﬁnitions provide context for the guidance in this topic, and examples are provided in the [Using  addresses in examples](.) section of this topic:

###### Protocol

A protocol is a set of rules that control the communication and transfer of data between two or more devices or systems in a communication network. The protocols that are used in web addresses are HTTP and HTTPS. Other protocols, such as FTP, GOPHER, and Telnet are sometimes supported by browsers. If the protocol is HTTP, you can typically omit the protocol name, colon, and forward slashes (http://) because most browsers default to an HTTP connection. However, some tools convert addresses into live links and require the full address, including the protocol name. If the protocol is not HTTP, always include the protocol name in the web address.

###### IP address

An Internet Protocol (IP) address is a unique address for a network device or network logical unit that uses the Internet Protocol standard. Two versions of Internet Protocol are commonly used: IP Version 4 (IPv4) and IP Version 6 (IPv6).

**URL**

A URL is the unique address of an information resource that is accessible in a network such as the Internet. The URL includes the abbreviated name of the protocol that is used to access the information resource, and the information that is used by the protocol to locate the information resource. A web address is a speciﬁc type of URL.

###### Web address

A web address is a unique identiﬁer of a web page. A web address is composed of the abbreviated name of the protocol that is used to access the web page (http or https), a host name or host IP address, and optional elements such as a port number, directory name, and ﬁle name. Use speciﬁc punctuation to separate the elements of a web address: insert a colon and two forward slashes after the abbreviated protocol name, insert a colon before a port number, and insert a forward slash before a directory name or ﬁle name.

###### Email address

An email address is composed of a user name, the at sign (@), and a domain name.

#### Referring to web addresses

When you refer to a web address, use the same capitalization of the web address that you are linking to.

When you refer to a web page, use a meaningful descriptive label. Meaningful text is particularly helpful for users of screen readers because users can click through a list of links that are provided by the software to activate the appropriate link. In the label, try to include text that mirrors the title of the linked site, so that users are conﬁdent that they are at the correct site. Also, try to include keywords in the label; the inclusion of keywords improves search results. Avoid using phrases such as, “Click here”.

In online information, apply the link to the descriptive label. Users can identify the web address by hovering over the label. Do not include the web address in parentheses after the linked text.


Click [here](http:/yoururl) for more information.


For more information, see the [CICS Explorer  website.](http:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer)

In PDF ﬁles and printed books, include the complete web address in parentheses after the descriptive label; even an outdated web address can provide useful information that can help users locate the target content. If you include an active link in a PDF ﬁle, apply the link to the descriptive label, and do not include the word “website” in the link. The PDF generation tool might also apply the link to the web address in parentheses.


[*For PDF ﬁles: For more information, see the CICS Explorer  website (https://www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer).*](https:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer)


[*For printed books: For more information, see the CICS Explorer website (https://www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer).*](https:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer)

When you create links, and when you add web addresses in parentheses, you can include or exclude the http:// or https:// protocol. Most browsers can interpret links without the protocol, but you can include the protocol if you believe that it might be helpful. See speciﬁc guidance for [Videos](.) . See speciﬁc guidance for [Marketing](.) .

Use the following verbs and prepositions with web addresses:


To direct readers to a website or web page, use *see* or *go to* .


For more information about the product, see [CICS Explorer .](http:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer)


To obtain videos for software support, go to the [IBM Software Subscription and Support  website.](http:/www.ibm.com/software/passportadvantage/software_subscription_support_ov.html)


To describe where information is located, use *on* .


See the latest product information on the [CICS Explorer  website.](http:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/cics-explorer)


Find information about database management systems on the [IBM Db2 Database  page.](https:/www.ibm.com/products/db2-database?p1=Search&p4=43700050328224062&p5=b&cm_mmc=Search_Google-_-1S_1S-_-WW_NA-_-%2Bdb2%20%2Bdatabase_b&cm_mmca7=71700000060951778&cm_mmca8=aud-382859943482%3Akwd-25069703066&cm_mmca9=CjwKCAjw4rf6BRAvEiwAn2Q76nLfxjuh9by2AGfV_mSanRxwlPh0pAAN5e9i1XJBTX7WDV2UD_KgRRoCtZwQAvD_BwE&cm_mmca10=406148470451&cm_mmca11=b&gclid=CjwKCAjw4rf6BRAvEiwAn2Q76nLfxjuh9by2AGfV_mSanRxwlPh0pAAN5e9i1XJBTX7WDV2UD_KgRRoCtZwQAvD_BwE&gclsrc=aw.ds)


To describe where to download a ﬁle, use *from* .


Download the video from the [IBM Software Subscription and Support  website.](http:/www.ibm.com/software/passportadvantage/software_subscription_support_ov.html)

When the link text for a web address is part of a sentence, do not use a colon between the verb or preposition and the link text. When you list the web address on a separate line, precede it with a complete sentence ending in a colon. You can list multiple web addresses inline or on separate lines.


More information is available at: [IBM Software  and](http:/www.ibm.com/software)

#### IBM web addresses

Most IBM web addresses, whether used as links in online information or displayed in PDF ﬁles and printed books, should use the format [www.ibm.com/sitename](http:/www.ibm.com/sitename) even if the host name of the address is not [www.ibm.com](http:/www.ibm.com) . Always remove the domain information from a URL, even if the URL is hidden in a link. Always test links and conﬁrm whether a redirect has been created.

IBM only IBM addresses might include the *sitename* element immediately after “www” or they might include characters that are appended to “www,” such as “-01” or “-03.” For example, “01” represents the Southbury CT hosting center and “03” represents the Boulder CO hosting center; if an application is moved from one hosting center to another, the URL might break.


[https://www.storage.ibm.com](http:/www.storage.ibm.com)


[https://www-03.ibm.com/software/products/en/category /digital-experience](http:/www-03.ibm.com/software/products/en/category/digital-experience)

#### Creating shortened URLs


IBM only Long URLs can be difﬁcult to remember, share, and track. They might also take up too much space or be confusing. To shorten long URLs, you can use [Snip , a product developed by IBM. You can also use](https:/snip.innovate.ibm.com)


*Original* : [https://www.ibm.com/software/products/en/ibm-cloud-orchestrator](http:/www.ibm.com/software/products/en/ibm-cloud-orchestrator)


*Shortened with Snip* : [https://ibm.biz/BdXEwU](https:/ibm.biz/BdXEwU)

Before you shorten a URL, remove any IBM proprietary domain information such as “-01” or “-03” from the URL, as described in the [IBM web addresses](.) section.


If you are concerned that readers might not trust shortened URLs, check with your organization for speciﬁc guidelines. To expand a shortened URL to show its destination, you can use a service such as [longurl .](https:/rdrr.io/cran/longurl/man/longurl.html)

#### Using addresses in examples

*Web addresses*

If you must use a web address as an example, do not create an address or use an address that links to (or might link to) an actual website. To avoid inadvertently using an address of an actual website, use addresses that are reserved for use in examples. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the following domain names to use for examples in testing and documentation:


[http://www.example.com](http:/www.example.com) [http://www.example.net](http:/www.example.net) [http://www.example.org](http:/www.example.org) [http://www.example.edu](http:/www.example.edu)

Do not use any other web domains except for those owned by IBM.


[http://www.test.com](http:/www.test.com) [http://www.mycompany.com](http:/www.mycompany.com) [http://www.test-company.com](http:/www.test-company.com)

A host name is the portion of the address up to the ﬁrst period. If the host name is used alone, it is an unqualiﬁed host name. A fully qualiﬁed host name is the host name plus its domain. In abc.rtp.raleigh.ibm.com, abc is the host name, and rtp.raleigh.ibm.com is the domain name. To convert this address into an example for documentation, replace either the full domain name or a portion of it with example.com. If you replace the domain name, the example becomes abc.example.com. If you need the subdomains in the example, replace a portion of the domain name; for example, abc.rtp.example.com.

[Start of page](.)

*IPv4 addresses*

If you must use an IP address in an example, use an address that is reserved for examples, and not one that relates to a particular company, unless that is required. For example, all addresses in the range 9.0.0.0/8 (or 9.*.*.*) are owned by IBM. Three ranges of addresses are reserved for use in documentation:


192.0.2.0/24 (or 192.0.2.*)


198.51.100.0/24 (or 198.51.100.*)


203.0.113.0/24 (or 203.0.113.*)


[The asterisk (*) in those ranges represents any number in the range 0 - 255. For more information, see Special Use IPv4 Addresses](http:/tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5735) [and](http:/tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5735) [IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation.](http:/tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5737)

You can also use the IP loopback address, which is 127.0.0.0/8 (127.*.*.*), although typically, only 127.0.0.1 is used for loopback purposes.

You can include wildcard characters in examples of IPv4 addresses to illustrate that a range of values is permitted; for example, 127.*.*.12 includes all addresses that start with 127 and end with 12. If you use wildcards, do not use identiﬁable companies' addresses in documentation. For example, using 192.*.*.12 is permissible because the 192.0.0.0/8 range covers a variety of uses.

[Start of page](.)

*IPv6 addresses*

If you must use an IPv6 address as an example, as with IPv4 addresses, avoid using an address that is assigned to a real entity. Use the range of addresses that is reserved for use in documentation:


2001:0DB8::/32 (long form: 2001:0DB8:0:0:0:0:0:0/32)


This address range includes 2001:0DB8:0:0:0:0:0:0 through 2001:0DB8:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF:FFFF. For more information, see [IPv6 Address Preﬁx Reserved for Documentation .](http:/tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3849)

*Email addresses*

If you must use an email address as an example, use a user name, the at sign (@), followed by a domain name that is reserved by IANA, for example, username@ example.com .

#### Formatting and punctuating web addresses

**No highlighting** : Present the address without any highlighting. When it is displayed on the web as a link, the label for the linked address is highlighted.


**Periods** : When the address or link text is at the end of a sentence, follow it with a period.  For more information, see [WebSphere Application Server .](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server)


Conﬁrm that you can connect to the IBM website at [https://www.ibm.com .](http:/www.ibm.com)

If the link is at the end of a sentence and the link text itself ends in a question mark or exclamation point, do not follow it with a period.


For more information, see [How do I set up the application serving  environment?](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/en/was-nd/9.0.5?topic=suase-how-do-i-set-up-application-serving-environment)

**No trailing forward slashes** : Do not include a forward slash at the end of a web address.


[https://www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server/](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server)

**Long addresses in PDF ﬁles and printed books** : If a web address does not ﬁt on one line, do not edit the web address to make the text more readable. For example, do not insert a hyphen or line break, or indent any part of a web address. Such editing might break a link or make a URL unusable when it is pasted into a browser.

However, in some output formats, a long URL might result in formatting problems, such as overlapping a page margin or table cell, If you must show the entire URL in a small space, end the ﬁrst line after an existing forward slash (/), double forward slash (//), or period, and continue the address on the next line. Do not add a hyphen to indicate a break. Do not indent any part of a web address.


[https://www.ibm.com/products/websphere-](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-) [application-server](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server)


[https://www.ibm.com/products/](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server) [websphere-application-server](https:/www.ibm.com/products/websphere-application-server)

IBM only Alternatively, consider replacing the long URL with a shortened URL, as described in the [Creating  shortened URLs](.) section in this topic.

#### Linking strategies

Link to and cite only reliable, authoritative websites. Do not link to websites, such as blogs or wikis, where the information can be edited by unreliable or irresponsible contributors.

IBM only You can link to blogs and wikis that are owned and maintained by IBM, but consider the cost of maintaining such links and the risk of broken links as such websites change or information is updated. Wikipedia is well moderated and is generally safe to link to. However, before linking to Wikipedia, consider whether the article has problems that are flagged within it; whether it is simply factual or expresses opinions; whether the information is outdated; or even whether the web page has a history of multiple changes.

When you consider using a deep link, be aware of the risk that the website you are linking to might be changed or removed in the future. A deep link is a link to a speciﬁc page or image on a website instead of to the main or home page of a website. When you use a deep link, you assume responsibility for maintaining that link.

### Claims and recommendations

Unsubstantiated claims and recommendations can cause legal problems for IBM. If you have questions about whether speciﬁc wording constitutes a claim, consult your legal department.


IBM only You can ﬁnd detailed guidance in the [IBM Legal Marketing  community. Do not make unsubstantiated claims about the following items:](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/legal-marketing-community)


**Product performance:** Instead of writing that a certain utility “improves” performance, state that it “can improve” performance or that it “is designed to improve” performance. Remember that performance testing does not reflect every customer environment.


**Perceived beneﬁts or characteristics of a product:** Avoid phrases such as “simple to use”, “effortless”, “user-friendly”, “future-proof”, and “easy to understand”. Users might not ﬁnd these statements true, and inflated language can reduce the credibility of the information.


With IBM product X you can future-proof your IT.

No technology is future-proof, but the IBM widget A is designed for longevity.


**Environmental beneﬁts:** Your legal department must approve the use of environmental terms, such as “green”, “eco-friendly”, and “environmentally friendly”, and environmental claims about products, such as that products are “free of” a substance, “made with renewable” energy or materials, or “recycled”. If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.


**Future product releases:** Avoid claims that are related to the content or timing of a future product or release.


**Publications that are not yet available:** If you must refer to a publication that is not yet available, consult your local legal department for guidelines.


**Best practices:** Use the term *best practice* with caution, to recommend a procedure to solve a problem or achieve a speciﬁc outcome. Otherwise, it can imply that information in other content types is less valuable. Also, your team or organization becomes obligated to ensure that anything it asserts as a best practice is still supported and correct. Instead, write more descriptive text to guide the user.


**Product security:** Avoid making general statements that a product or service is “secure” when you discuss the security capabilities of a product or service. Stating that a product is “secure” or provides “secure functionality” could expose IBM to liability. You can use phrases such as “security enhanced” or “in a security-rich environment”. In most cases, avoid “recommending” that users do something, especially if the recommendation is vague or unexplained. Instead, describe why the action is problematic or beneﬁcial.


If you have a large data set, you are recommended to disable the automatic search. If you have a large data set, disable the automatic search to improve performance.


It is recommended that you encrypt the server databases to increase the security of local replicas. To increase the security of local replicas, encrypt the server databases.


The JVM requires a minimum of 4 GB of server memory. We recommend 6 GB.

The JVM requires a minimum of 4 GB of server memory. To avoid occasional memory reallocation, allow 6 GB for the JVM.


IBM only **Use of “free”:** If a communication contains the word “free”, the client must be entitled to the item or service that is offered for “free” without any extra considerations such as purchasing another product. If the intention is to recover any costs


associated with the “free” offering, such as “buy one, get one free”, use the words “at no additional charge”, “complimentary”, or similar language instead of the word “free.” If there are limitations to what is “free” (such as resource or function limits, or a [speciﬁc timeframe), communicate those limitations conspicuously. For more information, go to Legal Marketing  Guidelines Deceptive Claims to Avoid .](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/legal-marketing-community?query=Use%2Cof%2Cthe%2CTerm%2C%22Free%22)


Review this free offer.

Review this offer, which is free for residents of Canada.


Get IBM Db2 free.

Get IBM Db2 Free Edition.

#### Fictitious company names

Unless your team has legal permission to do so, avoid making up names. Instead, use descriptive words based on a characteristic of the company or organization. For example, use “a large insurance company” or “a regional bank”.

When you need to refer to a company by a proper name, use generic names such as “Bank A” or “Insurance Company 1”.

### Copyright notices

Each IBM publication, online document, video, and program must have a copyright notice. Linking to the ibm.com copyright page does not protect IBM’s copyright. For information about videos, see the legal section of the corporate video guidelines. Important online illustrations might also require a copyright notice.

If you are publishing work that does not belong solely to IBM, you might have to add a copyright notice that is not from IBM. Make sure that you take the following steps:


Follow the copyright stipulations in the contract that IBM has with the other party.


Consult your Intellectual Property Law department to ensure that you are using the correct copyright notice and that it is correctly placed in the publication.

#### Placement

Each printed external support document must have the main copyright notice on the cover, on the front or back of the title page, or on the page that contains the edition notice. Also, copyright notices must be placed in a margin on the ﬁrst page of each chapter or major section of a document.


IBM only For information about copyright notices for topic-based information, see the [Copyrights  page on the IBM Content site.](https:/www.ibm.com/docs/en/technical-content?topic=standards-copyrights)

In IBM Documentation, the copyright statement must appear on the welcome page for the product documentation. The copyright statement is not required at the bottom of every page.


[IBM only For information about the placement of copyright notices in code or on title screens for software, see Copyright notice process  in the Legal Information for Business Clients wiki.](https:/w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/legal-for-business/copyright-notice-registration-archival/copyright-notice-process)

#### Dates

The copyright statement must show the ﬁrst and last publication years of the material. The ﬁrst date in the copyright notice is the earliest year in which at least 5% of the material was originally copyrighted. The second date is the year in which the current edition was copyrighted. Separate the two dates with a comma. If the material is all new, use one date only.


© Copyright IBM Corporation 2005, 2014

In information that is published in XHTML format, include the copyright years in the metadata for each topic. ID Workbench can retrieve these years from a DITA map. Components in the same product documentation set might have different copyright dates. Navigation ﬁles do not require copyright information because such ﬁles are not considered to be content.

When IBM and one or more vendors jointly produce documentation, the attribution statement must also cover these other companies. Use the wording *and others* in the attribution statement.


© Copyright IBM Corporation and others 2008, 2014 [Start of page](.)

#### Wording

The words, IBM Corp., IBM CORP., or IBM Corporation can all be used interchangeably to denote that IBM is the copyright owner. Do not use any other names without ﬁrst consulting with your local Intellectual Property Law counsel.

The only legal abbreviation for the word *Copyright* in a notice is *Copr* . Use this abbreviation only where there are serious space constraints. Although section 7.2.2 of the Corporate Standard *Proprietary Protection for IBM Materials (Including Copyright)* states that either the word *Copyright* or its abbreviation must follow the copyright symbol ©, the current advice of Corporate IP Law Department is that it is acceptable to leave *Copyright* or its abbreviation out, and include only the copyright symbol. However, do not use the symbol alone in cases where, due to lack of character set support, it might be rendered invisible or unreadable.

If the character set that you are using does not include the copyright symbol ©, you can use a capital C in parentheses *(C)* . Do not use a lowercase *c* in parentheses *(c)* in place of the copyright symbol ©. At the recommendation of the Corporate IP Law Department, do not include the words *All rights reserved* as part of the copyright notice.


(c) Copyright IBM Corp. 1999, 2015

(c) IBM Corp. 2015

All rights reserved. © Copyright IBM Corp. 1999, 2015.


© Copyright IBM Corp. 1999, 2015

© COPYRIGHT IBM CORP. 1999, 2015

© Copyright IBM Corporation 2015

© IBM Corporation 1999, 2015 (only in cases where character support exists for the © symbol)

© 2022 IBM Corporation (only in cases where character support exists for the © symbol)

(C) Copyright IBM Corp. 1999, 2015 [Start of page](.)

#### Type size

In legal notices, use a type size that corresponds to a minimum of 8 points. Some legal jurisdictions do not accept into evidence notices with text that is smaller than 8 points. For details, see [Type size](.) .

### Personal information

Personal information includes any information that identiﬁes or can reasonably be used to identify, contact, or locate the individual to whom such information pertains. Personal information includes names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, and photographs.

Treat personal information with care and protect it adequately. Reproduce personal information only with the written permission of the individual concerned. Instead of using real personal information, even with written consent, consider using ﬁctional information. Be sure to clear any ﬁctitious names with your legal department and add the following disclaimer to the legal notices:

“This information contains examples of data and reports used in daily business operations. To illustrate them as completely as possible, the examples include the names of individuals, companies, brands, and products. All of these names are ﬁctitious, and any similarity to the names and addresses used by a real business enterprise is entirely coincidental.”

To avoid usage that is culture speciﬁc and possibly confusing, use the term *given name* instead of *ﬁrst name* or *Christian name* , and use the term *surname* instead of *last name* . Particularly in the West, a surname is sometimes called a last name because people write their surnames last, after their given names, which are also known as ﬁrst names. In other parts of the world, particularly in Asia, the practice is often the reverse: people’s names are shown with their surnames before their given names.

For more information, see [Names and titles](.) .

### Republishing existing content

Be cautious about republishing content. Before you copy any existing content into a new publication or format, carefully consider the copyright and permission implications. To protect an existing IBM copyright, to avoid plagiarism, or to prevent copyright infringement, you might require explicit written permission to republish text, images, code, and other information.

#### Contents


[Republishing  IBM content](.)


[Republishing  content from other companies and sources](.)

#### Republishing IBM content

In most cases, you can copy content that IBM owns (copyrighted or not) into a copyrighted IBM publication without obtaining permission to republish the material. In this context, ownership applies to IBM and its worldwide subsidiaries, but not to companies that IBM formerly owned or to products and services that IBM divested to other companies.

Be careful about republishing IBM content in these situations, because you might risk losing the copyright or require permission:


**Reproducing material from a copyrighted IBM publication in a noncopyrighted publication** Because IBM could lose copyright on the copied material, consult the owner of the copyrighted material and obtain permission to republish it.


**Reproducing material from an IBM Conﬁdential publication in an unclassiﬁed publication** Verify that the information is not restricted and that you have permission to distribute it.


**Reproducing an IBM computer program or code** Before you publish any code or program, you must obtain permission from the IBM owner to distribute it.

Check carefully to ensure that the material that you are copying is owned by IBM or is in the public domain. If the source IBM publication indicates that the information was originally copied with permission (for example, if the source IBM publication contains an acknowledgment or credit line), you might have to obtain new permission. Some permissions do not include the right to transmit or distribute the information electronically.

#### Republishing content from other companies and sources

Before you republish content from any source outside of IBM (whether or not the source bears a copyright notice or other restrictive legend), consider whether republishing the material is necessary or whether you can link to the information instead. If you must republish the material, get advice and consent from an Intellectual Property legal representative before you request permission to republish the source.

You cannot republish material from a copyrighted publication (other than an IBM publication) in an IBM publication without the written consent and permission of the copyright owner. Copyright owners generally specify how they want the copyright acknowledgment worded and where it should be located. The permission must constitute worldwide permission to copy, print, and translate the material in the proposed publication and in future revisions and editions of the publication. If there are any plans to modify or adapt the copied material, the written permission must include express authorization to modify and adapt the material.

You cannot republish material from a source other than IBM on an IBM website or any web page without the written permission of the owner. This permission must include the right to electronically transmit and distribute the work worldwide. You might also need permission to modify or revise the work. If you reproduce software in a publication, you must make sure that you have an appropriate copyright license or that the software is truly in the public domain. Before you publish anyone’s name, voice, verbal statement, or likeness on the Internet, obtain signed model release forms that indicate permission to do so. You must acknowledge any material that you place on the IBM website with permission from the owner by using wording that is acceptable to the owner.

If you have questions or concerns about republishing content from other companies or sources, consult your Intellectual Property legal department.

#### Special characters


**#**

Use *number sign* to refer to the *#* character, unless you are referring to the character at the beginning of a hashtag, in which case, use hash sign.

An example of valid use of the *#* character is “Gartner ranks IBM #1 in cloud innovation report”.

See the table of [Common punctuation marks and special characters](.) in the Punctuation and symbols topic.

#### 0-9


**1H, 2H, 1Q, 2Q, 3Q, 4Q** ***noun***

When abbreviating business and ﬁscal halves and quarters of a year, put the numeral ﬁrst, then the uppercase letter. For more information about abbreviating segments of a year, see the Business calendar periods section of the [Dates and times](.) topic in IBM Style.


**10BASE-2** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *10BASE2* .


**10BASE2** ***noun***

Write as shown: uppercase *BASE* . Do not use a hyphen when a number follows *BASE* , but do use a hyphen when a letter follows (for example, *10BASE-T* ).


**10BASE-T** ***noun***

Write as shown: uppercase *BASE* . Use a hyphen when a letter follows *BASE* , but do not use a hyphen when a number follows (for example, *10BASE2* ).


**10BASET** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *10BASE-T* .


**24x7** ***adjective***

Use this abbreviation to indicate high availability, nonstop operation or support, such as for database and e-commerce applications or monitoring.

Do not use this abbreviation to indicate the general availability of something, such as service.

Whenever possible, use descriptive wording: for example, “High-availability databases not only are universally available but also have high reliability and serviceability”, or “Operations are monitored 24 hours a day, every day of the week.” However, 24x7 is acceptable usage, provided that you are consistent within a document or library.


**24/7** ***adjective***

Do not use this abbreviation to indicate high availability, nonstop operation or support, such as for database and e-commerce applications or monitoring.

Do not use to indicate the general availability of something, such as service. If you must use an abbreviation, use *24x7* instead.

*24x7* is acceptable usage, provided that you are consistent within a document or library. However, if possible, use descriptive wording instead.

**case folding** ***noun***

In character string processing, the act of converting characters to a single case (all uppercase or all lowercase) to determine whether strings are equivalent. Unlike case mapping, case folding cannot be relied upon to produce output that is suitable for display.


**case mapping** ***noun***

In character string processing, the act of converting characters to a single case (all uppercase or all lowercase) for display purposes. Contrast with *case folding* .

**CD-ROM drive** ***noun***

Use to refer to a read-only CD drive.

**CD-RW drive** ***noun***

Use to refer to a CD drive that can be read from and written to (a CD read/write drive).

If the read/write characteristic of the drive varies, cannot be predicted, or is irrelevant, use *CD drive* .

**complete** ***verb***

Use only as a transitive verb. For example, write “the program completes the operation successfully”, not “the program completes”. Alternatively, use simpler wording, such as “the process ends” or “the script ﬁnishes”.


**componentization** ***noun***

Use only when *componentization* is part of the existing product terminology. Otherwise, use *component-based development* , *component model* , *component architecture* , *shared components* , or a similar phrase.

**compress** ***verb***

Use *compress* to refer to compressing data with a compression utility. Do not use *gzip* , *jar* , *tar* , or *zip* .

Because the terms *zip* and *ZIP* are registered trademarks of other companies, using them might result in a trademark infringement.


**comprised of** ***verb***

Do not use. Use *consists of* or *composed of* to describe parts of a whole (for example, “the library is composed of ﬁve books”).

*Comprised of* is often used to mean *consists of* or *composed of* , but this usage is incorrect. Because *comprise* (which means *to include* ) is frequently used incorrectly, consider replacing it with a clearer alternative when possible.


Incorrect: The array is comprised of ﬁve disks.


Incorrect: Five disks comprise the array.


Correct: The array comprises ﬁve disks.


Correct: The array consists of ﬁve disks.


**compute** ***adjective, noun***

Use with caution. Use as an adjective or noun only when referring to infrastructure or resources that serve as the basis for building apps in the cloud, for example, *compute resource* or *compute infrastructure* .

If using the word in a general sense, use *computation* instead, for example, “The computation requires a signiﬁcant amount of memory.”

In some cases, it might be appropriate to use *computational* as an adjective before the appropriate noun, for example, “The system can create a virtual version of a computational resource.”

##### coordinated universal time noun

Do not use *coordinated universal time* (UTC) and *Greenwich mean time* (GMT) interchangeably.

Coordinated universal time (UTC) is the time scale, based on the Système International (SI) second, as deﬁned and recommended by the Comité Consultatif International de la Radio (CCIR) and maintained (using an atomic clock) by the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM). The Système International is based on three fundamental units of measure (the meter, the kilogram, and the second) and is sometimes called the *MKS system* because of these units. For most practical purposes, UTC is equivalent to the mean solar time at the prime meridian (0 degrees longitude) of Greenwich, England, which is known as Greenwich mean time. Do not use *Zulu time* as an alternative to *UTC* .

**decompiled** ***adjective***

Use *decompiled* to refer to data that was previously compiled. Use *uncompiled* to refer to data that was not previously compiled.

Use *decompress* to refer only to converting compressed data to its expanded or original size. See also *extract* .

Use *DMZ* . Instead of using *demilitarized zone* to explain *DMZ* at its ﬁrst occurrence, use a description such as *a ﬁrewall conﬁguration for securing local area networks* .


**demon** ***noun***

Do not use to describe a program that runs unattended. Use *daemon* .

Use the shortened form ( *demo* ) only when a conversational tone is appropriate and the meaning is clear from the context.


**demo, demonstration** ***noun***

Use the shortened form ( *demo* ) only when a conversational tone is appropriate and the meaning is clear from the context.

Do not use. Use *dismount* in documentation for a Windows system, or use *unmount* in documentation for hardware or for a UNIX system.

Do not use, as in “the deploy code”. Use *deployment* (for example, *deployment code* ).


**deploy** ***noun***

Do not use, as in “the deploy”. Use *deployment* .


**deploy** ***verb***

Use only as a verb. The noun or adjective is *deployment* .


**deprecated** ***adjective***

Describes the status of a feature, function, or API method that continues to be available from the product or software and is supported but is no longer recommended and is planned for removal. A deprecation of function is announced beforehand to inform customers about the upcoming removal and, when possible, to provide information about an alternative way to implement the function. Do not use to mean *removed* .


**depress** ***verb***

Do not use to refer to pressing keys, buttons, or latches or typing on a keyboard. Use *press* or *type* to refer to a keyboard, and use

Do not use. Use *unregister* .

**designed to** ***verb***

In technical information, do not write *designed to* to describe a concrete product function. For example, do not write “product X is designed to provide …”; instead, write “product X provides…”

In some situations, it is appropriate to use *designed to* , for example, to refer to potential performance beneﬁts. If in doubt, consult with your local IP lawyer to ensure that you do not make a false claim.
