#### E


**e, e-** ***adjective***

Do not create terms using the preﬁx *e* or *e-* .


**easy** ***adjective***

Use with caution. It is normally not accurate to say, *With IBM’s service products, installation of your new POWER system will be easy.* It may be accurate to say, *IBM’s service products can be used to make installation of your new POWER system easier than if you tried to manage your own installation.*


**earlier** ***adverb***

Use to refer to a previous software version or ﬁx level.


**e-book** ***adjective, noun***

Do not use. Use *ebook* .


**ebook** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated. If this term occurs at the beginning of a sentence or title, use *Ebook* .


**e-business** ***noun***

Do not use. IBM strategy no longer uses or associates the term *e-business* with IBM products or services.

IBM marketing strategy changes over time, as does the terminology that supports that strategy. Contact the branding or naming representative for your department or division for the latest terminology information.


**e-care** ***noun***

Do not use. Also, do not use *eCare* , which is a trademark of another company. In internal documentation only, use *eSupport* .


**eCare** ***noun***

Do not use because it is a trademark of another company. In internal documentation only, use *eSupport* .


**Eclipse** ***noun***

Use *Eclipse* , not *IBM Eclipse SDK* or *IES* .


**eco-friendly** ***adjective***

Do not use to describe environmental features or beneﬁts of IBM products unless the claim is clearly explained, can be substantiated, and is approved for use by an IBM legal representative.


Vague or unsubstantiated environmental claims can cause legal issues and mislead readers. For more information about the IBM policy on using environmental terms, see [IBM Environmental Marketing  Claims . For information about making any claims in content, see  in IBM Style. If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.](http:/w3.tap.ibm.com/medialibrary/media_view?id=192864)


**e-commerce** ***noun***

Write as shown: hyphenated and lowercase.


**ecosystem** ***noun***

Do not use to mean a computer network environment. Use only to refer to a biological environment or to a business community of interacting organizations and individuals.


**e-discovery** ***noun***

Write as shown: hyphenated and lowercase, except when referring to IBM product names that include the word eDiscovery.


**EEPROM** ***noun***

This abbreviation stands for *electrically erasable programmable read-only memory* , not *electronically erasable programmable read-only memory* .

EEPROM is a special type of PROM that can be erased by exposing it to an electrical charge.


**effortless** ***adjective***

Use with caution. This is a subjective claim that might not reflect all users' experiences.


**eﬁx, e-ﬁx, eFix, e-Fix** ***noun***

Do not use. Use the appropriate term, such as *ﬁx* , *interim ﬁx* , *program temporary ﬁx* , or *test ﬁx* .


**e.g.** ***conjunction***

Do not use. Use *for example* .


**either** ***adjective***

Use to mean *any one of two* .

Although *either* can be used to mean *each* , as in “close the latch on either side of the cover”, avoid this usage. Use *each* to avoid confusion or imprecision.


**EJB** ***adjective***

Use only as an adjective, as in *EJB server* or *EJB component* .

The artifact that is created by EJB programmers is called enterprise beans, EJB beans, or EJB components, not EJBs. Note that if the noun following *EJB* is uppercase, you should consult your IPL, because the term is a proper noun.


**e-learning** ***noun***

Write as shown: hyphenated and lowercase.


**e-mail** ***adjective, noun***

Do not use. Use *email* .


**email** ***adjective, noun, verb***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated. If this term occurs at the beginning of a sentence or title, use *Email* .


**embed** ***verb***

Write as shown: not *imbed* .


**enable** ***verb***

Use to describe the action of making an interface control or product function available to users. Avoid stating that inanimate objects grant abilities to people, as in “the product enables you to…”. Whenever possible, use a direct, user-focused alternative such as “you can use the product to …” or “with this product, users can…”.


**enabled** ***adjective***

Use only to describe an interface control or a product function that has been made available. An interface control or product function that is enabled can also be disabled.


**endpoint** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**end user** ***noun***

Write only when you need to differentiate between different types of user. Otherwise write *user* . For example, security software content might need to distinguish between the *user* of its software (the administrator of the security management software) and an *end user* (the user of the device that the security software protects).


**engineer** ***noun***

Use only to refer to a person who has a degree in engineering. Otherwise, use *professional* , *scientist* , *specialist* , *representative* (as in *support representative* ), or other alternative. This is a legal requirement. In some jurisdictions, the term must not be used for those without an appropriate academic qualiﬁcation.


**ensure** ***verb***

Use as a synonym of *verify* or *make sure* . Avoid using to suggest a guarantee of some performance standard without prior legal review. Such use is acceptable only if you can substantiate the accuracy of the claim or if it is appropriately qualiﬁed, such as *helps ensure* .

Do not confuse with the words *insure* or *assure* .


**enter** ***verb***

Use *enter* or *type* to refer to entering text in ﬁelds in a graphical interface. Use *type* , *enter* , *issue* , or *run* to refer to entering a command on a command line or at a command prompt; use one term consistently throughout your information.


##### environmentally friendly, environmentally preferable adjective

##### 

Do not use to describe environmental features or beneﬁts of IBM products unless the claim is clearly explained, can be substantiated, and is approved for use by an IBM legal representative.


Vague or unsubstantiated environmental claims can cause legal issues and mislead readers. For more information about the IBM policy on using environmental terms, see [IBM Environmental Marketing  Claims . For information about making any claims in content, see  in IBM Style. If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.](http:/w3.tap.ibm.com/medialibrary/media_view?id=192864)


**EPUB** ***adjective, noun***

Do not use *EPUB* as a noun to refer to an EPUB ﬁle. For example, do not write *in an EPUB* nor *Download the EPUB* . It is acceptable to use *EPUB* as a noun in constructions such as “The following ﬁle types are supported: EPUB, HTML, PDF,…”.


**error message** ***noun***

Write as shown, not *error* , to refer to a message that notiﬁes the user of an error. Use *message* as a generic term to refer to an informational message, a warning message, or an error message.


**e-sign** ***verb***

Write as shown, hyphenated and lowercase, as an acceptable alternative to *sign electronically* . If this term occurs at the beginning of a title or sentence, use *E-sign* .


**e-signature** ***noun***

Write as shown, hyphenated and lowercase, to refer to an electronic signature. If this term occurs at the beginning of a title or sentence, use *E-signature* .


**eSupport** ***noun***

Use only in internal documentation. In customer information, use a term such as *IBM Software Support* or *IBM Hardware Support* .


**etc.** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *and so on* when you list a clear sequence of elements, such as *1, 2, 3, and so on* or *Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and so on* . When you list items that do not form a clear sequence, use appropriate descriptive wording, such as *device drivers, ﬁrmware, and other code* .


**Ethernet** ***noun***

Write as shown, with an initial uppercase E.


**euro** ***noun***

Write as shown: lowercase.

The word *euro* has a lowercase initial *e* , just as the United States *dollar* has a lowercase initial *d* . Although the European Union speciﬁes *euro* as the plural form in its own ofﬁcial publications, use the usual English plural form by adding an *s* . This usual usage has been authorized by the EU and adopted by many publishers.


**evangelist, evangelize** ***noun, verb***

Do not use. Use another term such as influencer, advocate, or ambassador. This term is outdated and has religious connotations that might be disturbing to some people.


**executable** ***adjective***

Use only as an adjective that precedes a noun (for example, *executable ﬁle* ).


**executable** ***noun***

Do not use as a noun. Use *executable program* , *executable routine* , or another term, as appropriate.


**execute** ***verb***

Use only if a simpler term, such as *run* , *issue* , *start* , or *enter* is inappropriate.


**exit** ***adjective***

Do not use to mean *exit routine* or *exit program* .


**exit** ***noun***

Do not use to mean *exit routine* or *exit program* .

Use *exit* as a noun only to refer to the point in a program from which control exits and goes to an external exit routine or exit program.


**expandable section** ***noun***

Write as shown to refer to an interface element that users click to expand an area or section. Like any interface element, only refer to the element by its type if you cannot refer to the element by its label.


**exploit** ***verb***

Use only to mean *to make productive use of* . In most cases, write *use* . *Exploit* can have negative connotations, implying that an unfair advantage is being gained.


**exportation** ***noun***

##### GenAI, GENAI, genai, genAI noun

The deﬁnitions of *generally* , *normally* , *typically* , and *usually* are similar, and in some cases, more than one of these terms might be applicable. Use your judgment in deciding which term best applies.

Although FLOPS is the acronym for *floating-point operations per second* , when the acronym is used as part of a term such as *gigaflop* , common usage is to use all lowercase letters.

**GMT** ***noun***

Do not use *Greenwich mean time* (GMT) and *coordinated universal time* (UTC) interchangeably.

Greenwich mean time (GMT) is the mean solar time at the prime meridian (0 degrees longitude) of Greenwich, England. Greenwich mean time is sometimes called Z time or Zulu time. Although Greenwich mean time and coordinated universal time are sometimes used interchangeably, they are not synonyms. Greenwich mean time is an approximate time. Because the second is no longer deﬁned in terms of astronomical phenomena, the preferred name for this time scale is coordinated universal time (UTC).

Use these terms if you know that your intended audience is familiar and comfortable with what they represent, but in most cases you can write instructions that tell how to access the graphical user interface without using a generic noun.

Avoid *in the GUI, do this* or *in the interface, do that* . In tasks, refer to the speciﬁc part of the graphical user interface, such as the name of a window, ﬁeld, pane, or view. Use *GUI* or *graphical user interface* when you need contrast with named non-GUI components or character-based interfaces, such as the DB2 command-line interface.

If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.](http:/w3.tap.ibm.com/medialibrary/media_view?id=192864)

In most cases, use a more precise term such as *3270 application* , *5250 application* , or *character-based interface* .

*Green screen* is occasionally used to refer to monochrome display devices that have been obsolete for 20 years. However, the term *green screen* has a different meaning in the ﬁlm and video industry, and it probably means little to translators or to a younger generation of programmers. Use more precise terms to refer to 3270 or 5250 applications, data streams, or emulation mode. If you need a term to contrast with *GUI* , use *character-based interface* . If you must use *green screen* , for example because you believe your audience will use it as a search term, write the ﬁrst occurrence in italics to indicate that it is a nonstandard term, clarify what it means, and thereafter use preferred alternatives. For example, write “You can use this tool to add a web interface to 5250 character-based applications (sometimes called *green screen applications* )” and then, having established the equivalence, use *5250 application* for subsequent references in the same document.

Greenwich mean time (GMT) is the mean solar time at the prime meridian (0 degrees longitude) of Greenwich, England. Greenwich mean time is sometimes called Z time or Zulu time. Although Greenwich mean time and coordinated universal time are sometimes used interchangeably, they are not synonyms. Greenwich mean time is an approximate time. Because the second is no longer deﬁned in terms of astronomical phenomena, the preferred name for this time scale is coordinated universal time (UTC).

**if … then** ***conjunction***

Avoid using *then* to introduce an independent clause that follows an *if* clause. For example, write “If you set a password, access is restricted”, not “If you set a password, then access is restricted”.

Use the *if … then* construction only to clarify that a conditional relationship exists between two actions or events. For example, the *if*

*… then* construction can improve clarity when you are joining two long clauses.


**iﬁx, i-ﬁx, iFix, i-Fix** ***noun***

**if versus whether** ***conjunction***

Use *if* to express a condition and *whether* to express an alternative.

Example of correct usage: *If the job is canceled, you must determine whether any other jobs exist.* Example of incorrect usage: *Inform the administrator if the printer has been started.* This second example can have either of the following meanings: 1. If the printer has been started, tell the administrator. (Tell the administrator only if the printer has been started.) 2. Tell the administrator whether the printer has been started. (Regardless of the situation, you must tell the administrator.)

Use the abbreviation KB or kB, not the spelled-out form. If your audience needs to see the spelled-out form of an abbreviation, include the spelled-out form parenthetically on ﬁrst use only, and use only the abbreviation in all other occurrences.

In SI metric style, the abbreviation of the preﬁx kilo is lowercase k. However, IBM Style distinguishes between uppercase K (meaning 1,024, or 2 to the power of 10) and lowercase k (meaning 1,000, or 10 to the power of 3). Therefore, KB means 1,024 bytes, and kB means 1,000 bytes.

Clients depend on servers, and agents depend on managers. Regarding requests, clients request services from servers, and managers request services from agents.


**man day** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *person day* .


**man hour** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *person hour* or *labor hour* .


**manipulation button** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *right mouse button* .


**map** ***verb***

In character string processing, to convert characters to a single case (all uppercase or all lowercase) for display purposes. Contrast with *fold* .


**market** ***noun***

Do not use to mean *marketplace* or *market segment* .

It is OK to use in phrases such as: *market share* and *go to market* .


**mash-up, mash up** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *mashup* .


##### mash-up, mash up, mashup verb

Do not use as a verb. Use *create* or another, similar verb. For example, write “create a mashup of your reports”, not “mashup your reports”.


**mashup** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**massage** ***verb***

Do not use to refer to changing or working with data or other information.

The term *massage* implies the selective manipulation of data or information to present a biased or skewed perspective.


**master** ***noun, adjective***

Do not use *master* when it is paired with *slave* . Use another term such as *controller* , *leader* , or *primary* .

Recommendations by function for *master* : *controller* , *director* , *coordinator* (when used with *worker* or *agent* to represent an entity that controls or directs another entity), *main* , *primary* (when used with *replica* to represent an entity from which a copy of a main or primary entity is derived), *parent* (when used with *child* to indicate a dependent relationship), *primary* , *principal* (when used with *secondary* where it is not necessary to specify the function)


**masterbrand** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *corporate brand* when referring to an overarching brand name or anchor point for product offerings.


**master repository** ***noun***

Replace when possible or appropriate. Consider using *main* or *primary* in place of *master* before *repository* in new products and functions.


**may** ***verb***

Use only to indicate permission. Otherwise, use *can* to indicate ability, or use *might* to indicate possibility.

*May* is overused in technical information. In most cases, use *can* or *might* instead.


**MCP** ***noun***

Do not use MCP or Mini Control Program to refer to the embedded operating system. Do not refer at all to the embedded operating system unless it is clearly technically required to either use or service an IBM product or service. If the context of the communication clearly requires a technical reference to the embedded operating system, use the term *Linux kernel 2.6.x* , where x is the modiﬁcation level.

IBM wants to make sure that all messaging with respect to embedded operating systems in IBM is clear and consistent.


**medium, media** ***noun***

Traditionally, *media* is a plural noun and its singular form is *medium* . However, use of the singular *media* is becoming more widespread. Whichever singular noun you use, be consistent throughout your information. If possible, rewrite singular-form sentences to specify the medium. For example, instead of *The storage medium is inaccessible* , write “The tape volume is inaccessible”.


**medtech** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown, lowercase. If the term might be unfamiliar to your intended audience, write “medical technology, or *medtech* ” on ﬁrst occurrence.


**megaflop** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown: all lowercase. Add an *s* only to pluralize the noun ( *megaflops* ). Do not use *megaflops* as part of a compound adjective, as in “2-megaflops increase”. Instead, write “2-megaflop increase”.

Although FLOPS is the acronym for *floating-point operations per second* , when the acronym is used as part of a term such as *metaflop* , common usage is to use all lowercase letters.


**memory stick** ***noun***

Do not use. This term is a trademark of Sony. Use *USB flash drive* .


**menu bar** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words.


**menubar** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *menu bar* .


**message** ***noun***

Use *message* as a generic term to refer to an informational message, a warning message, or an error message.


**meta data, meta-data** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *metadata* .


**metadata** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**methodology** ***noun***

Use only to refer to a group or system of methods, procedures, or approaches in a discipline. Do not use to refer to a single method, procedure, or approach.


**metro** ***adjective***

Use metro as an abbreviation for metropolitan to represent a region and its surrounding areas. If the term might be unfamiliar to your intended audience, write *metropolitan* on ﬁrst occurrence.


**mice** ***noun***

Use *mice* as the plural of *mouse* .


**microcomputer** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *personal computer* or *PC* .


**middleware** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**Mid-Market** ***adjective***

Use only to refer to the Mid-Market Program Framework. In other contexts, use *midmarket* : one word, lowercase.


**midmarket** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown: one word, lowercase, unhyphenated. Use *Mid-Market* to refer to the Mid-Market Program Framework.


**midsize, midsized** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**might** ***verb***

Use *might* to indicate possibility. To indicate ability, use *can* . In most cases, use *can* or *might* , not *may* .


**migrate** ***verb***

Do not use to mean *upgrade* or *port* .

The terms *migrate* , *upgrade* , and *port* are not synonyms. To migrate is to move data, users, or applications to a new program, platform, or environment. Migration can occur between unlike systems, for example, between two different vendors' databases, and migrating usually involves more work than upgrading. To upgrade is to replace software with a new release or ﬁx level of the same program or to replace hardware with a newer model or more powerful technology. An upgrade involves little work on the user’s part. To port is to move an application program from the operating system for which it was developed to a different operating system.

Porting requires less effort than redevelopment. With open technologies such as Java, porting might require no extra work at all.


**mixed case** ***adjective***

Hyphenate the term if you use it before a noun that it modiﬁes (for example, *a mixed-case password* ).


**mobile** ***adjective***

Use *mobile* only as a general term to refer to laptops and handheld devices.

The IBM Terminology database provides the following deﬁnition: *Pertaining to computing that is performed on a portable computer or a handheld device by a user who is frequently moving among various locations and might be using different types of network connections (for example, dial-up, LAN, or wireless)* .


**motherboard** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *system board* .


**mount point** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words.


**mountpoint** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *mount point* .

Do not use. Use *left mouse button* .


**mouse button 2** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *right mouse button* .


**mouse over** ***verb***

Do not use. Use *point to* or *move the mouse pointer over* .

*Mouse* is not a verb, and *mouse over* is probably impossible to translate.


**move** ***verb***

Use *move* to refer to moving a cursor, not *position* .


**multi-channel** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *multichannel* .


**multichannel** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**multi-core** ***adjective***

Write as shown: hyphenated.

Although most terms that begin with the preﬁx *multi* are not hyphenated, *multi-core* is hyphenated to maintain consistency with other

*core* words, such as *dual-core* and *quad-core* .


**multifactor** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**multijobbing** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *multitasking* .


**multimedia** ***noun, adjective***

Write as shown: one word.


**multitasking** ***noun***

Use *multitasking* , not *multijobbing* .


**multi-tier** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *multitiered* .


**multi-tiered** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *multitiered* .


**multitiered** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated.


**must** ***verb***

Use *must* , not *have to* or *need to* , unless *must* is too restrictive. For example, *you do not have to* is not the same as *you must not* . For a mandatory action, either use the imperative, as in “back up your data”, or use *must* , as in “you must back up your data”.


**MVS** ***noun***

Do not confuse *MVS* with *z/OS* .

*MVS* has been used to refer to operating systems such as OS/MVS, MVS/XA, and MVS/ESA. The code that was known as the operating system called MVS/ESA is the basis for z/OS. The combination of MVS/ESA SP-JES2 (or JES3) and MVS Data Facility Product (MVS/DFP or DFSMS/MVS) composed the MVS/ESA operating system. In addition, the old OpenEdition MVS base services were integrated into MVS/ESA SP. Optional features such as OpenEdition MVS Shell and Utilities, OpenEdition MVS Debugger, MICR/OCR, ESCON Director, and others were also included in MVS/ESA SP. In z/OS, the term *MVS* refers to those services and functions that were provided by the Base Control Program (BCP) of the MVS/ESA operating system. MVS (or BCP, as it is sometimes called) is a base element of z/OS. You might need to use *MVS* as an adjective, but you should do this only if the context requires you to identify the Base Control Program of z/OS. For example, if you are writing about the speciﬁc set of commands that deal with the MVS element of z/OS and it is important for the reader to understand that you are referring to only that set of commands (and not to TSO, RACF, JES2, or JES3 commands), write *MVS commands* .


**M.V.** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *major vector* .

#### N


**N/A** ***adjective***

Write as shown to mean *not available* or *not applicable* . Use this abbreviation only when it is not practical to spell it out. In a table, use an en dash instead.


**name server** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words.


**nameserver** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *name server* .


**name space** ***noun***

Use with caution. Write as shown only when updating existing content that uses the two-word spelling. For new content, use

*namespace* .


**namespace** ***noun***

Write as shown unless updating existing content that uses *name space* .


**name-value pair** ***noun***

Write as shown: hyphenate *name-value* .

Do not use. This term is no longer used in IBM.


For more information, see *globalization* in the [Terminology database .](http:/w3.ibm.com/standards/terminology)


##### national language version (NLV) noun

Do not use. This term is no longer used in IBM.


For more information, see *globalization* in the [Terminology database .](http:/w3.ibm.com/standards/terminology)


**native** ***adjective***

Use only if the term is part of the existing product terminology, for example, *cloud native* or *develop a native app for iOS* . Do not use when a less ambiguous term such as *local* , *basic* , *original* , or *default* applies.


**navigate** ***verb***

Use only when a more direct verb, such as *click* , *select* , *browse* , or *go to* , is not applicable. Use only to provide direction to a location (for example, “Navigate to the directory that contains the ﬁles that you want to edit”).


**navigation** ***noun***

Do not use as a noun to refer to the area of an interface that you use to move between items. For example, do not write “In the navigation, click **Conﬁgure** .” Use only as an adjective in such cases, for example, “In the navigation tree, click **Conﬁgure** .”


**near real-time** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown. If you can, provide more speciﬁc information about the speed or duration of a process. Otherwise, use this term to indicate a short but perceptible delay before an event occurs. See also *real time* .


**need to** ***verb***

Use *need to* only when *must* is too restrictive. For example, *you do not need to* is not the same as *you must not* .

For a mandatory action, either use the imperative, as in “back up your data”, or use *must* , as in “you must back up your data”. However, for a conditional action, you can write “you might need to back up your data”.


##### network-centric computing noun

Do not use. Use *network computing* .


**new** ***adjective***

Do not use *new* to describe products, functions, features, technologies, or standards, other than in topics such as *Summary and changes* or *What’s new* that are updated for each release.

A topic that describes something as *new* might be in circulation long after the *new* item is established or obsolete. Using *new* can also be redundant, for example, “Create a new ﬁeld”.


**new-collar** ***adjective***

Write as shown: lowercase and hyphenated. For example, *new-collar jobs* . To refer to the IBM initiative to develop non-traditional recruitment programs, write as two capitalized unhyphenated words. For example, *a New Collar program* .


**new-line** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *newline* .


**newline** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated. For example, write *newline character* .


**newsfeed** ***noun***

Do not use. Write as two words *news feed* .


**news feed** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words.


**newton-meter** ***noun***

Write as shown: hyphenated.

In the English system, torque is measured in foot-pounds or inch-pounds. One newton-meter equals 0.738 foot-pound or 8.851 inch-pounds; one foot-pound equals 1.356 newton-meters; and one inch-pound equals 0.113 newton-meter.


**nextgen** ***adjective***

Do not use unless you are referring to a product name that includes *nextgen* . *NextGen* is a registered trademark. Instead, write *next generation* .


**NFS** ***noun***

Use *NFS* as an abbreviation for *Network File System* , not *network ﬁle server* . An NFS server is a Network File System server.


**no.** ***noun***

Do not use as an abbreviation of *number* . Spell out *number* .

The abbreviation *no.* causes problems for translation tools. Because the period marks the end of a translatable segment, translation tools would not associate *no.* with the text that follows, and translators might interpret *no.* as the word *no* at the end of a sentence, not as an abbreviation of *number* .


**non-English** ***adjective***

Do not use *non-English* to refer to the language in which information, software, or other text is written. Use *in languages other than English* or *non-English-language* . Use *non-English-language* only as an adjective, as in “non-English-language document”.


**non-IBM** ***adjective***

Use *non-IBM* or *third-party* to refer to products or services from companies other than IBM. Do not use to refer to an IBM Business Partner product; use *IBM Business Partner product* or the product name.


**nonpageable** ***adjective***

Use to indicate memory that is not capable of being paged in. To indicate memory that is capable of being paged in, but is not yet paged in, use *nonpaged* .


**nonpaged** ***adjective***

Use to indicate memory that is capable of being paged in, but is not yet paged in. To indicate memory that is not capable of being paged in, use *nonpageable* .


**nonrecoverable** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *unrecoverable* .


**non-toxic** ***adjective***

Do not use to describe environmental features or beneﬁts of IBM products unless the claim is clearly explained, can be substantiated, and is approved for use by an IBM legal representative.


Vague or unsubstantiated environmental claims can cause legal issues and mislead readers. For more information about the IBM policy on using environmental terms, see [IBM Environmental Marketing  Claims . For information about making any claims in content, see  in IBM Style.](http:/w3.tap.ibm.com/medialibrary/media_view?id=192864)

If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.


**normally** ***adverb***

Use to mean *in a manner that does not deviate from a standard pattern* . For example, write “The process is running normally”.

The deﬁnitions of *generally* , *normally* , *typically* , and *usually* are similar, and in some cases, more than one of these terms might be applicable. Use your judgment in deciding which term best applies.


**notebook** ***noun***

Use *notebook* to refer to an interface element that resembles a physical notebook with pages and tabs.


**NULL** ***adjective***

Write as shown (uppercase) only if the user is to enter it that way, or if it is a keyword that is spelled that way. Most occurrences of *null* are not written in uppercase.


**null** ***adjective***

Use *null* only as an adjective, for example, “If a ﬁeld is null.” For the noun form, use *null value* , for example, “Enter a null value.”

It is preferable to use *null* as an adjective because *null* has various interpretations, such as a blank, a zero value, and a class with no members.


**number sign** ***noun***

Use to refer to the # character, unless you are referring to the character at the beginning of a hashtag, in which case, use *hash sign* .


**numeric** ***adjective***

Use *numeric* to mean of, relating to, or employing numbers. Do not use to mean arranged in an order based on numbers. Example: The Date ﬁeld contains numeric data.


**numerical** ***adjective***

Use *numerical* to refer to an order or range. Do not use to mean of, relating to, or employing numbers. Example: Enter the values in numerical order, from lowest to highest.


**NWSAA** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *NetWare for SAA* .

**O2C** ***adjective, noun***

Spell out as *order to cash* on ﬁrst use. Although *O2C* is primarily used to refer to an *order-to-cash* process, it can have other meanings. The phrase is unhyphenated when used as a noun and hyphenated when used as an adjective before a noun. Do not use *OTC* to mean *order to cash* .


**object oriented** ***adjective***

Hyphenate the term if you use it before a noun that it modiﬁes (for example, *object-oriented programming* ).


**obsolete** ***verb***

For IBM Systems and IBM Cloud and Cognitive Software, use *product manager* . For other areas of IBM, use *offering manager* until further notice.

Do not use. Use *offline* .

Write as shown (lowercase, unhyphenated) when using as an isolated adjective, as in the phrase *the software is open source* .

**OTC** ***adjective, noun***

**our** ***pronoun***

Do not use to refer to IBM in technical information, as in "we recommend”. Do not use to refer collectively to both the authors and the audience, as in “we can proceed to the next step”. Use only in the question portion of frequently asked questions (FAQs), in marketing proposals, or in information that has listed authors and in which the authors describe their own actions or opinions.

Uncertainty about the identity of *our* , *us* , and *we* , and whether the pronouns refer to the authors, product management, or the management of IBM Corporation, can cause a potential marketing or legal problem for IBM.

For exceptions, see [Personal pronouns](.) .


**out of the box, out-of-the-box** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use text that is suitable for the context and the noun to which this adjective applies. For example, write *applications that you can rapidly integrate into the system* , *items that are ready for immediate use* , *default settings* , *initial values* , or *built-in components* .

*Out-of-the-box* typically refers to something that IBM provides that is ready for customers to use as is, without modiﬁcation.


**output** ***verb***

Do not use if a clearer and more direct alternative is available. For example, *to produce a report* is better than *to output a report* .


**outside the box, outside-the-box** ***adjective, adverb***

Do not use this phrase to refer to creative thinking or to an unconventional approach.


**overhead** ***noun***

Do not use. Use terminology that is more speciﬁc. For example, write “running large queries can increase processor usage”, not “running large queries can increase overhead”.

*Overhead* is ambiguous.

#### P


**P/N** ***noun***

Write the abbreviation of *part number* as shown: uppercase with a forward slash.


**page** ***noun***

Use to refer to the part of a notebook or wizard where a user makes selections or types data, or use to describe a web-based user interface that is displayed in a browser, For example, a browser-based application on a PDA displays pages. Do not confuse *page* with *tab* , *panel* , or *window* .


**pain point** ***noun***

Do not use in external technical information. Use a term such as *challenge* , *concern* , *difﬁculty* , or *issue* .


**pane** ***noun***

Do not use *pane* , *page* , *window* , *panel* , and *screen* interchangeably. A pane is a framed section of a window that provides different views of the same document or independent but related information.


**panel** ***noun***

Do not use *panel* , *page* , *window* , *pane* , and *screen* interchangeably. A panel sits flush to either the left or right side. Left panels are used for a product’s navigation. Right panels are used for additional system-level actions and are sometimes used for general tasks.


**parent-child** ***adjective***

Write as shown: hyphenated.


**parent/child** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *parent-child* .


**parent topic** ***noun***

Do not use to refer to a topic in online product documentation, except when you write instructions about navigating. Whenever possible, refer to the speciﬁc topic title, not the relationship of topics to one another.

The term *parent* is often used in IBM products to describe a hierarchy of objects. Ensure that you use the term consistently in your product documentation.


**partner** ***noun***

A member of the IBM partner ecosystem, such as a Business Partner or other organization that collaborates with IBM to promote IBM products. See also Business Partner. Write as shown, lowercase, to refer generically to any company that is part of the IBM partner ecosystem.


**partner** ***verb***

A *DMZ* , also referred to in the industry as a *demilitarized zone* or *perimeter network* , is a conﬁguration that includes multiple ﬁrewalls. These ﬁrewalls add layers of protection between a corporate intranet and a public network, such as the Internet.


**permit** ***verb***

Do not use in the sense of an inanimate object granting abilities to people, as in “the product permits you to…”, unless the object is a type of authorization that does grant abilities, as in “DBADM authority permits you to create database objects”. Whenever possible, use a direct, user-focused alternative such as “you can use the product to…” or “with this product, users can…”.


**persist** ***verb***

**port** ***verb***

Do not use to mean *migrate* or *upgrade* .

The terms *port* , *migrate* , and *upgrade* are not synonyms. To port is to move an application program from the operating system for which it was developed to a different operating system. Porting requires less effort than redevelopment. With open technologies such as Java, porting might require no extra work at all. To migrate is to move data, users, or applications to a new program, platform, or environment. Migration can occur between unlike systems, for example, between two different vendors' databases, and migrating usually involves more work than upgrading. To upgrade is to replace software with a new release or ﬁx level of the same program or to replace hardware with a newer model or more powerful technology. An upgrade involves little work on the user’s part.

**tab** ***noun***

Do not use *tab* , *pane* , *page* , *window* , and *screen* interchangeably. A tab is an interface element that is used to organize distinct sets of information and to provide an easy way to navigate between these sets. Tabs are used on websites, in applications, and in notebooks. The control that you select to show the information is always called a tab, and the name of the area that contains the information can vary depending on the interface: it might be a page, pane, view, or tab.

**TCP/IP network** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *Internet Protocol network* or *IP network* .

*IP network* is more accurate than *TCP/IP* network because (1) the transmission control protocol (TCP) is not a required protocol when IP is used and (2) the network consists of subnetworks that are connected with IP. The use of *TCP/IP network* can lead people to believe that the network is connection-oriented because TCP is a connection-oriented protocol; actually, the network has the characteristics of IP: it is connectionless. However, almost every vendor’s product that allows users to connect with this network has *TCP/IP* in the product name. Thus, the use of *TCP/IP network* is common despite its inaccuracy.

**that** ***conjunction***

Use *that* , without a comma, to introduce a restrictive clause. Use *which* , preceded by a comma, to introduce a nonrestrictive clause. See the IBM Style topics [Commas](.) , [Conjunctions](.) , and [Pronouns](.) for more information.


**then** ***adverb***

In a two-step procedure that is written as one sentence, punctuate *then* as shown in the following examples: (1) *Do this, and then do that.* (2) *Do this; then do that.*

The ﬁrst example is preferable, but you can use the style shown in the second example if you need to save space. Note that *then* is not a coordinating conjunction (such as *and* , *or* , and *but* ). Using *then* as a coordinating conjunction creates a run-on sentence, as in the following example: *Do this, then do that* .


**there is, there are** ***verb***

Avoid at the beginning of an independent clause. In most cases rewrite to remove the phrase. For example, instead of *There are three recovery control data sets in the product* , write *The product includes three recovery control data sets* .

**translation** ***noun***

**transparent** ***adjective***

*Transparent* can be interpreted to have either of two opposite meanings (undetected or readily detected). To avoid ambiguity, use other terms to describe what you mean when possible.

Do not use *transparent* to describe something that is not visible to a human observer or detectable by an entity such as an application (for example, *transparent process migration* ). Instead, use such terms as *undetectable* , *imperceptible* , *seamless* , *automatic* , or *unnoticeable* .

It is acceptable to use *transparent* to describe something that is readily observed and understood (for example, a *transparent decision-making process* ) when you cannot use alternative terms, such as *apparent* , *discernible* , *evident* , *observable* , or *open* .

Do not use to refer to the structure of topics in online product documentation. Use *navigation tree* .

Use the US deﬁnitions for *billion* and *trillion* : one billion means one thousand million, and one trillion means one million million.

The Republic of Turkey ofﬁcially renamed itself the Republic of Türkiye as of 31 May 2022 to avoid confusion with the bird of the same name in English. Accordingly, the United Nations, NATO, the World Trade Organization, and UNESCO have started to refer to the country as Türkiye with an umlaut. Use that spelling, or simply Turkiye without the umlaut, when you refer to the country.


**Türkiye, Turkiye** ***noun***

This spelling with or without an umlaut is the preferred reference for the country formerly known as the Republic of Turkey.

The deﬁnitions of *generally* , *normally* , *typically* , and *usually* are similar, and in some cases, more than one of these terms might be applicable. Use your judgment in deciding which term best applies.

**UNIX** ***adjective***

Write as shown (uppercase) to refer to the UNIX operating system.

The Open Group holds the trademark on this term; its trademark guidelines indicate that the preferred usage is *the UNIX system* . Use the UNIX trademark only when you refer to the fact that AIX is a UNIX system or when you refer to products that are certiﬁed UNIX operating systems. Do not use as a generic descriptor to refer to other operating systems that are similar to the UNIX system, such as Linux. For example, do not write *On UNIX operating systems, enter the…* . Instead, write *On operating systems such as AIX or Linux, enter the…* . For complete trademarking rules, see [The Open Group’s guidelines](https:/www.opengroup.org/trademarks) . Reviewed and approved 29 July 2005 by Marilyn Dawkins, IP attorney, Austin.

**upgradable** ***adjective***

Do not use. Use *upgradeable* .


**upgrade** ***verb***

Do not use to mean *migrate* or *port* .

The terms *upgrade* , *migrate* , and *port* are not synonyms. To port is to move an application program from the operating system for which it was developed to a different operating system. Porting requires less effort than redevelopment. With open technologies such as Java, porting might require no extra work at all. To migrate is to move data, users, or applications to a new program, platform, or environment. Migration can occur between unlike systems, for example, between two different vendors' databases, and migrating usually involves more work than upgrading. To upgrade is to replace software with a new release or ﬁx level of the same program or to replace hardware with a newer model or more powerful technology. An upgrade involves little work on the user’s part.


**upgradeable** ***adjective***

Write as shown: not *upgradable* .


##### upper left, upper right noun

Accessibility and globalization requirement: People who have limited vision, or who use interfaces that are translated into a bidirectional language, might not understand information if it is conveyed only by location. Provide more descriptive information. For example, write *The tables are displayed in the Table List pane, which is in the upper right of the window* , not *The list of tables is displayed in the upper right of the window* .


**upper-left, upper-right** ***adjective***

Accessibility and globalization requirement: People who have limited vision, or who use interfaces that are translated into a bidirectional language, might not understand information if it is conveyed only by location. Provide more descriptive information. For example, write *The tables are displayed in the Table List pane, which is in the upper-right corner of the window* , not *The list of tables is displayed in the upper-right corner of the window* .

Such uncertainty can cause a potential marketing or legal problem for IBM. For exceptions, see [Personal pronouns](.) .

Write as shown: not *useable* .

Do not use. Use *usable* .

**user ID** ***noun***

Write as shown (two words, uppercase *ID* ) unless you are referring to a variable, which should be written as *userid* (one word and lowercase *ID* ).


**userid** ***noun***

Use only as a variable. Otherwise, use *user ID* .


**user interface, UI** ***noun***

Use these terms if you know that your intended audience is familiar and comfortable with what they represent, but in most cases you can write instructions that tell how to access the user interface without using a generic noun.

Avoid *in the UI, do this* or *in the interface, do that* . In tasks, refer to the speciﬁc part of the user interface, such as the name of a window, ﬁeld, pane, or view. Use *UI* or *user interface* when you need to contrast with named non-UI components or character-based interfaces, such as the DB2 command-line interface.


**user name** ***noun***

Use with caution. Write as shown only when updating existing content that uses the two-word spelling. For new content, use

*username* .


**username** ***noun***

Write as shown unless updating existing content that uses *user name* .


**using** ***noun***

To avoid ambiguity, replace this gerund with either *by using* or *that uses* .

To refer to something *using* one thing or another is often ambiguous. For example, the sentence *Back up the server using ABC* might mean *Back up the server by using ABC* or *Back up the server that uses ABC* . This advice also applies to gerunds other than *using* . For more information, see the style and grammar tips in the [Global audiences](.) topic in IBM Style.


**usually** ***adverb***

Use to mean *in a manner that can be expected* or *in most instances* . For example, write *The failure of a device is usually indicated by a lit system-error LED* .

The deﬁnitions of *generally* , *normally* , *typically* , and *usually* are similar, and in some cases, more than one of these terms might be applicable. Use your judgment in deciding which term best applies.


**UTC** ***noun***

Do not use *Zulu time* as an alternative for *UTC* . Do not use *coordinated universal time* (UTC) and *Greenwich mean time* (GMT) interchangeably.

Coordinated universal time (UTC) is the time scale, based on the Système International (SI) second, as deﬁned and recommended by the Comité Consultatif International de la Radio (CCIR) and maintained (using an atomic clock) by the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM). The Système International is based on three fundamental units of measure (the meter, the kilogram, and the second) and is sometimes called the *MKS system* because of these units. For most practical purposes, UTC is equivalent to the mean solar time at the prime meridian (0 degrees longitude) of Greenwich, England, which is known as Greenwich mean time.


**utilization** ***noun***

Do not use unless the term is part of the existing product terminology. Use the simpler word *use* or *usage* .


**utilize** ***verb***

Do not use. Use the simpler word *use* .

For example, instead of "By using the **lookup** command, you can get the resource name with the resource ID and vice versa", you can rewrite it as, "By using the **lookup** command, you can get the resource name from the resource ID or the resource ID from the resource name."

Write as shown (two words, lowercase w, lowercase s) except in product or function names such as *Web Services Deﬁnition Language* .


**web site** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *website* .


The terms *website* , *home page* , and *web page* have different meanings and should not be used interchangeably. See the deﬁnitions in the [IBM Terminology database .](http:/w3.ibm.com/standards/terminology)


**website** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word, lowercase w.


**WebSphere** ***adjective***

Write as shown: one word, uppercase W and S.


**whether or not** ***conjunction***

Use *whether or not* only to mean *regardless of whether* (for example, “Log shunting runs whether or not log archiving is enabled”). Otherwise, use *whether* .


**which** ***pronoun***

Use *which* , preceded by a comma, to introduce a nonrestrictive clause. Use *that* , without a comma, to introduce a restrictive clause. See the IBM Style topics [Commas](.) , [Conjunctions](.) , and [Pronouns](.) for more information.


**while** ***conjunction***

Use *while* only to refer to a period of time. To avoid potential ambiguity, do not use the term as a synonym for *although* or *though* in documentation.


**whilst** ***conjunction***

Do not use. Use *while* .


**White** ***adjective***

Write as shown, with initial uppercase W, to refer to a person.


**white** ***adjective***

Do not use the terms *white* or *black* in a context where white is represented as good or black is represented as bad, such as *whitelist*

and *blacklist* . Such usage reinforces a model that promotes racial bias.


**white hat hacker** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *offensive security researcher* . Do not use the terms *white* or *black* in a context where white is represented as good or black is represented as bad, such as *white hat hacker* and *black hat hacker* . Such usage reinforces a model that promotes racial bias.


**whitelist** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *allowlist* . Do not use the terms *white* or *black* in a context where white is represented as good or black is represented as bad, such as *whitelist* and *blacklist* . Such usage reinforces a model that promotes racial bias.


**white paper** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words.


**whitepaper** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *white paper* .


**white space** ***noun***

Write as shown: two words, except in programming languages that use *whitespace* as one word.


**whitespace** ***noun***

In programming languages that use the word *whitespace* , write as shown: one word. Otherwise, write as two words, *white space* .


**widget** ***noun***

Write as shown: lowercase w.


**Wi-Fi** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown (hyphenated, with uppercase W and F) for speciﬁc and ofﬁcial references to the Wi-Fi Alliance and the services that it certiﬁes. For generic references to a wireless connection, use *wiﬁ* .

*Wi-Fi* is a registered trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance.


**WiFi, Wiﬁ, wi-ﬁ** ***adjective, noun***

Do not use. For generic references to a wireless connection, use *wiﬁ* . For speciﬁc and ofﬁcial references to the Wi-Fi Alliance and the services that it certiﬁes, use *Wi-Fi* .

*Wi-Fi* is a registered trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance.


**wiﬁ** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown (one word, unhyphenated, with lowercase w and f) for generic references to a wireless connection. For speciﬁc and ofﬁcial references to the Wi-Fi Alliance and the services that it certiﬁes, use *Wi-Fi* .

*Wi-Fi* is a registered trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance.


**wild card** ***adjective, noun***

Do not use. Use *wildcard* .


**wildcard** ***adjective, noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**wildcard** ***verb***

Do not use as a verb; use only as a noun or adjective.


**window** ***noun***

Do not use *window* , *pane* , *page* , *panel* , and *screen* interchangeably. A window is an area of the screen with visible boundaries that displays information or program content. A window might comprise multiple panes.

Note that a window *opens* ; it does not *appear* or *display* .


**Windows** ***adjective***

Use *Windows operating system* or *Windows system* , as appropriate.


##### Windows 32-bit operating system noun

Write as shown: not *32-bit Windows operating system* . Use this term only for experienced users and only if referring to the applicable operating systems by name is impractical.

This term refers to 32-bit Microsoft Windows operating systems such as Windows 95, Windows 98, Windows NT, Windows 2000, and Windows XP. It excludes Windows 3.1 (a 16-bit operating system) and earlier versions.

*Windows 32-bit operating system* is appropriate for experienced users, but novice users might not understand the 32-bit distinction.


**Windows for Workgroups** ***noun***

Write as shown: *Workgroups* as one word.


**wiring closet** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *telecommunications closet* .


**wish** ***verb***

Do not use. Use *want* .


**wizard** ***noun***

Write as shown: lowercase. Use this generic term when you are writing about a speciﬁc wizard (for example, the TCP/IP conﬁguration wizard). Do not capitalize *wizard* except in places such as titles and headings where you always use initial capital letters.

If you use initial capital letters when the name of the wizard is not part of a title or heading, you run the risk of trademark infringement, because many wizard names have been trademarked by other companies. If you have any questions about this, contact your IBM Legal department.


**w/o** ***preposition***

Do not use. Spell out *without* . Likewise, do not abbreviate *with* as *w/* .


**word** ***noun***

Use *word* , not *fullword* , unless *fullword* has special signiﬁcance or is part of system or programming terminology.


**workaround** ***noun***

Write as shown when used as a noun: one word. Although commonly considered to be programming jargon, *workaround* is acceptable for use if it is restricted to documentation written for programmers.


**workbench** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**work flow** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *workflow* .


**workflow** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**work group** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *workgroup* .


**workgroup** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**work load** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *workload* .


**workload** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**worksheet** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**work space** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *workspace* .


**workspace** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**work station** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *workstation* .


**workstation** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


**world wide, world-wide** ***adjective, adverb***

Do not use. Use *worldwide* .


**worldwide** ***adjective, adverb***

Write as shown: one word, unhyphenated. The only exception is *World Wide Web* , which is the name created by the consortium.


**World Wide Web** ***noun***

Write as shown: three words, initial uppercase letters.


**would** ***verb***

Use only to refer to an unfulﬁlled condition or hypothesis and to express the future in the past, for “The command was rejected because it would have resulted in the ClusterName attribute being blank.” Do not use as an auxiliary verb, for example, “You would need administrator authority to create an app.” Instead, use the present tense, for example “You need administrator authority to create an app.”

#### X


**XSA** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *extended subarea addressing* .


**xterm** ***noun***

Write as shown: one word.


##### X Window System noun

Write as shown, except in speciﬁc AIX terms such as *Enhanced X-Windows* and *Enhanced X-Windows toolkit* . Do not use *X-Windows* or

*X-Window System* .

#### Y

#### Z


**zero** ***verb***

Use *zero* , not *zero out* , to refer to resetting to zero.


**zero emissions** ***noun***

Do not use to describe environmental features or beneﬁts of IBM products unless the claim is clearly explained, can be substantiated, and is approved for use by an IBM legal representative.

Vague or unsubstantiated environmental claims can cause legal issues and mislead readers. For information about making any claims in content, see [Claims and recommendations](.) in IBM Style. If content includes claims about complying with standards, ensure that the legal notices include the appropriate compliance information that your templates and legal representatives require.


**zeroes** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *zeros* .


**zero out** ***verb***

Do not use. Use *zero* to refer to resetting to zero.


**zeros** ***noun***

Write as shown, not *zeroes* .


**zero trust** ***adjective*** **,** ***noun***

Write as shown, lowercase, without a hyphen, to refer to the approach that brings together the functions of many security domains, such as network, identity, data, and application, into a uniﬁed threat protection strategy.


**zip** ***verb***

Do not use *zip* to refer to compressing data with a compression utility. Use *compress* , which applies to several formats and utilities. The terms *zip* and *ZIP* are registered trademarks of other companies. Using *zip* or *ZIP* can result in a trademark infringement.


**ZIP code** ***noun***

Use only for an address in the US, a US territory, or the Philippines. Otherwise, use *postal code* .


**zip code** ***noun***

Do not use. For an address in the US, a US territory, or the Philippines, use *ZIP code* . Otherwise, use *postal code* .


**zip ﬁle, zipped ﬁle** ***noun***

Do not use to refer to a compressed ﬁle. Use *archive* or *compressed ﬁle* , which applies to several formats and utilities. To refer to a ﬁle that has an extension of *zip* , it is acceptable to use *.zip ﬁle* . Do not use *.ZIP ﬁle* .

The terms *zip* and *ZIP* are registered trademarks of other companies. Using *zip* or *ZIP* can result in a trademark infringement.


**z/OS** ***noun***

Always write as shown, with a lowercase z. On the ﬁrst occurrence, include IBM before the term, as in IBM z/OS. When z/OS appears at the start of a sentence, include IBM before the term to avoid starting the sentence with a lowercase letter.


**zSystems, z Systems** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *IBM Z* instead. Although IBM Z was rebranded as zSystems in March 2022, branding reverted back to IBM Z in October 2023.


**Zulu time** ***noun***

Do not use. Use *Coordinated Universal Time* .
